A similar example is what ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb did when he saw a man who had diluted milk with water for sale: he poured it away. This is authentically reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him. A group of jurists who accepted this principle issued rulings accordingly, based on the report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “forbade diluting milk with water for sale.” This differs from mixing it with water for drinking, because once it is mixed, the buyer cannot tell how much is milk and how much is water. Thus, ʿUmar destroyed it.

A comparable case is the ruling issued by a group of jurists who accepted this principle permitting the destruction of fraudulently manufactured goods. For example, garments woven poorly may be torn up and burned. Likewise, when ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb saw Ibn al-Zubayr wearing a silk garment, he tore it while the boy was wearing it. Al-Zubayr said, “You have frightened the boy!” He replied, “Do not clothe them in silk.” Another example is “ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar’s burning of his safflower-dyed garment at the command of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

This is comparable to destroying the part of the body through which the sin was committed: the thief’s hand is amputated, and the brigand’s hand and foot are amputated. Similarly, destroying the object involved in a wrongful act serves to deter a return to that wrongdoing. Such destruction is not obligatory in every case. Rather, if retaining the object entails no harm, it may also be spared, either for Allah’s sake or to be given in charity. If ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb destroyed milk diluted for sale, then giving it in charity is permissible with even greater reason. This punishes the adulterator and deters him from repeating the offence, while allowing the poor to benefit from it is more useful than destroying it. ʿUmar destroyed it because he provided people with sufficient means through stipends, so the poor in Medina under his rule were either few or nonexistent. For this reason, a group of scholars permitted giving it in charity and disapproved of destroying it.

Al-Mudawwana reports from Mālik ibn Anas that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb used to pour adulterated milk onto the ground to discipline its owner. According to Ibn al-Qāsim’s transmission, Mālik disapproved of this and held that it should be given in charity. Scholars differ, however, over whether a small amount should be given in charity; there are two views.

Ashhab also transmitted from Mālik that financial punishments are prohibited, reporting him as saying: “No sin makes a person’s property lawful to take, even if he has killed someone.” The former view, however, is more widely reported from him. He approved of giving adulterated milk in charity: this punishes the adulterator by depriving him of it and benefits the needy by giving it to them, rather than pouring it away.

Mālik was asked, “Do you regard saffron and musk in the same way?”

He replied, “How similar they are to that! If the adulteration is his doing, it is like the milk.”

As for alteration, an example is what Abū Dāwūd narrated from ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar concerning the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“He forbade breaking the Muslims’ coinage that was current among them, unless there was a fault in it.”

Thus, if the dirhams or dinars in circulation have a fault, they are to be broken. Another example is altering three-dimensional and two-dimensional images when they are not placed underfoot, as in the report narrated by Abū Hurayrah, who said:

translated_text:
“Gabriel came to me and said, ‘I came to you tonight, and nothing prevented me from entering the house where you were except that it contained a statue of a man, a thin curtain bearing images, and a dog.’ He then instructed that the statue’s head be cut off so that it would resemble a tree, that the curtain be cut up and made into two cushions laid aside to be trodden upon, and that the dog be taken out. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, complied. The dog turned out to be a puppy belonging to al-Hasan and al-Husayn, beneath their clothes rack.”

This was narrated by Imam Ahmad, Abū Dāwūd, and al-Tirmidhī, who graded it authentic.

The Muslims agree that anything prohibited in its substance or configuration is to be removed or altered. Examples include pouring away wine belonging to a Muslim, dismantling musical instruments, and altering images. Their disagreement concerns only whether the objects containing or bearing these prohibited things may also be destroyed along with them. The correct view is that this is permissible, as indicated by the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations. This is also the apparent position of Mālik, Ahmad, and others.

The correct view is that every intoxicating food or drink is forbidden. This includes mead, grain beer, cannabis, and other such substances.

As for financial penalties, an example is what Abū Dāwūd and other compilers of the Sunan narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

Likewise, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb ruled that compensation for a concealed stray animal should be doubled. A number of scholars, including Ahmad and others, upheld all these rulings. ʿUmar and others doubled the compensation for a Bedouin’s she-camel taken by hungry slaves: he imposed double compensation on their master and spared the slaves the penalty of amputation. ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān ruled that a Muslim who deliberately killed a non-Muslim under Muslim protection must pay double the blood money, since the blood money for such a non-Muslim is half that for a Muslim. Ahmad ibn Hanbal adopted this position.

Section

Reward and punishment correspond in kind to the deed, both in Allah’s decree and in His revealed law. This is part of the justice by which the heavens and the earth are upheld. As Allah Most High says:

“Whether you reveal something good or conceal it, or pardon an evil, Allah is ever Pardoning and All-Powerful.”

He also says:

“Let them pardon and overlook. Would you not love for Allah to forgive you?”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever shows no mercy will be shown no mercy.”

He also said:

“Allah is One and loves what is odd-numbered.”

He also said:

“Allah is beautiful and loves beauty.”

He also said:

“Allah is pure and accepts only what is pure.”

He also said:

“Allah is clean

and loves cleanliness.”

For this reason, He ordained that the thief’s hand be cut off, and prescribed cutting off the hand and foot of one who wages war. He also prescribed retribution for bloodshed, property, and bodily injuries. Whenever punishment can correspond in kind to the sin, that is what is prescribed, insofar as possible. An example is the report that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, ordered that a false witness be mounted backwards on an animal and have his face blackened. Since he had turned the account around, he was made to face backwards; and since he had blackened his face with lies, his face was blackened. A number of scholars, including followers of Ahmad and others, have mentioned this among the discretionary punishments for a false witness.

For this reason, Allah Most High says:

“Whoever is blind in this life will be blind in the Hereafter and even further astray.”

He also says:

“But whoever turns away from My remembrance will have a life of hardship, and We will raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection.”

“He will say, ‘My Lord, why have You raised me blind when I used to see?’”

“He will say, ‘Thus Our signs came to you, but you forgot them; so today you will be forgotten.’”

A hadith states:

“The tyrannical and arrogant will be gathered in the form of tiny ants, trampled under people’s feet.”

Because they humiliated Allah’s servants, Allah will subject them to humiliation at His servants’ hands. Likewise, whoever humbles himself for Allah’s sake, Allah raises him in rank and causes His servants to show humility toward him.

May Allah Most High set us and all our believing brothers aright, and guide us and all our believing brothers to the words and deeds He loves and is pleased with. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah bless our master Muhammad and all his family and Companions.

Chapter:

(*)
On Enjoining What Is Right and Forbidding What Is Wrong

Enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong—the teaching for which Allah revealed His Books and sent His messengers—is part of religion. Allah’s message consists either of statements or of prescriptions. Statements concern Himself and His creation, such as teachings about His oneness and narratives, which include promises and warnings. Prescriptions consist of commands, prohibitions, and permissions.

This accords with what has been mentioned concerning the fact that “Say: He is Allah, the One” is equivalent to one-third of the Quran, because it contains the third devoted to Allah’s oneness; for the Quran consists of narratives, teachings about His oneness, and commands.

His words, glorified be He, describing our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—

“He enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong, makes lawful for them good things, and forbids them foul things”—

explain the completeness of his message. For it was through him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that Allah commanded everything right, prohibited everything wrong, made every good thing lawful, and forbade every foul thing. Thus, it is reported that he said:

“I was sent only to perfect noble character.”

And in the hadith agreed upon by al-Bukhārī and Muslim, he said:

“Because of wrongdoing by the Jews, We forbade them good things that had been lawful to them.”

And not all foul things were necessarily forbidden to them, as Allah Most High said:

“All food was lawful to the Children of Israel except what Israel had forbidden himself before the Torah was revealed.”

Prohibiting foul things falls within the meaning of “forbidding what is wrong,” just as making good things lawful falls within “enjoining what is right,” because forbidding good things is among the matters Allah has prohibited. Likewise, enjoining everything right and forbidding everything wrong attained completeness only with the Messenger, through whom Allah perfected noble character, which falls within what is right. Allah Most High said:

“Today I have perfected your religion for you, completed My favor upon you, and chosen Islam as your religion.”

Thus Allah has perfected our religion for us, completed His favor upon us, and chosen Islam as our religion.

Likewise, He described this nation in the same terms as He described its Prophet, saying:

; they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.” For this reason, Abū Hurayra said:

“You are the best people for mankind: you bring them in shackles and chains until you bring them into Paradise.”

Thus He, glorified be He, made clear that this nation is the best of all nations for mankind: its people bring them the greatest benefit and show them the greatest kindness. For they have brought the practice of enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong to its fullest, in both nature and extent: they enjoin everything right and forbid everything wrong upon everyone, and uphold this through jihad in Allah’s cause with their lives and wealth. This is the fullest benefit that can be brought to creation.

The other nations did not enjoin everything right upon everyone, nor forbid everyone from everything wrong, nor wage jihad to that end. Some of them did not wage jihad at all. As for those who did, such as the Children of Israel, their fighting was mostly to repel their enemy from their land, as one fights an unjust aggressor—not to call those they fought to faith, enjoin what is right upon them, and forbid them from what is wrong. Thus Moses said to his people:

“My people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has assigned to you, and do not turn back, lest you become losers.”

“They said, ‘Moses, there is a people of great strength in it. We will never enter it until they leave. If they leave, we will enter.’”

“They said, ‘Moses, we will never enter it as long as they remain there. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. We are staying right here.’”

‘Then I was told, “Look!” I saw a vast multitude filling the horizon. Then I was told, “Look this way and that!” I saw a vast multitude filling the horizon, and I was told, “These are your nation. With them are seventy thousand who will enter Paradise without being called to account.”’

“The people dispersed without his having explained further. translated_text:
‘Am I among them, O Messenger of Allah?’ He replied, ‘Yes.’ Another man stood up and asked, ‘Am I among them?’ He replied, ‘ʿUkkāsha has preceded you in this.’”

For this reason, the consensus of this nation constitutes authoritative proof: Allah Most High has declared that they enjoin everything right and forbid everything wrong. Were they to agree on permitting something forbidden, dispensing with an obligation, forbidding something lawful, or making a false statement about Allah Most High or His creation, they would be enjoining wrong and forbidding right in matters of good speech and righteous deeds. Indeed, the verse implies that whatever the nation does not enjoin is not right, and whatever it does not forbid is not wrong. Since it enjoins everything right and forbids everything wrong, how could the entire nation enjoin something wrong or forbid something right?

Just as Allah Most High has declared that this nation enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong, He has also made this a collective obligation upon it, saying:

“Let there be among you a group who call to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. It is they who will be successful.”

His declaration that this nation enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong does not require that the injunctions and prohibitions issued by its members reach every morally accountable person in the world. This is not even a requirement for conveying the divine message, so how could it be required for something that follows from it? Rather, the requirement is that those who are accountable should have access to it. Then, if they are negligent and fail to seek it out, even though the person undertaking this task has fulfilled his duty,

the negligence is theirs, not his.

Likewise, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is not an individual obligation upon everyone; rather, it is a collective obligation, as the Quran indicates. Since jihad completes this duty, it too is a collective obligation. If it is not adequately carried out, everyone capable incurs sin according to his ability, for each person is obliged to act according to his ability. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever among you sees a wrong, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot, then with his tongue; and if he cannot, then with his heart. That is the weakest level of faith.”

This being so, it is clear that enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and completing this through jihad are among the greatest good deeds we have been commanded to perform. Hence the saying: “Let your enjoining of right and forbidding of wrong not itself be wrong.” Since this is among the greatest obligatory and recommended deeds, the benefit of such deeds must outweigh their harm. For this is what the Messengers were sent with and the Scriptures were revealed for. Allah does not love corruption; rather, everything Allah commands is conducive to righteousness.

Allah has repeatedly praised righteousness, those who set things right, and those who believe and do righteous deeds, while condemning those who spread corruption. Thus, whenever the harm caused by enjoining and forbidding outweighs its benefit, it is not something Allah has commanded, even if an obligation has been neglected and a forbidden act committed. translated_text:
His words, Exalted is He:

“O you who believe, take care of yourselves. Those who go astray will not harm you if you are rightly guided.”

Being rightly guided is only complete through fulfilling one’s obligations. Thus, when a Muslim fulfills his duty to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, just as he fulfills his other obligations, the misguidance of those who go astray will not harm him. This duty is carried out sometimes with the heart, sometimes with the tongue, and sometimes with the hand. As for rejecting wrong in the heart, this is obligatory in all circumstances, since doing so causes no harm. Whoever does not do so is not a believer, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“That is the lowest—or weakest—level of faith.”

He also said:

“Beyond that there is not a mustard seed’s weight of faith.”

Ibn Masʿūd was asked, “Who is dead among the living?” He replied, “The one who neither recognizes what is right nor rejects what is wrong.” This is the person who has succumbed to temptation described in the hadith of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yamān.

Two groups of people fall into error here. One group neglects the obligatory duty of enjoining right and forbidding wrong because of its interpretation of this verse. As Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, said in his sermon:

“You recite this verse, ‘Take care of yourselves. Those who go astray will not harm you if you are rightly guided,’ but you apply it where it does not belong. I heard the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say: ‘When people see wrongdoing and do not change it, Allah may soon afflict them all with punishment from Him.’”

The second group consists of those who seek to enjoin right and forbid wrong, whether by word or by hand, without qualification, understanding, forbearance, patience, or consideration of which actions are appropriate and which are not, and what lies within their ability and what does not. As Abū Thaʿlabah al-Khushanī related in the hadith:

“I asked the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about this verse. He replied: ‘Rather, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. But when you see avarice obeyed, desires followed, worldly life preferred, and everyone admiring his own opinion, and you encounter a situation beyond your ability to handle, then attend to yourself and leave the affairs of the general public alone. For ahead of you are days when remaining patient will be like grasping burning embers. Whoever acts rightly during those days will have the reward of fifty men doing the same deeds.’”

Such a person enjoins and forbids, believing that he is thereby obeying Allah and His Messenger, while actually overstepping the prescribed limits. Many adherents of innovation and desires have taken this course, such as the Khawārij, the Muʿtazilah, the Rāfidah, and others who erred in their efforts to enjoin right, forbid wrong, and wage jihad for that purpose. The harm they caused outweighed the good they did. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded patience with the injustice of rulers and forbade fighting them so long as they maintained the prayer. He said:

“Give them their due rights, and ask Allah for your rights.”

We have discussed this at length elsewhere. Thus, among the principles of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah are adhering to the united Muslim community, refraining from fighting the rulers, and abstaining from fighting during civil strife. As general categories, however, right is to be enjoined without qualification, and wrong is to be forbidden without qualification. When the matter is unclear, the believer seeks clarification until the truth becomes clear to him. He does not undertake an act of obedience except with knowledge and intention. This principle also explains why the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) left ‘Abdullāh ibn Ubayy and similar leaders of hypocrisy and wickedness alone, because of their supporters. Eliminating his wrongdoing through some form of punishment would necessarily have cost a greater good, by provoking his people’s anger and tribal zeal, and by driving people away when they heard that Muhammad was killing his companions.

Thus, when he addressed the people as he did concerning the slander, asking them to acknowledge his justification for taking action against him, and Sa‘d ibn Mu‘ādh gave his commendable response, Sa‘d ibn ‘Ubādah was stirred by tribal zeal to defend him, despite the soundness of his faith.

The underlying principle is that a person’s love of right and hatred of wrong, his desire for the former and aversion to the latter, should accord with Allah’s love and hatred, will and aversion, as expressed in His revealed law. His pursuit of what is loved and his efforts to avert what is disliked should be within his strength and ability. Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity, and He has said:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

As for the heart’s love and hatred, desire and aversion, these should be complete and resolute. Any deficiency in them can only be due to deficient faith. Bodily action, however, is according to one’s ability. Whenever the heart’s desire and aversion are complete and wholehearted, and the servant acts accordingly to the extent of his ability, he is granted the reward of one who performs the deed fully, as we have explained elsewhere.

Some people’s love and hatred, desire and aversion accord with their own personal likes and dislikes, not

with what Allah and His Messenger love and hate. This is a form of personal desire; whoever follows it has followed his own desire:

“And who is more astray than one who follows his own desire without guidance from Allah?”

Personal desire is rooted in what the soul loves, and what it hates follows from that. A person is not blamed for the inclination itself—that is, the love and hatred within the soul—for this may be beyond his control. Rather, he is blamed for following it. As Allah the Exalted says:

“O David, We have made you a successor upon the earth, so judge between people in truth and do not follow desire, lest it lead you astray from the way of Allah.”

And the Exalted says:

“And who is more astray than one who follows his own desire without guidance from Allah?”

The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Three things bring salvation: fearing Allah in private and in public, moderation in poverty and wealth, and speaking the truth in anger and contentment. And three things bring ruin: avarice that is obeyed, desire that is followed, and a person’s admiration for himself.”

Love and hatred give rise to a felt experience in the presence of what is loved or hated, as well as emotion, desire, and other responses. Whoever follows these without the command of Allah and His Messenger is among those who follow their own desires without guidance from Allah. Indeed, this may go so far that he takes his own desire as his god.

Following desires in matters of religion is more grievous than following desires in matters of appetite. The former is the condition of those who disbelieve among the People of the Book and the polytheists. As Allah the Exalted says:

“But if they do not respond to you, then know that they only follow their own desires. And who is more astray than one who follows his own desire without guidance from Allah?”

And the Exalted says:

“He sets forth for you

an example from your own lives: Do you have, among those whom your right hands possess, any partners in what We have provided for you?”—to the end of the verse—until He says:

“Rather, those who do wrong follow their own desires without knowledge.”

And the Exalted says:

“He has already explained to you what He has forbidden you, except that to which you are compelled by necessity. Indeed, many lead others astray through their own desires, without knowledge”—to the end of the verse.

And the Exalted says:

“O People of the Book, do not go to extremes in your religion beyond the truth, and do not follow the desires of people who went astray before, led many astray, and strayed from the right way.”

And the Exalted says:

“Neither the Jews nor the Christians will ever be pleased with you until you follow their religion. Say, ‘Indeed, Allah’s guidance is the true guidance.’ If you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have neither protector nor helper against Allah.”

And the Exalted says in another verse:

“If you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would then surely be among the wrongdoers.”

And He says:

“And judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires.”

For this reason, scholars and worshippers who depart from what the Book and the Sunnah require are counted among the people who follow their own desires, as the early generations used to call them. This is because whoever does not follow knowledge follows his own desire, and knowledge of religion comes only through the guidance of Allah with which He sent His Messenger.

Thus, the Exalted says in one passage:

“Indeed, many lead others astray through their own desires, without knowledge.”

And He says in another:

“And who is more astray than one who follows his own desire without guidance from Allah?”

The servant must therefore examine his love and hatred themselves, and the degree of his love

and hatred: do these conform to the command of Allah and His Messenger—the guidance Allah revealed to His Messenger—so that this love and hatred are commanded, without his putting himself ahead of Allah and His Messenger? For He has said:

“Do not put yourselves before Allah and His Messenger.”

Whoever loves or hates before Allah and His Messenger command him to do so is, to some extent, putting himself ahead of Allah and His Messenger. Love and hatred are, in themselves, personal inclinations; what is forbidden, however, is following one’s love and hatred without guidance from Allah. For this reason, He says:

“Do not follow your own desire, lest it lead you astray from Allah’s way. Indeed, those who go astray from Allah’s way will have a severe punishment.”

He thus tells us that whoever follows his own desire will thereby be led astray from Allah’s way: the guidance with which He sent His Messenger, and the path leading to Him.

To clarify this, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong are among the most binding, virtuous, and excellent deeds. The Exalted has said:

“That He may test you as to which of you is best in deeds.”

This means, as al-Fudayl ibn ‘Iyād—may Allah have mercy on him—said, the most sincere and the most correct. For if a deed is sincere but not correct, it will not be accepted until it is both sincere and correct. Sincerity means that it is for Allah, and correctness means that it accords with the Sunnah. A righteous deed must therefore be done seeking the Face of Allah Most High, for Allah Most High accepts only deeds done seeking His Face alone. As reported in the Sahih, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah says: ‘I am wholly self-sufficient and have no need of partners. Whoever performs a deed in which he associates another with Me, I am free of it, and it belongs entirely to the one he associated with Me.’”

translated_text:
This is the monotheism that forms the foundation of Islam. It is Allah’s religion, with which He sent all His messengers and for which He created creation. It is His right over His servants: that they worship Him and associate nothing with Him.

Alongside this, the deed must be righteous—that is, something commanded by Allah and His Messenger. This is obedience: every act of obedience is a righteous deed, and every righteous deed is an act of obedience. It is action prescribed by the revealed law and the Sunnah, for what they prescribe is commanded either as an obligation or as a recommendation. Such action is righteous, good, virtuous, and beneficial. Its opposite is disobedience, corrupt action, evil, wickedness, and wrongdoing.

Every action necessarily involves two things: intention and activity. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The truest names are Hārith and Hammām.”

Everyone is a worker and one who forms intentions: everyone has deeds and intentions. Yet the praiseworthy intention that Allah accepts and rewards is to seek Him through that deed. The praiseworthy deed is the righteous one: that which He has commanded. This is why ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, would say in his supplication:

“O Allah, make all my deeds righteous, make them sincerely for Your Face, and let no one else have any share in them.”

Since this is the definition of every righteous deed, whoever enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong must himself meet these requirements. His action cannot be righteous unless it is based on knowledge and understanding. As ‘Umar ibn ‘Abd al-‘Azīz said: “Whoever worships Allah without knowledge

does more harm than good.” Likewise, in the report of Mu‘ādh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him:

“Knowledge guides action, and action follows it.”

This is clear: intentions and actions not grounded in knowledge amount to ignorance, misguidance, and following one’s desires, as explained above. This is what distinguishes the people of pre-Islamic ignorance from the people of Islam. One must therefore know what is right and what is wrong and distinguish between them. One must also understand the circumstances of the person being instructed or prohibited. Acting righteously also requires enjoining and forbidding by the straight path—the most direct way to achieve the intended purpose.

Gentleness is indispensable in this, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Gentleness never enters anything without adorning it, and harshness never enters anything without marring it.”

He also said:

“Allah is gentle and loves gentleness in all matters. He grants through gentleness what He does not grant through harshness.”

One must also be forbearing and patient in the face of harm, for one will inevitably suffer harm. Without forbearance and patience, one will do more harm than good. As Luqmān said to his son:

“Enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and patiently endure whatever befalls you. Indeed, that is a matter requiring firm resolve.”

For this reason, Allah commanded the messengers—who are the leaders in enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong—to be patient, as in His words to the final Messenger. Indeed, patience is coupled with conveying the message. When he was first sent as a messenger, the surah “O you wrapped in your cloak” was revealed to him, after the revelation of the surah “Read!” through which he had been made a prophet.

So Allah said:

“O you wrapped in your cloak,
arise and warn,
and magnify your Lord,
and purify your garments,
and shun idols,
and do not give in order to receive more,
and be patient for the sake of your Lord.”

He began the verses commissioning him to convey the message to creation with the command to warn, and ended them with the command to be patient. Warning itself consists of enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. Thus, it is clear that patience is required afterward. He also said:

“Be patient with your Lord’s decree, for you are under Our eyes.”

And He, Most High, said:

“Be patient with what they say, and leave them graciously.”

“So be patient, as were the messengers of firm resolve.”

“So be patient with your Lord’s decree, and do not be like the companion of the fish.”

“And be patient; your patience is only through Allah.”

“And be patient, for Allah does not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

These three qualities are therefore indispensable: knowledge, gentleness, and patience. Knowledge comes before enjoining and forbidding, gentleness accompanies it, and patience follows it—although all three must remain present throughout these stages. This accords with a report from some of the early generations, which has also been narrated with attribution to the Prophet. Judge Abū Ya‘lā mentioned it in al-Mu‘tamad:

“None should enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong unless he understands what he enjoins and understands what he forbids; is gentle in what he enjoins and gentle in what he forbids; and is forbearing in what he enjoins and forbearing in what he forbids.”

It should be understood that the requirement to possess these qualities when enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong proves difficult for many people. A person may therefore imagine that this absolves him of the duty and abandon it. Such abandonment harms him more than enjoining without these qualities—or

less. For neglecting the obligatory duty to enjoin what is right is a sin. Someone who moves from one sin to a greater sin is like someone seeking refuge from scorching ground in a fire. We know, through the signs Allah has shown us in the world around us and within ourselves, and through what He has testified to in His Book, that sins cause calamities. “Whatever calamity befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned, and He pardons much.”

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

He, Most High, says:

He says:

“When a calamity befell you, although you had inflicted twice as much, did you say, ‘How has this happened?’ Say, ‘It is from yourselves.’”

He says:

“Or He could destroy them for what they have earned, yet He pardons much.”

He says:

“But if some evil befalls them because of what their own hands have sent forth, then man is indeed ungrateful.”

He, Most High, says:

“Allah would not punish them while you were among them, nor would Allah punish them while they sought forgiveness.”

And He, glorified be He, has told us of the punishments He inflicted in this world upon sinful nations: the people of Noah, ‘Ād, Thamūd, the people of Lot, the people of Midian, and Pharaoh’s people. He has also told us of the punishments He will inflict upon them in the Hereafter. Thus, the believer from Pharaoh’s household said:

“My people, I fear for you a day like that of the allied peoples.”

“Like the fate of the people of Noah, ‘Ād, Thamūd, and those after them. Allah wills no injustice for His servants.”

“My people, I fear for you the Day of Mutual Calling.”

“The day you turn and flee, with none to protect you from Allah. Whoever Allah leaves astray will have no guide.”

He, Most High, says:

“Such is the punishment, but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater.”

He says:

“We shall punish them twice; then they will be returned to a tremendous punishment.”

He says:

“We shall surely make them taste the lesser punishment before the greater punishment, so that they may return.”

He says:

“Watch, then, for the day when the sky brings forth a visible smoke.”

Up to His words:

“On the day We seize them with the greatest seizure, We shall surely exact retribution.”

Thus, in most surahs containing warnings, Allah mentions the punishments He inflicted upon evildoers in this world and what He has prepared for them in the Hereafter. Sometimes, a surah mentions only what is promised in the Hereafter, for its punishment is greater, its reward is greater, and it is the enduring abode. Whatever He mentions of reward and punishment in this world is mentioned only secondarily, as in His words in the account of Joseph:

“Thus We established Joseph in the land, to settle wherever he wished. We bestow Our mercy upon whom We will, and We do not let the reward of those who do good go to waste.”

“And the reward of the Hereafter is better for those who believe and are mindful of Allah.”

He says: “So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the finest

reward of the Hereafter.” He says:

“And those who emigrated for Allah’s sake after suffering oppression—We shall surely grant them a good abode in this world, but the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.”

“Those who remained patient and put their trust in their Lord.”

He says of Abraham, peace and blessings be upon him:

“We gave him his reward in this world, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous.”

As for His mention of punishment in this world and the Hereafter, in the surah beginning:

“By those who wrench out forcefully,”

“And those who draw out gently,”

He then says:

“On the Day the quaking blast comes,”

“Followed by the next.”

Thus, He mentions the Resurrection in general terms, then says:

“Has the story of Moses reached you?”

“When his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwā,”

“Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed,”

Up to His words:

“Surely in that is a lesson for whoever fears Allah.”

He then describes the beginning of creation and the resurrection in detail, saying:

“Are you more difficult to create, or the heaven which He built?”

Up to His words, Most High:

“Then, when the Great Overwhelming Calamity comes,”

And up to His words, Most High:

“As for whoever transgressed,”

“And preferred the life of this world,”

“Hell will surely be his home.”

“But whoever feared standing before his Lord and restrained his soul from desire,”

“Paradise will surely be his home,”

And so on to the end of the surah.

Likewise, in al-Muzzammil, He says:

“Leave Me to deal with the deniers who enjoy lives of luxury, and give them a little respite.”

“Indeed, with Us are shackles and a blazing Fire,”

“And food that chokes, and a painful punishment,”

Up to His words, Most High:

“Just as We sent a messenger to Pharaoh.”

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger, so We seized him with a severe punishment.”

Likewise, in Surah al-Hāqqah, He recounts the stories of the nations, such as Thamūd, ‘Ād, and Pharaoh.

then He, Most High, says:

“Then, when the Trumpet is blown with a single blast,

“And the earth and mountains are lifted up and crushed in a single stroke,”

Continuing through His account of Paradise and Hell.

Likewise, in Surah Nūn wa-l-Qalam, He recounts the story of the owners of the garden who withheld what was due from their wealth, and the punishment He inflicted upon them. Then He says:

“Such is the punishment; but the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew.”

Likewise, in Surah al-Taghābun, He says:

“Has the news not reached you of those who disbelieved before? They tasted the evil consequences of their deeds, and they will have a painful punishment.”

“That was because their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they said, ‘Shall mere human beings guide us?’ So they disbelieved and turned away. Yet Allah had no need of them. Allah is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.”

Then He says:

“Those who disbelieve claim that they will never be resurrected. Say, ‘Yes indeed, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected.’”

Likewise, in Surah Qāf, He describes the condition of those who opposed the messengers, and mentions the promise of reward and the warning of punishment in the Hereafter. In Surah al-Qamar, too, He mentions both. The same applies to the Hā Mīm surahs, such as Hā Mīm Ghāfir, al-Sajdah, al-Zukhruf, al-Dukhān, and others. There are countless further examples.

al-Bukhārī, from Yūsuf ibn Māhak, who said:

“I was with ‘Ā’ishah, the Mother of the Believers, when an Iraqi man came to her and asked, ‘Which kind of shroud is best?’

“She replied, ‘Woe to you! What difference does it make to you?’

“He said, ‘Mother of the Believers, show me your copy of the Quran.’

“She asked, ‘Why?’

“He said, ‘So that I may arrange the Quran according to it, for it is being recited out of order.’

“She replied, ‘What harm does it do you whichever part you read first? The first revelation from it was a surah from the Mufassal—the section of shorter surahs—mentioning Paradise and Hell. Then, when people embraced Islam, rulings on the lawful and unlawful were revealed. Had the first thing revealed been, “Do not drink wine,” they would have said, “We will never give up wine.” Had it been, “Do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse,” they would have said, “We will never give up unlawful sexual intercourse.” The following was revealed to Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in Mecca while I was still a young girl playing: “But the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter.” Surahs al-Baqarah and al-Nisā’ were not revealed until I was living with him.’”

He said: “She then brought out the copy of the Quran for him and dictated to him the verses of the surahs.”

Since disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience cause evil and aggression, a man or a group may commit a sin, while others remain silent instead of enjoining right and forbidding wrong, making that silence one of their sins. Still others may condemn them in a prohibited manner, making that condemnation one of their sins. Thus division, discord, and evil arise. This has been among the greatest sources of strife and evil, in both past and present, for man is deeply unjust and ignorant, and wrongdoing and ignorance take many forms. The wrongdoing and ignorance of the first may be of one kind, while those of the second and third may each be of another kind.

Whoever reflects on the strife that has occurred will recognize this as its cause. He will see that this lies at the root of the strife among the community’s rulers and scholars, the kings and shaykhs who became involved, and the ordinary people who followed them. This includes the causes of misguidance and waywardness: religious and sensual passions, namely, innovations in religion and immorality in worldly affairs. For the causes of misguidance and waywardness—innovations in religion and immorality in worldly affairs—are common to the children of Adam because of the wrongdoing and ignorance within them. Through his sin, a person wrongs himself and others, as in unlawful sexual intercourse, whether sodomy or otherwise; drinking wine; wrongdoing involving wealth through betrayal of trust, theft, or usurpation; and similar acts.

It is well known that although these sins are repugnant and blameworthy according to both reason and religion, they are also desired. It is in the nature of souls to dislike others having exclusive enjoyment of them; rather, they want to obtain what others have obtained. This is the desire to have the same as another, which is the lesser of the two forms of envy. The soul wants to rise above others and reserve things for itself to their exclusion; or it envies another and wishes that person’s blessing to disappear, even if it does not obtain that blessing itself. Within it are desires for supremacy and corruption, arrogance and envy, which impel it to reserve the objects of desire for itself to the exclusion of others. How, then, will it react when it sees someone else monopolizing these things and enjoying them to its exclusion?

The moderate person among them in this regard is the one who desires sharing and equality; the other is deeply unjust and envious. These two attitudes occur both in permissible matters and in matters whose prohibition concerns Allah’s right. Thus, whatever is

“And whoever is protected from the covetousness of his own soul—it is they who will succeed.”

ʿAbd al-Rahmān ibn ʿAwf was seen circumambulating the House and saying, “My Lord, protect me from the covetousness of my own soul. My Lord, protect me from the covetousness of my own soul.” When asked about this, he replied, “If I am protected from the covetousness of my own soul, then I am protected from miserliness, injustice, and severing ties”—or words to that effect.

This covetousness—the soul’s intense greed—leads to miserliness through withholding what one owes, and to injustice through taking another’s property. It also leads to severing kinship ties and to envy: resenting what someone else alone enjoys. Envy involves both miserliness and injustice: miserliness over what another has been given, and injustice in seeking to deprive him of it. If this is the case with desires for permissible things, what, then, of unlawful desires:

translated_text:
such as unlawful sexual intercourse, drinking wine, and the like?

When someone claims exclusive enjoyment of these things, there are two grounds for hating them. The first is the exclusivity and injustice involved, just as with things that are permissible in kind. The second is the violation of Allah’s right involved.

Thus, sins fall into three categories:

The first involves wronging people, such as unlawfully taking their property, withholding their rights, envy, and the like.

The second involves wronging people alone, such as drinking wine and unlawful sexual intercourse, when their harm does not extend to others.

The third combines both: for example, when someone in authority takes people’s wealth and uses it to engage in unlawful sexual intercourse and drink wine; or when he has unlawful sexual intercourse with someone whom he consequently elevates above other people, harming them—as happens with those who are enamoured of certain women and boys.

Allah Most High has said:

“Say, ‘My Lord has only forbidden shameful deeds, whether open or secret, sin, unjust aggression, associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about Allah what you do not know.’”

translated_text:
People’s worldly affairs function more soundly with justice—even when accompanied by shared involvement in various sins—than with violations of people’s rights, even when no sin is shared. Hence the saying:

“Allah sustains a just state even if it is unbelieving, but does not sustain an unjust state even if it is Muslim.”

It is also said:

“Worldly life endures with justice and unbelief, but does not endure with injustice and Islam.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No sin brings swifter punishment than aggression and severing ties of kinship.”

The aggressor is therefore brought down in this world, even if he is forgiven and shown mercy in the Hereafter. This is because justice holds everything in order. When worldly affairs are founded on justice, they endure, even if the one responsible for them has no share in the Hereafter. Whenever they are not founded on justice, they do not endure, even if the one responsible for them possesses faith for which he will be rewarded in the Hereafter.

The soul harbours an impulse to wrong others by exalting itself above them, envying them, and violating their rights. It also harbours an impulse to wrong itself by indulging in vile desires, such as unlawful sexual intercourse and consuming foul things. Thus, it may wrong someone who does not wrong it, and favour such pleasures even without indulging in them. When it sees its peers committing injustice and indulging in these pleasures, its own impulse towards such pleasures or injustice becomes much stronger.

It may exercise restraint, yet this arouses within it a hatred and envy of the other person, and a desire for his punishment and the loss of his blessings, that it had not previously harboured. In its own view, it has grounds in both reason and religion: that other person has wronged himself and the Muslims; commanding him to do what is right and forbidding him to do what is wrong is obligatory; and striving to that end is part of religion.

 وَهَؤُلَاءِ هُمْ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ وَهُمْ مِنْ خَيْرِ أُمَّةٍ أُخْرِجَتْ لِلنَّاسِ:
translated_text:
In this regard, people fall into three groups:

Some take a stand only to serve their own desires. They are pleased only with what they are given and angered only by what they are denied. If one of them is given the lawful or unlawful pleasures he desires, his anger disappears and he becomes content. What he formerly regarded as an evil—to be forbidden and punished, and whose perpetrator he condemned and resented—now becomes acceptable to him. He begins doing it himself, sharing in it, helping others engage in it, and opposing anyone who forbids or condemns it. This is prevalent among the children of Adam; one sees and hears countless examples of it.

The reason is that man is deeply unjust and ignorant. Consequently, he does not act justly; indeed, he may be unjust in both situations. One sees people condemning a ruler for his injustice and aggression against his subjects, only for those critics to be won over by some benefit and turn into his supporters. At best, they cease condemning him. Likewise, you see them condemning those who drink wine, commit unlawful sexual intercourse, and listen to music, until the offenders draw one of these critics into joining them or win him over with a share of those pleasures. Then you find that he has become their supporter. Through their condemnation, these people may end up in a worse state than they were in before, or in something less than that or comparable to it.

Others take a stand out of genuine religious devotion, sincerely seeking Allah’s sake and setting matters right through their actions. They remain steadfast in this, even to the point of patiently enduring the harm inflicted on them.

These are those who believe and do righteous deeds, and they belong to the best nation brought forth for mankind:

they enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in Allah.

A third group combines both tendencies. These constitute most believers: people who have religious devotion as well as desires. Their hearts contain both the desire to obey and the desire to disobey, and sometimes one prevails, sometimes the other.

This threefold division corresponds to the saying that souls are of three kinds: those that urge evil, those at peace, and those that reproach themselves. The first group have souls that urge them to do evil. The second group have souls at peace, of which it is said:

“O soul at peace,
return to your Lord, well pleased and pleasing to Him.
Enter among My servants,
and enter My Paradise.”

The last group have self-reproaching souls: they commit a sin, then reproach themselves for it. They fluctuate between one state and another, mixing righteous deeds with evil ones.

Thus, in the time of Abū Bakr and ‘Umar, whom the Muslims were commanded to follow—as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Follow the two who come after me: Abū Bakr and ‘Umar”—people were closer in time to the prophetic message and greater in faith and righteousness. Their leaders fulfilled their duties more faithfully and were more firmly established in inner peace. Consequently, no strife arose, for they fell within the second category.

Toward the end of ‘Uthmān’s caliphate and during ‘Alī’s caliphate, the third group grew more numerous. Desires and doubts came to coexist in them with faith and religious devotion, and this came to be found among some of the governors

translated_text:
and some of their subjects. This then became more widespread, giving rise to strife whose cause was what has already been explained: on both sides, piety and obedience were not pure, but were mixed with a measure of desire and disobedience. Each side believed, on the basis of its own interpretation, that it was enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and upholding truth and justice. Yet this interpretation was accompanied by a measure of desire, and thus involved some conjecture and indulgence of the soul’s desires—even though one of the two groups was closer to the truth than the other.

The believer must therefore seek Allah’s help and rely upon Him to keep his heart upright, not let it deviate, and make it steadfast upon guidance and piety. He must not follow his desires, as the Most High says:

“So call people to this faith, stand firm as you have been commanded, and do not follow their desires. Say, ‘I believe in whatever Scripture Allah has revealed, and I have been commanded to deal justly between you. Allah is our Lord and your Lord.’”

This is also the condition of the Muslim community in the doctrinal views and acts of worship over which it has divided and differed. Such matters greatly intensify the trials faced by believers.

They need two things: to protect themselves from the trials in religious and worldly affairs that have afflicted their peers, despite the presence of the factors that give rise to those trials. For they, like others, have their own souls and devils to contend with. When such things occur among their peers, the impulses toward them grow stronger within them, as experience shows. Thus the impulse within a person grows stronger, as does his devil, together with the incentive generated by the actions of others and his peers. How many people have had no intention of doing either good or evil until they saw someone else—especially a peer—

Thus, whoever initiates good or evil receives the same reward, or bears the same burden of sin, as those who follow him. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever establishes a good practice shall have its reward and the reward of everyone who acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection, without their rewards being diminished in the least. Whoever establishes an evil practice shall bear its burden of sin and the burden of everyone who acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection, without their burdens being diminished in the least.”

This is because they share the same essential nature, like cases are governed by the same rule, and like is drawn to like.

If these are two powerful incentives, how much more so when two others are added to them? Many who engage in wrongdoing love those who go along with them in what they do, and hate those who do not. This is evident in false religions: each group befriends those who agree with it and shows hostility toward those who oppose it.

Likewise, in worldly affairs and the pursuit of desires, they often choose and favor those who join them. This may be to gain their assistance, as with rulers who wield power by force, highway robbers, and the like. Or it may be to have others join in, as with those who gather to drink wine: they want everyone present to drink.

Or it may be because they dislike someone distinguishing himself from them through goodness. They may envy him for it, not wanting him to rise above them and receive praise instead of them. Or they may not want him to have an argument against them. Or they may fear that he will punish them himself, or through those to whom he reports their conduct; and they do not wish to be beholden to him or exposed to harm from him

Most High:

“But those who believe are stronger in their love for Allah.”

The incentive to do good is stronger. A person has an inner impulse urging him toward faith, knowledge, truthfulness, justice, and the fulfilment of trusts. When he finds someone else doing these things, he gains a second incentive, especially if that person is his peer, and particularly when there is competition between them. This is good and praiseworthy. If he finds believers and righteous people who want him to join them in these deeds and hate him if he does not, he gains a third incentive. If they command him to do so, show him loyalty for doing so, and oppose and punish him for neglecting it, he gains a fourth incentive. For this reason, believers are commanded to counter evil deeds with their opposites among good deeds, just as a physician counters an illness with its opposite.

The believer is commanded to reform himself through two things: doing good deeds and refraining from evil deeds, despite the presence of influences that hinder good deeds and prompt evil deeds. These constitute four categories. He is also commanded to reform others through these four categories, according to his ability and means. Allah Most High says:

“By time! Surely mankind is in loss, except those who believe, do righteous deeds, urge one another to uphold the truth, and urge one another to persevere.”

It is reported that al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “If all people reflected on Surah al-Asr, it would suffice them.” It is indeed as he said. Allah Most High has declared that all people are at a loss except those who are themselves believers and righteous, and who urge others to uphold the truth and to persevere. “The prophets, then the righteous, then those next best, in descending order. A man is tried according to his religious commitment. If his commitment is firm, his trials are increased; if it is weak, they are lightened. Trials continue to afflict the believer until he walks upon the earth without a single sin remaining.”

He therefore needs a degree of patience that others do not. This is what leads to leadership in religion, as Allah Most High says:

“We raised from among them leaders, guiding by Our command, when they patiently endured and had sure faith in Our signs.”

One must therefore persevere in doing the good that is commanded and refraining from the evil that is forbidden. This includes patiently enduring harmful deeds and words, bearing the hardships that befall one, restraining oneself from arrogant exultation when blessed, and other forms of patience. Yet a servant cannot remain patient unless he has something that gives him reassurance, delight, and nourishment: namely, certainty. Thus, in the hadith narrated by Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“O people, ask Allah for certainty and well-being, for after certainty no one has been given anything better than well-being. So ask Allah for both.”

People cannot endure bitterness without some sweetness; there is no other way. For this reason, Allah Most High commanded that hearts be won over, even assigning a share of the prescribed alms to those whose hearts are to be reconciled. Allah Most High said to His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Be gracious, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant.”

He also said:

“And they urged one another to patience and urged one another to mercy.”

One must therefore be patient and show mercy: this is courage and generosity. Thus Allah sometimes pairs prayer with zakah—which is kindness towards His creatures—and at other times mentions both together with patience.

All three are indispensable: prayer, zakah, and patience. The believers’ welfare, both in setting themselves right and in reforming others, cannot be secured without them. This is especially true as turmoil and trials intensify, for the need for these qualities then becomes greater. Generosity and patience are needed by all human beings; neither their religious nor their worldly welfare can be secured without them. Hence they all praise one another for courage and generosity; indeed, these qualities constitute most of what poets celebrate in their verse. Likewise, they blame one another for miserliness and cowardice. Matters upon which all human beings agree can only be true, as with their agreement in praising truthfulness and justice and condemning lying and injustice.

translated_text:
and said, ‘By Him in whose hand is my soul, if I had as many head of livestock as there are thorn trees here, I would distribute them among you. Then you would not find me miserly, cowardly, or given to lying.’”

Yet these qualities differ according to the purposes and characteristics involved. Actions are judged only by intentions, and each person will have only what he intended. Thus the Quran and Sunnah condemn miserliness and cowardice, and praise courage and generosity in Allah’s cause—not when exercised outside His cause. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The worst traits in a person are panic-driven avarice and paralyzing cowardice.”

He also said:

“Who is your chief, Banū Salimah?”

They replied, “Al-Jadd ibn Qays, although we regard him as miserly.”

He said, “What disease is worse than miserliness?”

Another narration reads:

“A chief cannot be miserly. Rather, your chief is the fair-skinned, curly-haired al-Barā’ ibn Ma‘rūr.”

Likewise, the Sahīh records that Jābir ibn Abdullah said to Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with them both, “Either give to me or withhold from me out of miserliness.” He replied, “You say, ‘Or withhold from me out of miserliness’? What disease is worse than miserliness?” Miserliness was thus counted among the gravest diseases.

In Sahīh Muslim, Salmān ibn Rabī‘ah reported that ‘Umar said:

“The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, distributed some wealth, and I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, by Allah, others are more entitled to it than these people.’ He replied, ‘They have given me a choice between asking me abusively and accusing me of miserliness, and I am no miser.’”

He means: “They make improper demands of me: either I give to them, or they say, ‘He is miserly.’ They have thus forced me to choose between two unwelcome things, allowing me no escape from one or the other: abuse and accusations of miserliness. Being accused of miserliness is worse, so I ward off

the worse of the two by giving to them.”

Miserliness is a general category encompassing different forms: some are major sins, while others are not. Allah Most High says:

“Let not those who withhold what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them. Rather, it is bad for them. What they withheld will be hung around their necks on the Day of Resurrection.”

He also says:

“Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents,”

up to His words:

“Indeed, Allah does not love those who are arrogant and boastful—those who are miserly and urge others to be miserly.”

Allah Most High says:

“Nothing prevents their contributions from being accepted except that they disbelieve in Allah and His Messenger, come to prayer only sluggishly, and spend only reluctantly.”

He also says:

“But when He gave them of His bounty, they withheld it and turned away in aversion. So He punished them with hypocrisy in their hearts until the Day they meet Him.”

And He says:

“Whoever is miserly is miserly only to his own detriment.”

He also says:

“So woe to those who pray, yet are heedless of their prayers—those who show off and withhold even small acts of kindness.”

And He says:

“Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in Allah’s cause—give them tidings of a painful punishment. On the Day it is heated in the Fire of Hell, their foreheads, sides, and backs will be branded with it,”

and so on to the end of the verse.

All the Quran’s commands to give, and its condemnation of those who fail to do so, constitute a condemnation of miserliness. Likewise, its condemnation of cowardice is frequent, as in His words:

“Whoever turns his back on them that day—unless maneuvering for battle or joining another group—has incurred Allah’s wrath. His refuge is Hell, and what an evil destination!”

And His words concerning the hypocrites:

“They swear by Allah

that they are indeed of you, but they are not of you; rather, they are a people who are afraid.”

“If they could find a refuge, caves, or somewhere to hide, they would turn towards it, rushing headlong.”

And His words:

“But when a clear, decisive surah is revealed and fighting is mentioned in it, you see those in whose hearts is disease looking at you with the gaze of someone overcome by death.”

And His words:

“Have you not seen those who were told, ‘Restrain your hands, establish prayer, and give zakah’? Then, when fighting was prescribed for them, some of them feared people as they feared Allah, or even more. They said, ‘Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You would grant us a little more time!’ Say, ‘The enjoyment of this world is brief, and the Hereafter is better for whoever fears Allah. You will not be wronged in the least.’”

All the Quran’s exhortations and encouragements to undertake jihad, and its condemnation of those who shrink from it or abandon it, constitute a condemnation of cowardice.

Since human well-being in both religious and worldly affairs cannot be complete without courage and generosity, He, glorified be He, explained that whoever turns away from undertaking jihad in person will be replaced by someone who will undertake it. He says:

“O you who believe, what is the matter with you that, when you are told to go forth in Allah’s cause, you cling heavily to the earth? Are you content with the life of this world rather than the Hereafter? Yet the enjoyment of this worldly life is but little compared with the Hereafter.”

“If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and replace you with another people. You will not harm Him at all, and Allah has power over all things.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Here you are, being called to spend in Allah’s cause, yet some of you are miserly. Whoever is miserly is miserly only to his own detriment. Allah is free of need, while you are the needy. If you turn away, He will replace you with another people, who will not be like you.”

translated_text:
Through courage and generosity in Allah’s cause, He gave precedence to the earliest believers, saying:

“Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest. They are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterwards, though Allah has promised the finest reward to all.”

He has mentioned jihad in His cause with one’s life and wealth, praising it in numerous verses of His Book. This is courage and generosity in obedience to Him, glorified be He. He says:

“How many a small company has overcome a large company by Allah’s permission! And Allah is with the patient.”

Allah Most High also says:

“O you who believe, when you encounter an enemy force, stand firm and remember Allah often, so that you may succeed.”

“And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute, lest you lose courage and your strength depart. Be patient; indeed, Allah is with the patient.”

Courage is not bodily strength: a man may be strong in body yet weak in heart. Rather, it is strength and firmness of heart. Fighting depends on bodily strength and skill in combat, as well as strength of heart and experience in fighting. What is praiseworthy in both is that which is guided by knowledge and understanding, rather than recklessness, whose possessor neither thinks nor distinguishes between what is praiseworthy and what is blameworthy. Thus, the truly strong and mighty person is the one who controls himself when angry, so that he acts rightly. As for someone overcome by his anger, he is neither courageous nor strong. As explained earlier, patience is what brings all this together; it is indispensable.

Patience is of two kinds: patience when angry and patience when afflicted by calamity. As al-Hasan said:

The truly courageous and strong person is the one who patiently endures pain. If the cause of pain can be repelled, it arouses anger; if it cannot be repelled, it arouses sorrow. Thus, the face reddens in anger because the blood surges when one feels capable, whereas it grows pale in sorrow because the blood recedes when one feels helpless.

This is why the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought the two together in the authentic hadith narrated by Muslim from Ibn Mas‘ūd, who said:

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, “Whom do you consider childless among you?”

They replied, “Someone to whom no child is born.”

He said, “That is not the truly childless man. Rather, the childless man is one none of whose children has preceded him in death.”

Then he said, “Whom do you consider a champion wrestler among you?”

We replied, “Someone whom other men cannot throw down.”

He said, “That is not so. Rather, the champion wrestler is the one who controls himself when angry.”

He thus mentioned what entails patience in calamity and patience in anger. Allah Most High says concerning calamity:

“And give glad tidings to the patient, who, when calamity strikes them, say, ‘Indeed, we belong to Allah, and indeed, to Him we shall return’”—the verse.

And He, Most High, says concerning anger:

“But none is granted this except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one blessed with great good fortune.”

This pairing of patience in calamity with patience in anger parallels the pairing of patience in times of blessing with patience in calamity, as in His words, Most High:

“And if We give him a taste of prosperity after hardship has touched him, he will surely say, ‘My troubles have gone from me.’ Indeed, he is exultant and boastful.”

“Except those who are patient and do righteous deeds; those will have forgiveness and a great reward.”

And He says:

“So that you may not grieve over what you have missed, nor exult over what He has given you.”

Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr described some of the Emigrant Companions in these terms, saying:

They do not exult when their swords strike others,
Nor panic when they themselves are struck.

Likewise, Hassān ibn Thābit said in describing the Ansār:

No boasting when they strike their enemy;
When struck, no weakness and no panic.

One of the Arabs described the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saying: “He prevails without arrogance, and is overcome without vexation.”

Since Satan urges people in both these situations to overstep the bounds with their hearts, their voices, and their hands, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade this. When he wept upon seeing Ibrāhīm in the throes of death, he was asked, “Do you weep? Did you not forbid weeping?”

He replied:

“I only forbade two foolish, sinful sounds: a sound accompanying a melody of amusement and play and the pipes of Satan; and a sound at a time of calamity, accompanied by slapping cheeks, tearing garments at the neckline, and crying out with the cries of the pre-Islamic age of ignorance.”

Thus he brought the two sounds together.

As for his prohibition of such conduct at times of calamity, examples include his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“He is not one of us who slaps his cheeks, tears his garments at the neckline, and cries out with the cries of the pre-Islamic age of ignorance.”

He also said:

“I disavow the woman who shaves her head, wails loudly, or tears her garments in mourning.”

And he said:

“What comes from the eyes and the heart is from Allah, while what comes from the hands and the tongue is from Satan.”

And he said:

“Allah does not hold anyone accountable for the tears of the eyes or the sorrow of the heart, but He punishes or shows mercy because of this”—and he pointed to his tongue. He then said: “Whoever is wailed over is punished because of the wailing over him.”

He stipulated that women, when pledging allegiance, must not wail, and he said:

“If a woman who wails does not repent before her death, she will wear a tunic of scabies and a garment of pitch on the Day of Resurrection.”

Concerning victory, calamities, and joy, he said:

“Allah has prescribed excellence in all things. So when you kill, kill in the best manner, and when you slaughter, slaughter in the best manner. Let each of you sharpen his blade and spare the animal he slaughters unnecessary suffering.”

And he said:

“The people of faith are the most restrained in how they kill.”

And he said:

“Do not mutilate, do not act treacherously, and do not kill a child.”

These are among his commands to uphold justice and refrain from aggression in jihad, in accordance with the saying of the Most High:

“Do not let the hatred of a people lead you to be unjust. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”

And His saying:

“Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors.”

He also forbade wearing silk, wearing gold rings, and drinking from vessels of gold

and silver, and letting garments trail, among other forms of extravagance and arrogance when enjoying blessings. He also condemned those who deem unlawful sexual intercourse, silk, wine, and musical instruments lawful, and declared that among them would be people swallowed by the earth and transformed.

Allah Most High has said:

“Indeed, Allah does not love those who are conceited and boastful.”

And He said concerning Qārūn:

“When his people said to him, ‘Do not exult. Indeed, Allah does not love the exultant.’”

These three matters, together with patiently refraining from transgression in the pursuit of desire, encompass the essentials of this subject.

A person faces both what he loves and desires and what he hates and dislikes. He pursues the former through his love and desire, and repels the latter through his hatred and aversion. When he obtains the former or averts the latter, this brings him joy and happiness; when the latter befalls him or the former is lost, he experiences sorrow. Thus, when experiencing love and desire, he needs patiently to restrain the transgression they may cause; when experiencing anger and aversion, he needs patiently to restrain the transgression they may cause; when experiencing joy, he needs patiently to restrain its excesses; and when calamity strikes, he needs patiently to refrain from giving way to anguish.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, therefore mentioned the two foolish, sinful sounds: the sound that leads to excess in joy until a person becomes exultant and boastful, and the sound that provokes anguish.

As for sounds that stir anger for Allah’s sake, such as the poetry chanted during jihad, these were not accompanied by instruments. Likewise, regarding sounds of desire at times of joy, he permitted such forms as are established in the Sunnah, such as beating the frame drum

at weddings and other celebrations, for women and children. Most poetry chanted to stir the soul falls into these four categories: love poetry; poetry of anger and zeal, namely martial verse and satire; poetry about calamities, such as elegies; and poetry celebrating blessings and joy, namely praise poetry. Poets habitually follow their natural impulses, as Allah Most High says:

“Do you not see that they wander in every valley,
and that they say what they do not do?”

For this reason, He states that the wayward follow them. A wayward person is someone who follows his desires without knowledge. This is waywardness, the opposite of sound judgment. Likewise, someone who is astray and does not know what benefits him stands in contrast to someone who is rightly guided. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, says:

“By the star when it descends,
your companion has neither strayed nor erred.”

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Adhere to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the upright, rightly guided caliphs after me.”

Thus you find poets praising courage and generosity as such. The absence of these two qualities is blameworthy without qualification, while their presence enables people to attain all manner of desired ends. Yet the good outcome belongs to those who fear Allah. Those who do not fear Him have immediate gains, but no good final outcome. Although this good outcome is realized in the Hereafter, it is also realized in this world. Thus, after recounting the story of Noah and his deliverance in the Ark, Allah Most High says:

“It was said, ‘O Noah, disembark with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon communities from among those with you. But there are communities whom We shall grant enjoyment, then a painful punishment from Us will afflict them.’”

Then, further on, He says:

“So be patient; indeed, the good outcome belongs to those who fear Allah.”

And He said:
