translated_text:
“Whoever attacks you, respond in equal measure to their attack. Fear Allah, and know that Allah is with those who fear Him.”

The criterion is to praise, among these qualities, what Allah and His Messenger have praised. For it is Allah Most High whose praise confers honor and whose censure brings disgrace—not poets, orators, or anyone else. Thus, when a man from Banū Tamīm said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “My praise confers honor, and my censure brings disgrace,” he replied, “That is Allah.”

Allah, glorified is He, has praised courage and generosity in His cause, as in the authentic report from Abū Mūsā, who said:

“The Messenger of Allah was asked, ‘A man fights to display courage, another fights out of partisan zeal, and another fights to be seen by others. Which of these is in Allah’s cause?’ He replied, ‘Whoever fights so that Allah’s word is supreme is fighting in Allah’s cause.’”

He, glorified is He, has also said:

“Fight them until there is no more fitnah (religious strife) and religion is entirely for Allah.”

This is the purpose for which creation was brought into being, as Allah Most High says:

“I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me.”

Whatever serves the purpose for which creation was brought into being is therefore praiseworthy before Allah, and it is what endures for the person who does it. These are righteous deeds.

People thus fall into four categories: those who act for Allah with courage and generosity—these are the believers who deserve Paradise; and those who act for other than Allah with courage and generosity—

they benefit from this in this world but have no share in the Hereafter. Those who act for Allah, but without courage or generosity, have a corresponding measure of hypocrisy and deficiency in faith. Those who neither act for Allah nor possess courage or generosity have neither this world nor the Hereafter.

The believer needs these qualities and deeds in general, and especially in times of severe trials and turmoil. Believers need to keep their souls upright and guard themselves against sins when faced with circumstances that put them to the test. They also need to command others to do right and forbid them from doing wrong, according to their ability. Both tasks entail considerable difficulty, though they are easy for those for whom Allah makes them easy. This is because Allah has commanded the believers to have faith and do righteous deeds, and has commanded them to call people to faith and righteous deeds and to wage jihad against them for that purpose. As Allah Most High says:

“Allah will surely help those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is All-Powerful, Almighty.”

“Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer, give zakah, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. And to Allah belongs the outcome of all matters.”

He also says:

“We will surely help Our messengers and those who believe, both in the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses stand forth.”

He also says:

“Allah has decreed, ‘I and My messengers will surely prevail.’ Indeed, Allah is All-Powerful, Almighty.”

He also says:

“And Our forces will certainly be victorious.”

Since enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and jihad in Allah’s cause entail trials and hardships that expose a person to temptation, some people resort to excuses

for neglecting these obligations by claiming that they seek to avoid temptation, as Allah said concerning the hypocrites:

“Among them is one who says, ‘Give me leave and do not put me to temptation.’ Surely, they have fallen into temptation”—to the end of the verse.

Quranic commentary gives the following account of its revelation:

“Al-Jadd ibn Qays, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered him to prepare for a campaign against the Byzantines—and I believe he said, ‘Would you like the women of Banū al-Asfar?’—replied, ‘O Messenger of Allah, I am a man who cannot bear to be without women, and I fear being tempted by the women of Banū al-Asfar. So give me leave and do not put me to temptation.’”

This al-Jadd was the one who stayed away from the Pledge of Divine Pleasure beneath the tree and hid behind a red camel. The hadith concerning him states:

“All of them have been forgiven except the man with the red camel. Allah Most High then revealed concerning him: ‘Among them is one who says, “Give me leave and do not put me to temptation.” Surely, they have fallen into temptation.’”

The meaning is that he asked to stay behind to escape temptation by women, lest he become infatuated with them and then have to guard against what is forbidden and struggle against his own desires, suffering as a result—or else commit the forbidden act and incur sin. For when someone sees beautiful people and is attracted to them, but cannot attain them—either because the Lawgiver has forbidden it or because he is unable to do so—his heart is tormented. If, however, he can attain them and commits what is forbidden, he is ruined. Even in what is lawful, dealing with women entails trials.

This explains his words:

“Do not put me to temptation.”

Allah Most High said:

“Surely, they have fallen into temptation.”

The meaning is that his very turning away from obligatory jihad and shrinking from it, his weak faith, and the sickness of his heart that made abandoning jihad seem appealing to him constitute a grave trial into which he has already fallen.

So how can he seek to escape a lesser trial that has not befallen him by falling into a greater trial that has already afflicted him? Allah says:

“And fight them until there is no more fitnah (tribulation) and religion is entirely for Allah.”

Thus, whoever abandons the fighting Allah has commanded for fear of tribulation has already fallen into it through the doubt in his heart, the sickness within it, and his abandonment of the jihad Allah has commanded. Reflect on this, for this is a perilous matter. People here fall into three groups:

One group enjoins right, forbids wrong, and fights, seeking to remove what they claim to be tribulation, yet their actions cause an even greater tribulation—as with those who fight one another in the strife that arises within the Muslim community.

Others shrink from enjoining right, forbidding wrong, and fighting through which religion becomes entirely for Allah and Allah’s word is supreme, lest they fall into temptation, although they have already fallen into tribulation. The tribulation mentioned in Surah Barā’ah includes temptation by beautiful people, for that was the occasion of the verse’s revelation. This is the condition of many religious people: they abandon their obligations of enjoining right, forbidding wrong, and engaging in jihad through which religion becomes entirely for Allah and Allah’s word is supreme, lest they be tempted by desires. Yet they have fallen into a tribulation greater than what they claim to have fled.

 الِاثْنَانِ فَمَا فَوْقَهُمَا جَمَاعَةٌ؛ لَكِنْ لَمَّا كَانَ ذَلِكَ اشْتِرَاكًا فِي مُجَرَّدِ الصَّلَاةِ حَصَلَ بِاثْنَيْنِ أَحَدُهُمَا إمَامٌ
translated_text:

When such a person fulfils his obligations of enjoining right, forbidding wrong, engaging in jihad, exercising authority, and the like, he will inevitably commit some prohibited acts. He must therefore consider which of the two considerations carries greater weight. If performing what is commanded brings a greater reward than refraining from that prohibited act, he should not abandon it for fear that it may be accompanied by something less harmful. If, however, refraining from the prohibited act brings a greater reward, he should not forfeit that reward in the hope of gaining a lesser reward by fulfilling an obligation. This is determined by the good deeds and sins that the two courses together entail for him. Such is the matter; explaining it in detail would take considerable space.

Every human being on earth inevitably receives commands and prohibitions and must also issue commands and prohibitions. Even someone entirely alone would command and forbid himself, directing himself either towards right or towards wrong. As the Most High says:

“Indeed, the soul is ever prone to evil.”

Commanding means seeking and willing that an action be done; forbidding means seeking and willing that it be left undone. Every living being necessarily has an inner will and desire through which it seeks action from itself and, where possible, from others. For the human being is a living creature who acts by his own will. The children of Adam cannot live without associating with one another. Whenever two or more come together, they must urge one another to do certain things and to refrain from others. Hence, the smallest congregation for prayer consists of two people. As it has been said:

“Two or more constitute a congregation.”

But since this involves participation only in prayer, two suffice, one of them being the imam

and the other following him, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Mālik ibn al-Huwayrith and his companion:

“When the time for prayer comes, give the call to prayer and the call for its commencement, and let the older of you lead you both.”

They were comparable in their Quran recitation.

As for ordinary affairs, the Sunan collections record that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“It is not lawful for three people travelling together to leave one of their number unappointed as their leader.”

Since commanding and forbidding are inseparable from human existence, whoever does not enjoin the right that Allah and His Messenger have commanded, forbid the wrong that Allah and His Messenger have prohibited, receive commands to do the right that Allah and His Messenger have commanded, and receive prohibitions against the wrong that Allah and His Messenger have prohibited, will nevertheless inevitably command and forbid, and be commanded and forbidden. This will concern either the opposite of those things or a mixture of the truth that Allah has revealed and falsehood that Allah has not revealed. If this is adopted as a religion, it becomes an innovated religion.

Similarly, every human being acts by his own will, forming intentions and undertaking actions. If his intention is not righteous and his deed is not a righteous deed performed for Allah’s sake, then his deed will either be corrupt or be performed for other than Allah’s sake. That is what is vain, as the Most High says:

“Indeed, your efforts are diverse.”

All such deeds are vain, of the same kind as the deeds of the disbelievers:

“Those who disbelieve and turn others away from Allah’s way—He will render their deeds worthless.”

The Most High also says:

“As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a lowland which a thirsty person mistakes for water, until, when he reaches it, he finds nothing there

and finds Allah there, who will settle his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning.”

He also says:

“And We will turn to whatever deeds they did and make them scattered dust.”

In His Book, Allah has commanded obedience to Himself, obedience to His Messenger, and obedience to those in authority among the believers. As the Most High says:

“O you who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is best and most excellent in outcome.”

Those in authority are those who possess the authority to command: they are the ones who give people commands. This applies both to people of power and authority and to people of knowledge and discourse. Thus, those in authority fall into two categories: scholars and rulers. When they are upright, the people are upright; and when they are corrupt, the people are corrupt. Thus, when the woman from Ahmas asked Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, “How long will we remain upon this way?” he replied, “As long as your leaders remain upright.”

They include kings, shaykhs, and administrative officials. Everyone who is followed is among those in authority. Each of them must command what Allah has commanded and forbid what He has forbidden. Everyone obliged to obey any of them must obey him in obedience to Allah, but must not obey him in disobedience to Allah. Thus, when Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, assumed leadership of the Muslims and addressed them, he said in his sermon:

“O people, the strong among you are weak in my eyes until I exact from them what is rightfully due;

Section

Since all good deeds must meet two requirements—that they be done for Allah’s sake and conform to the Sharia—these requirements apply to words and actions, to good speech and righteous deeds, and to matters of knowledge and worship. Thus, it is authentically reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The first three with whom Hell will be set ablaze are: a man who acquired knowledge and taught it, recited the Quran and taught others to recite it, so that people would say, ‘He is a scholar and a reciter’; a man who fought and strove in battle so that people would say, ‘He is brave and bold’; and a man who gave charity and bestowed gifts so that people would say, ‘He is generous and open-handed.’”

These three, who seek to show off and gain a reputation, stand in contrast to the three groups who rank after the prophets: the steadfastly truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous. Whoever learns the knowledge with which Allah sent His messengers and teaches it for Allah’s sake is among the steadfastly truthful. Whoever fights so that Allah’s word may be supreme and is killed is a martyr. Whoever gives charity seeking Allah’s pleasure is among the righteous.

This is why someone who neglects his duties concerning his wealth asks to return at the time of death. As Ibn ‘Abbās said:

“Whoever is given wealth but neither performs Hajj with it nor pays zakat asks to return at the time of death.”

He then recited the words of the Most High:

“And spend from what We have provided for you before there comes to any one of you

In these matters of knowledge and discourse, a person must ensure that what he relates about Allah, the Last Day, and what has happened and will happen is true and correct, and that what he enjoins and forbids accords with what the messengers brought from Allah. This is what is correct and consistent with the Sunnah and the Sharia, following the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger. Likewise, the acts of worship that people perform are true and correct, in accordance with what Allah sent His messengers with, when they are among those Allah has prescribed and Allah and His Messenger have commanded.

Whatever fails to meet this standard in either category belongs to falsehood, misleading innovations, and ignorance—even if some call it knowledge and rational understanding, worship and spiritual striving, or spiritual experiences and stations.

One must also enjoin something because Allah has commanded it, forbid something because Allah has forbidden it, and convey what Allah has revealed because it is truth, faith, and guidance, as conveyed by the messengers. Likewise, worship must be performed seeking Allah’s pleasure. If such things are said out of personal desire and partisan zeal, to display one’s knowledge and merit, or to gain a reputation and show off, this is like fighting out of bravery, partisan zeal, and ostentation.

the Book and the Sunnah, as well as statements that accord with them. Those of the latter group often perform acts of worship that Allah has not commanded—indeed, He may have forbidden them—or acts that combine prescribed and prohibited elements. Likewise, people often engage in fighting that contravenes the fighting commanded by Allah, or that combines commanded and prohibited elements.

In each of these three categories—what is commanded, what is prohibited, and what combines the two—the person involved may have a good intention, may be following his own desires, or may combine both. Thus, there are nine categories concerning these matters and the funds spent on them: state revenues, including fay’ (revenues acquired without fighting) and other funds; endowed funds; funds assigned through bequests or vows; and various gifts, charitable donations, and grants. All this involves mingling truth with falsehood and mixing righteous deeds with evil ones.

As for the evil involved, the person responsible may have acted mistakenly or forgetfully and be forgiven, like a qualified scholar who errs in exercising independent judgment, receives a reward, and has his error forgiven. It may be a minor sin expiated by avoiding major sins. It may also be forgiven through repentance or good deeds that erase evil deeds, or expiated through worldly afflictions and the like. Nevertheless, Allah’s religion, for which He revealed His Books and sent His messengers, consists in what was stated above: seeking Allah alone through righteous deeds.

This is Islam in its universal sense, besides which Allah accepts no other religion from anyone. Allah Most High says:

“Whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will never be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Allah bears witness

that there is no deity except Him, as do the angels and those endowed with knowledge; He upholds justice. There is no deity except Him, the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

“Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam.”

Islam encompasses two meanings. The first is submission and obedience, which exclude arrogance. The second is exclusive devotion, as in His words, “and a man belonging wholly to one man,” which excludes associating partners with Allah. It means that the servant submits himself to Allah, the Lord of all worlds, as Allah Most High says:

“Who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself? We certainly chose him in this world, and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous.”

“When his Lord said to him, ‘Submit,’ he said, ‘I have submitted to the Lord of all worlds.’”

“Abraham enjoined this upon his sons, as did Jacob: ‘My sons, Allah has chosen this religion for you, so do not die except as Muslims.’”

Allah Most High also says:

“Say, ‘Indeed, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, an upright religion, the faith of Abraham, who was devoted to Allah alone and was not one of those who associated partners with Him.’”

“Say, ‘Indeed, my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, the Lord of all worlds.’”

“‘He has no partner. This I have been commanded, and I am the first of those who submit.’”

The verb for submission is used intransitively, with the preposition li- (“to”), as in these verses and in the words of Allah Most High:

“Turn to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, for then you will not be helped.”

And His words:

“She said, ‘My Lord, I have indeed wronged myself, and I submit with Solomon to Allah, the Lord of all worlds.’”

And His words:

“Do they seek a religion other than Allah’s, when all those in the heavens and the earth have submitted to Him willingly

or unwillingly, and to Him they will be returned?” And His words:

“Say, ‘Shall we invoke besides Allah what can neither benefit nor harm us, and turn back on our heels after Allah has guided us, like someone whom the devils have led astray in the land, bewildered, while his companions call him to guidance, “Come to us”?’ Say, ‘Indeed, Allah’s guidance is the true guidance, and we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of all worlds.’”

“‘And to establish prayer and fear Him.’”

The verb is also used transitively, coupled with doing good, as in His words, Most High:

“They say, ‘None will enter Paradise unless they are Jews or Christians.’ Those are their wishful claims. Say, ‘Produce your proof, if you are truthful.’”

“Yes indeed! Whoever submits himself wholly to Allah while doing good will have his reward with his Lord. No fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.”

And His words:

“Who is better in religion than one who submits himself wholly to Allah while doing good and follows the faith of Abraham, who was devoted to Allah alone? And Allah took Abraham as a close friend.”

He thus denies that any religion could be better than this religion: submitting oneself wholly to Allah while doing good. He also declares that everyone who submits himself wholly to Allah while doing good will have his reward with his Lord, and that no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve. This comprehensive statement and universal proposition establish a rebuttal to those who claim that none will enter Paradise unless they follow Judaism or Christianity.

These two qualities—submitting oneself wholly to Allah and doing good—are the two principles mentioned earlier: that deeds be done sincerely for Allah and be correct, conforming to the Sunnah and the revealed law. For submitting oneself wholly to Allah entails directing one’s purpose and intention to Allah, as

someone said:

I seek Allah’s forgiveness for sins beyond my count—
The Lord of all servants: to Him are directed the face and the deed.

Four expressions are used here: submitting one’s face and setting one’s face, as in His words, Most High:

“Set your faces toward Him at every place of prayer.”

And His words:

“So set your face toward the religion, devoted to Allah alone—the natural disposition upon which Allah created mankind.”

And turning one’s face, as in the words of Abraham, Allah’s close friend:

“Indeed, I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth, devoted to Him alone, and I am not one of the polytheists.”

Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would say in the opening supplication of his prayer:

“I have turned my face toward Him who created the heavens and the earth, devoted to Him alone, and I am not one of the polytheists.”

In the two Sahīh collections, al-Barā’ ibn ‘Āzib reports that among the words the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would say upon retiring to bed were:

“O Allah, I have submitted myself to You and turned my face toward You.”

Thus, “face” encompasses the one who turns and that toward which he turns; it also encompasses the direction itself. For example, one asks, “Which way do you intend to go?” meaning, “What direction and destination are you heading toward?” This is because the two are inseparable: wherever a person turns, his face turns, and the orientation of his face necessarily entails his own orientation. This applies both inwardly and outwardly. These, then, are four aspects.

The inward is the foundation, while the outward is its completion and visible sign. When a person’s heart turns toward something, his physical face follows it. Thus, when a servant directs his purpose, desire, and attention toward Allah, his will and intention are sound.

translated_text:

The foundation of action is the heart’s action: love and reverence, which are incompatible with hatred and arrogance. They then said:

“Neither speech nor action is accepted without intention.”

This is clear, for Allah Most High does not accept speech or action unless it is sincerely devoted to Him. They then said:

“Neither speech, action, nor intention is accepted without conformity to the Sunnah.”

The Sunnah is the divinely prescribed law: what Allah and His Messenger have commanded. For speech, action, and intention that are not in accordance with the Sunnah, prescribed by Allah and commanded by Him, constitute innovation. They are not among the things Allah loves, so He does not accept them, nor are they sound—as with the deeds of the polytheists and the People of the Book.

The term “Sunnah,” as used by the early generations, encompasses the Sunnah in both worship and belief, although many who wrote works on the Sunnah intended to discuss matters of belief. This is illustrated by the saying of Ibn Mas‘ūd, Ubayy ibn Ka‘b, and Abū al-Dardā’, may Allah be pleased with them:

“Moderate effort in following the Sunnah is better than strenuous effort in innovation.”

There are other similar statements.

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May His blessings be upon Muhammad, his pure family, and all his Companions.

Shaykh al-Islām also said, after an earlier discussion:

The foundation of this is knowledge, for justice and injustice can only be recognized through knowledge. Thus, religion in its entirety consists of knowledge and justice; their opposites are injustice and ignorance.

Allah Most High said:

“But man undertook it; indeed, he was unjust and ignorant.”

Since man is unjust and ignorant—and this occurs sometimes among rulers, sometimes among their subjects, and sometimes among others—the knowledge and justice that we are commanded to observe include patiently enduring the injustice and oppression of rulers. This is among the fundamental principles of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded it in the well-known hadiths reported from him. He said:

“After me, you will encounter preferential treatment given to others, so be patient until you meet me at the Cistern.”

He also said:

“Whoever sees something he dislikes in his ruler should patiently endure it.”

There are other similar statements. He also said:

“Give them what is due to them, and ask Allah for what is due to you.”

And forbid fighting them so long as they continue to pray. This is because they retain the foundation that religion seeks to establish—affirming Allah’s oneness and worshipping Him—and they perform good deeds and refrain from many evil deeds. As for the injustice and oppression they commit, whether on the basis of a defensible interpretation or an indefensible one, it is not permissible to remove it through measures that entail injustice and oppression. Yet this is the habit of most people: they remove evil with something worse, and aggression with something more aggressive;

Their injustice must therefore be patiently endured, just as, when enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, one must often patiently endure the injustice of those being commanded or forbidden. Thus Allah says:

“Enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and patiently endure whatever befalls you.”

And He says:

“So be patient, as were the messengers of firm resolve.”

And He says:

“And patiently await your Lord’s judgment, for you are under Our watchful eyes.”

This applies equally to rulers and their subjects when they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. They must patiently endure whatever befalls them for Allah’s sake, just as those who strive in His cause patiently endure harm to themselves and their property. Patiently enduring affronts to one’s honour is therefore all the more incumbent. This is because the benefit of enjoining right and forbidding wrong cannot be fully achieved otherwise, and whatever is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation is itself obligatory. Rulers are included in this: they are required to show a degree of patience and forbearance not required of others, just as they are required to show a degree of courage and generosity not required of others, because the benefits of governance cannot be fully achieved otherwise.

Just as rulers must patiently endure the harm and injustice inflicted by their subjects when the public interest cannot otherwise be secured, since failing to do so would lead to even greater corruption, so too must subjects patiently endure their rulers’ oppression and injustice if failing to be patient does not entail a greater harm. Both ruler and subject owe the other rights that each must fulfil, some of which he mentioned in the “Book of Jihad and Adjudication.” Each must also be patient with the other and show forbearance

Section: The Degrees of Sin

The degrees of sin in the Hereafter are discussed elsewhere. The concern here is their degrees in this world with respect to blame and punishment.

I have previously mentioned that sins involving wrongdoing against others and harm to their religious or worldly affairs incur greater punishment in this world than sins that do not harm others, even if the punishment for the latter in the Hereafter is greater. Thus, Muslim offenders receive punishments that are not imposed upon non-Muslims living under a covenant of protection, even though the unbeliever’s punishment in the Hereafter is more severe than the Muslim’s.

The second is punished despite his uprightness—for example, someone who drinks nabīdh (a drink made by steeping fruit) believing it permissible on interpretive grounds, or rebels acting on interpretive grounds—in ways that a sinful person who conceals his sin is not. Punishment is also imposed on

translated_text:
those who call others to religious innovation and those who openly commit wrongdoing, in ways not imposed upon a hypocrite who conceals his hypocrisy without calling others to it. These are examples comparing an unbeliever with a sinful Muslim, a sinful person with an upright person, and a hypocrite with a believer who openly displays an innovation or sin. I have explained the reason for this: punishing these people serves to protect religious and worldly life from the wrongdoing of wrongdoers. By contrast, the punishment of someone who wrongs only himself rests with his Lord.

“The crux of the matter” is that all sins constitute wrongdoing: a person either wrongs himself alone or also wrongs others. Where others are wronged, punishment must be prescribed sufficient to protect religious and worldly life from the wrongdoer’s wrongdoing. As Allah Most High says:

“Permission to fight has been given to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged. And indeed, Allah is able to grant them victory.”

Thus, He made “because they have been wronged” the ground permitting the punishment of others by fighting them.

He also says:

“Fight them until there is no more persecution and worship is for Allah. But if they cease, then let there be no aggression except against the wrongdoers.”

He thus makes clear that aggression may be directed against the wrongdoer—that is, by exceeding the generally applicable limit in dealing with him, namely through punishment. This is permissible aggression, as He says:

“So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same measure as he has transgressed against you.”

Some say that this is not really aggression, but is called aggression only to mirror the wording describing the original act. They say the same concerning His words:

“The recompense of an evil is an evil like it.”

There is no need for this explanation. Aggression, in its general sense, means exceeding the generally applicable limit. This is not permissible in dealing with someone unless he himself transgresses; the limit may then be exceeded in dealing with him to the same extent that he exceeded it.

translated_text:
The term “evil” denotes whatever causes a person distress, for calamities and punishments are called “evils” in several places in the Book of Allah Most High.

Wrongdoing is of two kinds: failing to fulfil a right and transgressing a limit. The first consists in withholding what is due to another, such as failing to repay debts, return entrusted property, or discharge other financial obligations. The second consists in aggression against another, such as killing or taking property. Both are wrongdoing. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“Delaying repayment when one has the means is wrongdoing. If one of you is referred for payment to someone solvent, let him accept the referral.”

He thus described mere delay in payment, despite having the means, as wrongdoing. How much more so, then, is outright failure to pay!

Allah Most High also says:

“They ask you for a ruling concerning women. Say, ‘Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, as does what is recited to you in the Book concerning orphan girls to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them, yet whom you wish to marry’”

—up to His words:

“and that you deal justly with orphans.”

‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: “This refers to an orphan girl in her guardian’s care whom he wishes to marry without giving her a fair dowry.” Allah thus called giving the full dowry justice; its opposite is wrongdoing.

In general, this is clear and agreed upon among Muslims: justice may consist in fulfilling an obligation, refraining from something forbidden, or combining both. Among them is that those who hold authority among the Muslims—scholars, rulers, and those who follow them—each owe people certain duties that constitute the essential obligations of their position, even though these are neither required of nor binding upon those outside that category. These obligations apply to them rather than to those others.

Likewise, certain acts may be forbidden to someone by virtue of his position, even though they are not forbidden to those who do not hold that position, or the prohibition is less severe in their case.

Jihad is an example. It is a collective obligation upon the Muslims generally, and it may sometimes become an individual obligation. However, it is more emphatically obligatory upon soldiers who receive stipends from the fay’ revenues for the purpose of jihad. Indeed, it is an individual obligation upon them: obligatory under religious law; obligatory under the agreement they entered into when they pledged obedience to those in authority regarding jihad; and obligatory by virtue of the compensation they receive.

Even if it were not obligatory under religious law or through a pledge of allegiance to an imam, it would nevertheless become obligatory by virtue of the exchange agreed upon, just as an employee who has received his wages must perform the work, and a seller who has received the price must deliver what he has sold. This obligation arises from the contract of exchange and the receipt of compensation, just as the former is an obligation

under religious law and by the mere act of pledging allegiance to the imam. It is also obligatory because neglecting it exposes the Muslims to danger and causes them harm, just as fulfilling a guarantee is obligatory towards the one to whom it was given. For, by accepting their stipends, the “stipendiary soldiers” have undertaken to defend the Muslims. People have therefore felt secure in this undertaking, relied upon them, and refrained from defending themselves. Their reliance is greater than that of a principal upon his agent or an investor upon the person managing his capital. If some of these soldiers are negligent and fail in their duty, this causes the gravest harm to the Muslims.

By abandoning their obligation to fight in defence of the Muslims, they have inflicted immense harm upon them in their religious and worldly affairs. The resulting harm to the Muslims—in their religion, their worldly affairs, their lives, their offspring, and their wealth—is beyond anyone’s ability to measure. Thus, the wrongdoing committed by soldiers who abandon jihad in defence of the Muslims is among the gravest forms of wrongdoing. By contrast, the harm that befalls an individual soldier himself concerns wrongdoing against his own soul. The same applies to sins confined to himself, such as drinking wine and committing sexual immorality: these constitute wrongdoing against himself alone.

His punishment and the blame he deserves for abandoning jihad are therefore far greater than the blame and punishment he deserves for those sins. If both punishments cannot be imposed, punishment for abandoning jihad takes precedence over punishment for these sins, just as the benefit of jihad to him and to the Muslims may

translated_text:
be far greater than the benefit of deterring him from drinking wine and sexual immorality, if he does these things in secret and does not thereby wrong anyone else. Here, the greater of the two evils is averted by tolerating the lesser. Concerning such cases, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah supports this religion through a wicked man and through people who have no share in the Hereafter.”

Such a soldier is censured or reprimanded for his inability to undertake jihad or his negligence in it in a way that someone not assigned to jihad is not.

The same applies to the scholars who preserve the Book and the Sunnah for the Muslim community, both in wording and in meaning. Preserving them is a collective obligation upon the community as a whole, while some of this knowledge is individually obligatory: the knowledge that each Muslim must possess concerning his own personal affairs. Nevertheless, this obligation, both individual and collective, weighs more heavily upon scholars who have attained leadership in this field or receive stipends for it than upon others. This is because it is a general obligation under religious law, and it may become individually binding upon them because they are capable of fulfilling it while others are not.

Such capability includes intellectual aptitude, prior study, familiarity with the means of acquiring knowledge—written works, earlier scholars, and the various other sources of evidence—and the freedom to devote themselves to it without the preoccupations that occupy others.

Thus, the Sunnah has established that embarking upon the pursuit of knowledge or jihad makes its continuation binding, just as embarking upon Hajj does. This means that, with regard to the religious knowledge and knowledge of jihad he has retained, he is not permitted to

allow it to be lost, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever recites the Quran and then forgets it will meet Allah maimed.”

Reported by Abū Dāwūd.

He also said:

“The deeds of my community—both good and bad—were presented to me. Among their evil deeds, I saw a man whom Allah grants a verse of the Quran, but who then neglects it until he forgets it.”

And he said:

“Whoever learns archery and then forgets it is not one of us.”

Reported by Muslim.

The same applies to embarking upon jihad itself. When Muslims line up for battle against an enemy or lay siege to a fortress, they may not withdraw until they have gained victory. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“It is not fitting for a prophet, once he has put on his armour, to remove it until Allah judges between him and his enemy.”

Those assigned to the pursuit of knowledge owe it to the Muslim community to preserve religious knowledge and convey it. If they fail to convey religious knowledge to the community or neglect to preserve it, this constitutes one of the gravest wrongs against Muslims. For this reason, Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, those who conceal the clear proofs and guidance We have sent down, after We have made them clear to people in the Scripture, are cursed by Allah and by those who curse.”

The harm caused by their concealment extends even to animals and other creatures, so those who curse them include even the animals. By contrast, Allah bestows blessings upon the one who teaches good, and His angels pray for him. Everything seeks forgiveness for him, even the fish in the depths of the sea and the birds in the sky.

" سَمِعَ اللَّهُ لِمَنْ حَمِدَهُ "

He thus mentioned the hypocrites and the disbelievers who had made a truce, and stated that they listened to other people who had not come to you. This refers to the hypocrites and the disbelievers under a truce listening to the openly declared disbelievers who had made no truce. Likewise, among the believers there may be those who listen to the hypocrites, as He said:

“And among you are those who listen to them.”

Some people think this means that they listen on their behalf, like spies: they listen to what he says and convey it to them. Indeed, someone was asked, “Where in the Quran does it say, ‘Walls have ears’?” He replied, “In His words: ‘And among you are those who listen to them.’” Likewise, they interpret His words, “avid listeners to lies,” as meaning “so that they may lie,” taking the lām as indicating transitivity rather than following. But this is not the meaning of either verse. Rather, the meaning is that among you are those who listen to them—that is, respond to them and follow them.

Similarly, the expression:

“Allah hears whoever praises Him”

denotes Allah’s approval of whoever praises Him—that is, His acceptance of that person’s praise. One says, “So-and-so listens to so-and-so,” meaning that he responds to him and obeys him.

Although hearing originally denotes the act of hearing itself, which resembles perception, when what is heard is a request, its intended benefit and consequence are response and acceptance. When what is heard is a statement, its intended benefit is assent and belief. Thus, it came to encompass

its intended purpose and benefit within the meaning of the term, in both affirmative and negative usage. Thus, one says, “So-and-so listens to so-and-so,” meaning that he obeys his commands or believes what he tells him. And “So-and-so does not hear what he is told” means that he neither believes the statement nor obeys the command, as Allah has explained concerning the disbelievers’ hearing in several passages, such as His words:

“The example of those who disbelieve is like that of one who calls out to what hears nothing but cries and calls.”

And His words:

“The deaf do not hear the call.”

This is because hearing the truth entails accepting it, just as sensation entails movement, and knowledge in the heart entails movement of the heart. Awareness of what is congenial prompts movement toward it, while awareness of what is repellent prompts aversion to it. Thus, when the necessary consequence is absent, this indicates the absence of its originating cause. Hence the Most High said:

“Only those who hear respond. As for the dead, Allah will resurrect them.”

For this reason, He likened the disbelievers’ hearing to that of livestock hearing the voices of shepherds: they hear mere sounds, as animals do. They do not hear the combinations of letters conveying meanings within those sounds with the hearing that must involve the heart as well as the body.

The Most High said:

“Avid listeners to lies, listeners to other people who have not come to you. They distort words after they have been put in their proper places, saying, ‘If you are given this, accept it.’”

He means that they respond to “other people,” and those people “have not come to you.” Those people “distort words after they have been put in their proper places,” saying to those who have come to you:

“If you are given this, accept it; but if you are not given it, beware.”

Once this meaning becomes clear, the decisive answer becomes apparent concerning the obligation to judge between those under covenant from among non-Muslim belligerents—such as those granted safe-conduct, those covered by a truce, and protected non-Muslim subjects. There is a well-known disagreement among scholars on this matter. Some say that it is not obligatory, because he was given a choice. Others say that it is obligatory, and that this choice was abrogated by His words:

“And judge between them according to what Allah has revealed.”

Those holding the first view say: The command here is to judge according to what Allah has revealed if he judges. It therefore concerns how judgment is to be rendered, not whether judgment must be rendered in the first place. It is like His words:

“If you judge, then judge between them with justice,”

and His words:

“And when you judge between people, judge with justice.”

This is the more correct view, for abrogation cannot be established on the basis of a merely possible interpretation, let alone a less likely one.

The actual meaning of the verse is this: if someone heeds others who have not come to the Messenger, the Messenger is not obliged to judge between them. This includes a person under covenant—whether granted safe-conduct or otherwise—who refers matters back to his rulers and scholars in their own territory. It also includes a protected non-Muslim subject who accepts a judgment if it accords with his wishes, but otherwise returns to his leaders and scholars. Such a person chooses between obeying the judgment of Allah and His Messenger and turning away from it.

As for someone who submits only to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger and has no alternative to it—such as a wronged person seeking protection against his oppressor, with no one of his own religion to defend him—the verse grants no choice in such a case. If the covenant of protection requires defending him against non-Muslim belligerents, then it should, with even greater reason, require defending him against those among the protected non-Muslim subjects who wrong him.

Likewise, if someone seeking a judgment from a judge or scholar is among the hypocrites who choose between accepting what the Quran and Sunnah teach and disregarding it, the judge or scholar is not obliged to judge between them. This is part of the reasoning of many of the early generations who would not relate the Prophet’s hadiths—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—to those who openly professed religious innovations.

The same applies to someone whose aim in seeking a fatwa or judgment is not the truth, but merely to find someone who agrees with his desires, whoever that person may be and whether what he says is true or false. This is heeding something other than that with which Allah sent His Messenger; for Allah sent His Messenger only

وَمِنْ جِنْسِ مُوَالَاةِ الْكُفَّارِ الَّتِي ذَمَّ اللَّهُ بِهَا أَهْلَ الْكِتَابِ وَالْمُنَافِقِينَ:
 الْإِيمَانُ بِبَعْضِ مَا هُمْ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ الْكُفْرِ أَوْ التَّحَاكُمُ إلَيْهِمْ دُونَ كِتَابِ اللَّهِ كَمَا قَالَ تَعَالَى: 
{أَلَمْ تَرَ إلَى الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا نَصِيبًا مِنَ الْكِتَابِ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالْجِبْتِ وَالطَّاغُوتِ وَيَقُولُونَ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا هَؤُلَاءِ أَهْدَى مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا سَبِيلًا}

" الصَّارِمِ الْمَسْلُولِ "
 لَمَّا ذَكَرْنَا قَوْلَ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ

.
 وَنَظِيرُ هَذِهِ الْآيَةِ قَوْله تَعَالَى عَنْ بَعْضِ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ:
 
{وَلَمَّا جَاءَهُمْ رَسُولٌ مِنْ عِنْدِ اللَّهِ مُصَدِّقٌ لِمَا مَعَهُمْ نَبَذَ فَرِيقٌ مِنَ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ كِتَابَ اللَّهِ وَرَاءَ ظُهُورِهِمْ كَأَنَّهُمْ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ}
 
{وَاتَّبَعُوا مَا تَتْلُو الشَّيَاطِينُ عَلَى مُلْكِ سُلَيْمَانَ}
 الْآيَةَ. فَأَخْبَرَ أَنَّهُمْ اتَّبَعُوا السِّحْرَ وَتَرَكُوا كِتَابَ اللَّهِ كَمَا يَفْعَلُهُ كَثِيرٌ مِنْ الْيَهُودِ وَبَعْضُ الْمُنْتَسِبِينَ إلَى الْإِسْلَامِ مِنْ اتِّبَاعِهِمْ كُتُبَ السَّحَرَةِ - أَعْدَاءِ إبْرَاهِيمَ وَمُوسَى - مِنْ الْمُتَفَلْسِفَةِ وَنَحْوِهِمْ
translated_text:
with guidance and the religion of truth. The successors of the Messenger of Allah are therefore not obliged to issue him fatwas or judge his case, just as they are not obliged to judge between hypocrites and disbelievers who heed other people who have not responded to Allah and His Messenger.

Among the forms of allegiance to disbelievers for which Allah condemned the People of the Book and the hypocrites are accepting some of their unbelief or seeking their judgment instead of that of the Book of Allah. As the Most High says:

“Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture? They believe in jibt and tāghūt and say of the disbelievers, ‘These are better guided than the believers.’”

It is well known that this verse was revealed concerning Ka‘b ibn al-Ashraf, one of the Jewish leaders, when he went to the polytheists and declared their religion superior to the religion of Muhammad and his Companions. We have related this account in al-Sārim al-Maslūl when discussing the Prophet’s words—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Who will deal with Ka‘b ibn al-Ashraf? For he has harmed Allah and His Messenger.”

Similar to this verse are the words of the Most High concerning some of the People of the Book:

“And when a messenger from Allah came to them, confirming what was with them, a group of those who had been given the Scripture cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as though they did not know.”

“And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon”—to the end of the verse.

Thus, He tells us that they followed sorcery and abandoned the Book of Allah. This is what many Jews and some who profess Islam do when they follow the books of sorcerers—the enemies of Abraham and Moses—among the philosophers and others like them.

وَهُوَ كَإِيمَانِهِمْ بِالْجِبْتِ وَالطَّاغُوتِ؛

{الْعِيَافَةُ وَالطِّيَرَةُ وَالطَّرْقُ: مِنْ الْجِبْتِ}
 رَوَاهُ أَبُو دَاوُد.
 وَكَذَلِكَ مَا أَخْبَرَ عَنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ بِقَوْلِهِ:

 أَيْ: وَمَنْ عَبَدَ الطَّاغُوتَ فَإِنَّ أَهْلَ الْكِتَابِ كَانَ مِنْهُمْ مَنْ أَشْرَكَ وَعَبَدَ الطَّوَاغِيتَ. فَهُنَا ذَكَرَ عِبَادَتَهُمْ لِلطَّاغُوتِ وَفِي 
" الْبَقَرَةِ "
 ذَكَرَ اتِّبَاعَهُمْ لِلسِّحْرِ وَذَكَرَ فِي 
" النِّسَاءِ "
 إيمَانَهُمْ بِهِمَا جَمِيعًا: بِالْجِبْتِ وَالطَّاغُوتِ.
 وَأَمَّا التَّحَاكُمُ إلَى غَيْرِ كِتَابِ اللَّهِ فَقَدْ قَالَ:
 
{أَلَمْ تَرَ إلَى الَّذِينَ يَزْعُمُونَ أَنَّهُمْ آمَنُوا بِمَا أُنْزِلَ إلَيْكَ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ مِنْ قَبْلِكَ يُرِيدُونَ أَنْ يَتَحَاكَمُوا إلَى الطَّاغُوتِ وَقَدْ أُمِرُوا أَنْ يَكْفُرُوا بِهِ وَيُرِيدُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَنْ يُضِلَّهُمْ ضَلَالًا بَعِيدًا}
 
{وَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُمْ تَعَالَوْا إلَى مَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ وَإِلَى الرَّسُولِ رَأَيْتَ الْمُنَافِقِينَ يَصُدُّونَ عَنْكَ صُدُودًا}
 . وَالطَّاغُوتُ فعلوت مِنْ الطُّغْيَانِ. كَمَا أَنَّ الْمَلَكُوتَ فعلوت مِنْ الْمُلْك. وَالرَّحَمُوتُ وَالرَّهَبُوتُ والرغبوت. فعلوت مِنْ الرَّحْمَةِ
translated_text:
and this is like their belief in jibt and tāghūt; for tāghūt is a transgressing entity, whereas jibt pertains to deeds and words. As ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb said, “Jibt is sorcery, and tāghūt is Satan.” Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Divination through birds, belief in evil omens, and divination through pebbles or lines drawn on the ground are forms of jibt.”

Reported by Abū Dāwūd.

Likewise, Allah says concerning the People of the Book:

“Say, ‘Shall I inform you of those whose recompense with Allah is worse than that? They are those whom Allah has cursed and with whom He is angry, some of whom He turned into apes and pigs, and who worshipped tāghūt.’”

That is, those who worshipped tāghūt, for among the People of the Book were those who associated partners with Allah and worshipped false gods. Here He mentions their worship of tāghūt; in al-Baqara, He mentions their following sorcery; and in al-Nisā’, He mentions their belief in both jibt and tāghūt.

As for seeking judgment from anything other than the Book of Allah, He says:

“Have you not seen those who claim to believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you? They wish to seek judgment from tāghūt, although they were commanded to reject it. And Satan wishes to lead them far astray.”

“And when they are told, ‘Come to what Allah has revealed and to the Messenger,’ you see the hypocrites turning resolutely away from you.”

The word tāghūt follows the morphological pattern fa‘alūt, from tughyān (transgression), just as malakūt (dominion) follows the fa‘alūt pattern, from mulk (sovereignty). Likewise, rahamūt, rahabūt, and raghabūt follow the fa‘alūt pattern, derived from rahma (mercy)

وَالرَّهْبَةُ وَالرَّغْبَةُ.

 وَلِهَذَا سُمِّيَ مَنْ تُحُوكِمَ إلَيْهِ مَنْ حَاكَمَ بِغَيْرِ كِتَابِ اللَّهِ طَاغُوتٌ وَسَمَّى اللَّهُ فِرْعَوْنَ وَعَادًا طُغَاةً وَقَالَ فِي صَيْحَةِ ثَمُودَ:
 
{فَأَمَّا ثَمُودُ فَأُهْلِكُوا بِالطَّاغِيَةِ}
 .
 فَمَنْ كَانَ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْأُمَّةِ مُوَالِيًا لِلْكُفَّارِ:
 مِنْ الْمُشْرِكِينَ أَوْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ بِبَعْضِ أَنْوَاعِ الْمُوَالَاةِ وَنَحْوِهَا: مِثْلَ إتْيَانِهِ أَهْلَ الْبَاطِلِ وَاتِّبَاعِهِمْ فِي شَيْءٍ مِنْ مَقَالِهِمْ وَفِعَالِهِمْ الْبَاطِلَ: كَانَ لَهُ مِنْ الذَّمِّ وَالْعِقَابِ وَالنِّفَاقِ بِحَسَبِ ذَلِكَ؛ وَذَلِكَ مِثْلُ مُتَابَعَتِهِمْ فِي آرَائِهِمْ وَأَعْمَالِهِمْ؛ كَنَحْوِ أَقْوَالِ الصَّابِئَةِ وَأَفْعَالِهِمْ مِنْ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ وَنَحْوِهِمْ الْمُخَالَفَةِ لِلْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ؛ وَنَحْوِ أَقْوَالِ الْيَهُودِ وَالنَّصَارَى وَأَفْعَالِهِمْ الْمُخَالِفَةِ لِلْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ؛ وَنَحْوِ أَقْوَالِ الْمَجُوسِ وَالْمُشْرِكِينَ وَأَفْعَالِهِمْ الْمُخَالِفَةِ لِلْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ. وَمَنْ تَوَلَّى أَمْوَاتَهُمْ أَوْ أَحْيَاءَهُمْ بِالْمَحَبَّةِ وَالتَّعْظِيمِ وَالْمُوَافَقَةِ فَهُوَ مِنْهُمْ؛
 كَاَلَّذِينَ وَافَقُوا أَعْدَاءَ إبْرَاهِيمَ الْخَلِيلِ:
 مِنْ الْكَلْدَانِيِّينَ وَغَيْرِهِمْ
translated_text:
and rahba (fear) and raghba (desire).

Transgression means exceeding the bounds; it is wrongdoing and aggression. Whoever is worshipped besides Allah, without being averse to it, is a tāghūt. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, called idols tawāghīt (false gods) when he said in an authentic hadith:

“Those who worship false gods will follow those false gods.”

Anyone obeyed in disobedience to Allah, or obeyed in following something other than guidance and the religion of truth—whether his statements that contradict the Book of Allah are accepted, or his commands that contradict Allah’s commands are obeyed—is a tāghūt. Hence, someone to whom disputes are referred, who judges by other than the Book of Allah, is called a tāghūt. Allah called Pharaoh and ‘Ād transgressors, and said concerning the blast that struck Thamūd:

“As for Thamūd, they were destroyed by the overpowering blast.”

Any member of this community who shows allegiance to the disbelievers, whether polytheists or People of the Book, through some form of allegiance or the like—for example, by going to the adherents of falsehood and following them in some of their false statements and deeds—incurs blame and punishment, and has a share of hypocrisy, in proportion to that. This includes following their views and practices, such as the statements and deeds of the Sabians—philosophers and others like them—that contradict the Book and the Sunnah; the statements and deeds of the Jews and Christians that contradict the Book and the Sunnah; and the statements and deeds of the Magians and polytheists that contradict the Book and the Sunnah.

Whoever gives allegiance to their dead or their living through love, veneration, and agreement is one of them, like those who sided with the enemies of Abraham, the close friend of Allah, among the Chaldeans and others

translated_text:
among the polytheists who worshipped the heavenly bodies and practised sorcery; and those who sided with the enemies of Moses—Pharaoh and his people—in practising sorcery, or claimed that there is no Maker apart from what is made, no Creator apart from creation, and no God above the heavens, as the Ittihādiyya (advocates of the unity of Creator and creation) and other Jahmiyya maintain.

There are also those who agreed with the Sabians and philosophers in what they said about the Creator and His messengers, His names and attributes, the Resurrection, and other matters.

Although the unbelief of these groups is manifest, there is no doubt that many who have entered Islam—even those renowned for learning, worship, and leadership—have adopted much of their unbelief, revered them, and considered the principles they established and similar things authoritative. Such people have become numerous in later times, mixing the truth brought by the messengers with the falsehood followed by their enemies.

Allah Most High loves that the impure be distinguished from the pure, and truth from falsehood. It should therefore be recognized that these groups are hypocrites or have hypocrisy within them, even though they are among the Muslims. A person’s being outwardly Muslim does not preclude his being inwardly a hypocrite: all hypocrites are outwardly Muslim, and the Quran has explained their characteristics and the rulings concerning them.

If they existed during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when Islam was strong and the signs of prophethood and the light of the message were manifest, they are all the more prevalent when far removed from those signs and that light. This is especially so because the cause of hypocrisy is the same as the cause of unbelief: whatever opposes what the messengers brought.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

Whom is it obligatory or permissible to hate or shun, or both, for the sake of Allah Most High? What conditions must be met by someone who hates or shuns another for the sake of Allah Most High? Does refraining from greeting someone fall within shunning? If the person being shunned greets the person shunning him first, is the latter obliged to return his greeting? Should hatred and shunning for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, continue until it is established that the characteristic for which the person was hated and shunned has disappeared? Or is there a specified period for this? If there is, what is its limit? Give us your ruling, and may you be rewarded.

The Answer

He replied:

Shunning prescribed by Islamic law is of two kinds: the first consists in keeping away from wrongdoing, and the second in punishment for it.

The first is mentioned in the words of Allah Most High:

“When you see those who engage in offensive discourse concerning Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in another conversation. And if Satan should cause you to forget, then, after remembering, do not sit with the wrongdoing people.”

And in His words, Most High:

“He has already revealed to you in the Book that when you hear Allah’s verses being denied

and mocked, do not sit with them until they engage in another conversation. Otherwise, you would be like them.”

This means that one should not be present where wrongdoing occurs without a need to be there. For example, one must not sit with people drinking wine, nor accept an invitation to a wedding feast where there is wine and the playing of wind instruments, and so forth. This does not apply to someone who attends in order to condemn their wrongdoing, or who is present against his will.

Hence the saying:

“Someone present at wrongdoing is like the one committing it.”

And the hadith states:

“Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day must not sit at a table where wine is being drunk.”

This kind of shunning is akin to a person’s keeping himself from committing wrongdoing. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The emigrant is the one who abandons what Allah has forbidden.”

This category includes migration from a land of disbelief and wickedness to a land of Islam and faith. It means abandoning residence among disbelievers and hypocrites who do not allow a person to do what Allah has commanded. The words of Allah Most High also fall under this heading:

“And shun defilement.”

The second kind is shunning as a disciplinary measure. This means shunning someone who openly commits wrongdoing until he repents of it, just as

“the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Muslims shunned the three who were left behind until Allah revealed that He had accepted their repentance,”

when it became evident that, without an excuse, they had failed to undertake the jihad that was individually obligatory upon them. He did not, however, shun those who outwardly displayed goodness

translated_text:
even if such a person was a hypocrite. Here, shunning serves as a discretionary disciplinary punishment. Such punishment applies to those whose neglect of obligations and commission of forbidden acts have become evident: those who abandon prayer and zakah, openly commit injustice and indecency, or promote innovations that contradict the Quran, the Sunnah, and the consensus of the early generations of the Muslim community, and that have clearly been established as innovations.

This is the true meaning of the statement made by some of the early generations and leading scholars:

“The testimony of those who promote innovations is not accepted; they are not to be followed in prayer, knowledge is not to be taken from them, and marriage ties are not to be formed with them.”

These measures are a punishment for them until they desist. Hence, these scholars distinguish between those who promote innovations and those who do not. Someone who promotes them has openly displayed wrongdoing and thus deserves punishment, unlike someone who conceals it. The latter is no worse than the hypocrites whose outward professions the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, accepted, leaving their inner secrets to Allah, despite knowing the true condition of many of them.

Hence the statement in the hadith:

“When a sin is concealed, it harms only the one who commits it. But when it is committed openly and is not condemned, it harms the community at large.”

This is because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When people see wrongdoing and do not change it, Allah may soon encompass them all in a punishment from Him.”

Open wrongdoing must therefore be condemned, unlike concealed wrongdoing, for its punishment falls upon the one who commits it

translated_text:
alone.

This shunning varies according to the strength or weakness of those who practise it and whether they are few or many. Its purpose is to deter and discipline the person being shunned and to discourage the general public from following his example. If its benefits predominate, such that shunning him leads to evil diminishing and becoming less apparent, then it is prescribed. But if neither the person being shunned nor anyone else is deterred, and evil instead increases, while those practising the shunning are weak, so that its harm outweighs its benefit, then shunning is not prescribed. Rather, winning some people over is more beneficial than shunning them, while shunning others is more beneficial than winning them over.

For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would win some people over and shun others. The three who were left behind were better than most of those whose hearts were being won over. The latter were chiefs obeyed within their clans, so the interests of the religion lay in winning their hearts. The former were believers, and there were many other believers; thus shunning them strengthened the religion and purified them of their sins.

Similarly, what is prescribed in dealing with an enemy may sometimes be fighting, sometimes concluding a truce, and sometimes collecting the jizyah (poll tax). All of this depends on the circumstances and the benefits involved.

The answers given by leading scholars such as Ahmad and others on this subject are based on this principle. Hence, he would distinguish between places where innovations had become widespread—as Qadarism had in Basra, astrology in Khurāsān, and Shiism in Kufa—and those where this was not

translated_text:
the case. He would also distinguish between leaders whom people obeyed and others. When one understands the objective of Islamic law, one pursues the means most conducive to achieving it.

Once this is understood, prescribed shunning is among the deeds commanded by Allah and His Messenger. An act of obedience must be devoted sincerely to Allah and conform to His command, so that it is both sincere and correct.

Whoever shuns someone out of personal desire, or practises a form of shunning that has not been commanded, falls outside this category. How often people follow their own desires while imagining that they are acting in obedience to Allah!

Shunning someone for personal reasons is not permissible for more than three days, as reported in the two Sahīh collections from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“It is not lawful for a Muslim to shun his brother for more than three days. They meet, and each turns away from the other. The better of the two is the one who first offers the greeting of peace.”

He did not permit this kind of shunning for more than three days, just as he did not permit mourning for more than three days except in the case of a wife.

It is also reported in the two Sahīh collections that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The gates of Paradise are opened every Monday and Thursday, and every servant who associates nothing with Allah is forgiven, except a man between whom and his brother there is enmity. It is then said: ‘Let these two wait until they reconcile.’”

Thus, shunning someone over one’s own rights is forbidden; only certain instances have been permitted, just as a husband has been permitted to shun his wife in bed if she is defiantly disobedient, and as shunning for three days has been permitted. One must therefore distinguish between shunning to uphold Allah’s rights and shunning over one’s own rights.

original_text:
فَالْأَوَّلُ مَأْمُورٌ بِهِ وَالثَّانِي مَنْهِيٌّ عَنْهُ؛

{وَإِنْ طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا فَأَصْلِحُوا بَيْنَهُمَا فَإِنْ بَغَتْ إحْدَاهُمَا عَلَى الْأُخْرَى فَقَاتِلُوا الَّتِي تَبْغِي حَتَّى تَفِيءَ إلَى أَمْرِ اللَّهِ فَإِنْ فَاءَتْ فَأَصْلِحُوا بَيْنَهُمَا بِالْعَدْلِ وَأَقْسِطُوا إنَّ اللَّهَ يُحِبُّ الْمُقْسِطِينَ}
 إنَّمَا الْمُؤْمِنُونَ إخْوَةٌ فَجَعَلَهُمْ إخْوَةً
translated_text:
The former is commanded, whereas the latter is forbidden, for the believers are brothers. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“Do not sever ties with one another, turn your backs on one another, hate one another, or envy one another. Be brothers, O servants of Allah. A Muslim is the brother of a Muslim.”

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said in a hadith recorded in the Sunan collections:

“Shall I tell you of something higher in rank than prayer, fasting, charity, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong?” They replied, “Yes, O Messenger of Allah.” He said, “Reconciling people, for discord between people is the razor. I do not mean that it shaves off hair; rather, it shaves away religion.”

He also said in an authentic hadith:

“The believers, in their mutual love, mercy, and compassion, are like a single body: when one limb suffers, the rest of the body responds with fever and sleeplessness.”

This is because shunning falls under the category of penalties prescribed by Islamic law, and is thus of the same nature as jihad in Allah’s cause. It is practised so that Allah’s word may be supreme and religion may be devoted entirely to Allah. A believer must show enmity for Allah’s sake and loyalty for Allah’s sake. If someone is a believer, he must remain loyal to him even if that person wrongs him, for wrongdoing does not sever the bond of loyalty based on faith. Allah Most High says:

“If two groups of believers fight one another, make peace between them. But if one of them transgresses against the other, fight the transgressing group until it returns to Allah’s command. If it returns, then make peace between them with justice and act equitably. Indeed, Allah loves those who act equitably.”

“The believers are but brothers.”

He thus declared them brothers

 اسْتَحَقَّ مِنْ الْمُوَالَاةِ وَالثَّوَابِ بِقَدْرِ مَا فِيهِ مِنْ الْخَيْرِ وَاسْتَحَقَّ مِنْ الْمُعَادَاتِ وَالْعِقَابِ بِحَسَبِ مَا فِيهِ مِنْ الشَّرِّ فَيَجْتَمِعُ فِي الشَّخْصِ الْوَاحِدِ مُوجِبَاتُ الْإِكْرَامِ وَالْإِهَانَةِ فَيَجْتَمِعُ لَهُ مِنْ هَذَا وَهَذَا كَاللِّصِّ الْفَقِيرِ تُقْطَعُ يَدُهُ لِسَرِقَتِهِ وَيُعْطَى مِنْ بَيْتِ الْمَالِ مَا يَكْفِيهِ لِحَاجَتِهِ. هَذَا هُوَ الْأَصْلُ الَّذِي اتَّفَقَ عَلَيْهِ أَهْلُ السُّنَّةِ وَالْجَمَاعَةِ وَخَالَفَهُمْ الْخَوَارِجُ وَالْمُعْتَزِلَةُ وَمَنْ وَافَقَهُمْ عَلَيْهِ فَلَمْ يَجْعَلُوا النَّاسَ لَا مُسْتَحِقًّا لِلثَّوَابِ فَقَطْ وَلَا مُسْتَحِقًّا لِلْعِقَابِ فَقَطْ.
 وَأَهْلُ السُّنَّةِ يَقُولُونَ:
 إنَّ اللَّهَ يُعَذِّبُ بِالنَّارِ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكَبَائِرِ مَنْ يُعَذِّبُهُ ثُمَّ يُخْرِجُهُمْ مِنْهَا بِشَفَاعَةِ مَنْ يَأْذَنُ
translated_text:
even while they fought and transgressed and were commanded to be reconciled. Let the believer reflect on the distinction between these two kinds, for how often one is confused with the other! Let him know that loyalty to a believer is obligatory even if that believer wrongs him and transgresses against him, while enmity towards a disbeliever is obligatory even if that disbeliever gives him gifts and treats him kindly. For Allah, Glorified is He, sent the messengers and revealed the Scriptures so that religion would be devoted entirely to Allah: love for His allies and hatred for His enemies, honour for His allies and humiliation for His enemies, reward for His allies and punishment for His enemies.

When good and evil, wickedness, obedience and disobedience, adherence to the Sunnah and religious innovation coexist in one man, he deserves loyalty and reward in proportion to the good within him, and enmity and punishment in proportion to the evil within him. Thus, grounds for both honouring and humiliating a person may coexist, and he receives a share of each. This is like a poor thief whose hand is cut off for his theft, yet who is given enough from the public treasury to meet his needs.

This is the principle upon which Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah agree. The Khawārij, the Muʿtazilah, and those who agree with them oppose them on this point. They did not regard people as neither deserving of reward alone nor deserving of punishment alone.

Ahl al-Sunnah say:

Allah punishes in the Fire those perpetrators of major sins whom He punishes, then brings them out of it through the intercession of those whom He permits

to intercede, by His abundant mercy, as is established in numerous reports of the Sunnah from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, knows best. O Allah, bless Muhammad and all his family and Companions.

He also said—may Allah have mercy on him:

Section

In the questions recorded by Ishāq ibn Mansūr—which al-Khallāl also cited in his Book of the Sunnah, in the chapter on avoiding those who say that the Quran is created—Ishāq reports that he said to Abū Abd Allāh:

“What of someone who says, ‘The Quran is created’?”

He replied: “Attribute every evil to him.”

I said: “Should one openly show enmity towards them, or deal tactfully with them?”

He replied: “The people of Khurāsān are no match for them.”

This reply of his, together with his statement concerning the Qadariyyah—“If we were to abandon transmitting reports from the Qadariyyah, we would have to abandon transmitting from most of the people of Basra”—and his treatment of them during the inquisition, responding in the best manner and addressing them with proofs, explains his statements and actions concerning shunning them and forbidding others to sit or converse with them. Indeed, at another time he even shunned certain eminent figures and ordered that they be shunned because of some form of Jahmī belief.

translated_text:
For shunning is a form of disciplinary punishment, and punishment is a form of abandonment—that is, abandoning evil deeds. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The emigrant is one who abandons evil deeds.”

He also said:

“One who abandons what Allah has forbidden.”

This is abandonment as an expression of piety. Shunning as a disciplinary measure and a form of jihad includes the shunning of the three who were left behind: he ordered the Muslims to shun them until Allah accepted their repentance.

Thus, abandonment is sometimes an expression of piety, when it consists of abandoning evil deeds. As Allah Most High said:

“When you see those who engage in offensive discourse about Our verses, turn away from them until they turn to another subject. And if Satan causes you to forget, then after remembering, do not sit with the wrongdoing people.”

“Those who fear Allah are not accountable for them in any way, but must remind them, so that perhaps they may fear Him.”

He, Glorified is He, thus made clear that the God-fearing are distinct from the wrongdoers, and that those commanded to leave gatherings where people engage in offensive discourse about Allah’s verses are the God-fearing.

At other times, shunning is a form of jihad, enjoining right and forbidding wrong, and enforcing the prescribed legal penalties. It constitutes punishment of someone who has transgressed and committed wrongdoing. Punishing and disciplining a wrongdoer is conditional upon having the ability to do so.

For this reason, the religious ruling concerning these two forms of abandonment differs according to whether one has the ability or lacks it, and whether wrongful innovators are few or many, strong or weak. The ruling similarly varies according to these factors in all other forms of wrongdoing, including disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience. Everything Allah has forbidden is wrongdoing, whether it infringes solely upon Allah’s rights, upon the rights of His servants, or upon both.

The abandonment He has commanded—whether through abstaining and desisting, or through shunning as punishment and discipline—applies only when it involves no benefit

of religious significance that outweighs the harm of performing the act. Otherwise, if an evil deed contains an outweighing good, it is not evil. If punishment entails harm greater than that of the crime, it is not good; rather, it is evil. If the harms are equal, it is neither good nor evil.

Thus, abandonment may aim at avoiding the evil of religious innovation, which constitutes wrongdoing, sin, transgression, and corruption. Alternatively, shunning may aim at the good of jihad, forbidding wrong, and punishing wrongdoers so that they are deterred and restrained, and so that faith and righteous deeds are strengthened among those who uphold them.

Punishing a wrongdoer deters people from committing his wrongdoing and encourages them to pursue its opposite: faith, the Sunnah, and the like. If shunning him neither deters anyone nor causes anyone to desist, but instead prevents many commanded good deeds from being performed, then such shunning is not commanded. This is what Ahmad mentioned concerning the people of Khurāsān at that time: they lacked the strength to stand against the Jahmiyyah. When they were unable to show hostility towards them, the command to perform this good deed ceased to apply. Dealing tactfully with them would protect the weak believer from harm and might also win over the powerful evildoer. Likewise, when Qadarite doctrine became widespread among the people of Basra, abandoning the transmission of hadith from them would have caused the knowledge, Sunnah traditions, and transmitted reports preserved among them to die out.

If duties relating to knowledge, jihad, and other matters cannot be fulfilled except through someone whose religious innovation causes less harm than abandoning that duty, then securing the benefit of fulfilling the duty, despite the lesser harm accompanying it, is better than the reverse. For this reason, these questions require a nuanced discussion.

translated_text:
Many answers given by Imam Ahmad and other imams were responses to questions from people whose circumstances they knew, or were addressed to particular individuals whose circumstances they knew. Such answers are comparable to the Messenger’s rulings on particular cases—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—which apply only to analogous cases.

Some people have treated these answers as general rulings and consequently practised forms of shunning and denunciation that they were not commanded to practise, and which are therefore neither obligatory nor recommended. In doing so, they may have neglected obligatory or recommended deeds and committed forbidden acts.

Others have disregarded this matter altogether, failing to shun the evil practices rooted in religious innovation that they were commanded to shun. Instead, they have merely kept away from them out of indifference, rather than abstaining from them with aversion, or have fallen into them themselves. They may also abstain from them with aversion, yet neither forbid others to engage in them nor punish those who deserve punishment for them through shunning or similar measures. They have thus neglected the forbidding of wrong that they were commanded to undertake, whether as an obligation or a recommendation. They therefore either commit wrong or fail to forbid it, doing what they were forbidden to do or neglecting what they were commanded to do.

That is how matters stand. Allah’s religion is the middle way between those who go to excess in it and those who neglect it. And Allah, Glorified is He, knows best.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām was asked about a Muslim who, in his youth, committed a sin warranting shunning and avoidance. One group said, “He should seek Allah’s forgiveness, and he should be pardoned and all his past deeds overlooked.” Another group said, “It is not permissible to take him as a brother or keep his company.” Which of the two groups is closer to the truth?

He replied:

There is no doubt that whoever sincerely repents to Allah will have his repentance accepted by Allah, as the Most High says:

“He is the One who accepts repentance from His servants, pardons their sins, and knows what you do.”

The Most High also says:

“Say, ‘O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of Allah’s mercy. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.’”

That is, for those who repent. This being so, if the man repents, then does righteous deeds for a year without going back on his repentance, his repentance is to be accepted, and people may sit with him and speak to him. If, however, he repents but a year has not yet passed, the scholars have two well-known views concerning him.

Some say that people may sit with him immediately and his testimony may be accepted. Others say that a year must pass, as was the practice of ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb with Sabīgh ibn ‘Isl. This is one of
