in his eyes; a man whom a woman of rank and beauty invites to sin, but who says, ‘I fear Allah, Lord of all worlds’; and a man who gives charity so secretly that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends.”

In Sahīh Muslim, ‘Iyād ibn Himār, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The people of Paradise are of three kinds: a just ruler; a man who is merciful and tenderhearted towards every relative and every Muslim; and a wealthy man who is chaste and gives charity.”

In the Sunan collections, it is reported that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“One who collects charity justly is like one who strives in Allah’s cause.”

When commanding fighting in His cause, Allah Most High said:

“Fight them until there is no more fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked:

“O Messenger of Allah, a man fights out of bravery, another out of partisan zeal, and another for show. Which of these is in Allah’s cause?”

He replied:

“Whoever fights so that Allah’s word may be supreme is fighting in Allah’s cause.”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded this in their Sahīh collections.

The aim, then, is that religion should be entirely for Allah and that Allah’s word should be supreme. “Allah’s word” is a comprehensive term encompassing His words contained in His Book. Likewise, Allah Most High said:

“We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance, so that people may uphold justice.”

The purpose of sending the messengers and revealing the Scriptures is therefore that people should uphold justice concerning both the rights of Allah and the rights of His creation. Then Allah Most High said:

“And We sent down iron, in which is great strength and benefits for people, so that Allah may know those who support Him and His messengers though they do not see Him.”

Whoever departs from the Book is set right by iron. Thus, religion is upheld by the Quran and the sword. It is reported that Jābir ibn ‘Abd Allāh, may Allah be pleased with them both, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded us to strike with this—meaning the sword—whoever departs from this—meaning the Quran.”

Since this is the objective, it should be pursued through the means that come closest to achieving it, in order of priority. Of two candidates, whichever is better suited to achieving that objective should be appointed. If, for example, the office consists solely of leading the prayer, preference should be given to the person whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave precedence when he said:

“The people should be led in prayer by the one most proficient in reciting the Book of Allah. If they are equal in recitation, then by the one most knowledgeable about the Sunnah. If they are equal in knowledge of the Sunnah, then by the one who emigrated earliest. If they are equal in emigration, then by the oldest. No man should lead another in prayer within the latter’s sphere of authority, nor sit in his place of honour in his house, except with his permission.”

Muslim recorded it.

If two men are equally qualified and it is unclear which is more suitable, lots should be drawn between them. Thus, Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās drew lots among the people on the day of al-Qādisiyyah when they disputed over giving the call to prayer, following the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“If people knew what reward there is in the call to prayer and the first row, and could find no way to obtain them except by drawing lots, they would draw lots.”

When precedence is thus determined by Allah’s command where the proper choice is clear, and by His action—namely, the choice He determines through drawing lots when the matter is unclear—the appointing authority has discharged the trusts of public office by entrusting them to those entitled to them.

Section

The Second Category of Trusts: Property

Allah Most High says concerning debts:

“If one of you entrusts another, let the one entrusted discharge his trust, and let him fear Allah, his Lord.”

This category includes property and debts, both private and public: returning deposits for safekeeping; returning a partner’s property or property held under an agency or profit-sharing arrangement; and returning the property of those in one’s care, such as orphans and beneficiaries of endowments, and the like. It also includes settling debts arising from purchases, repaying loans, paying women’s dowries, and paying fees for the use of property or services, and the like.

Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, mankind was created anxious: distressed when evil touches him, and withholding when good touches him—except those who pray, who are constant in their prayer, and in whose wealth there is a known right for the beggar and the deprived.”

And later in the passage:

“And those who are faithful to their trusts and pledges.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth so that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you. And do not plead on behalf of the treacherous.”

That is, do not argue in their defence.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“The believer is one whom Muslims trust with their lives and wealth. The Muslim is one from whose tongue and hand Muslims are safe. The emigrant is one who abandons what

Allah has forbidden. The one who strives in Allah’s cause is one who strives against his own self for Allah’s sake.” This is an authentic hadith, parts of which appear in the Sahīh collections of al-Bukhārī and Muslim, and parts in Sunan al-Tirmidhī.

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“Whoever takes people’s wealth intending to repay it, Allah will repay it on his behalf; whoever takes it intending to squander it, Allah will bring him to ruin.”

Narrated by al-Bukhārī.

Since Allah has made it obligatory to return trusts lawfully received, this also indicates the obligation to restore property seized by force, stolen, or obtained through betrayal or similar wrongdoing. Borrowed property must likewise be returned.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, delivered a sermon during the Farewell Pilgrimage, in which he said:

“Borrowed property must be returned, property granted for use must be given back, debts must be repaid, and a guarantor is liable for payment. Allah has given everyone their due, so no bequest may be made to an heir.”

This category applies to both rulers and subjects: each must render to the other whatever is due. The ruler and his deputies responsible for disbursements must give everyone their due. Revenue collectors, such as the officials of the administrative bureaux, must deliver to the ruler whatever must be paid to him. The same applies to subjects who owe such dues.

Subjects have no right to demand from those administering public funds anything to which they are not entitled, thereby becoming like those of whom Allah Most High says:

“And among them are those who criticize you concerning the charitable funds. If they are given some, they are pleased; but if they are not given any, they become angry.”

“If only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them and had said, ‘Allah is sufficient for us. Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. To Allah alone we turn with hope.’”

Then He, glorified be He, explained who is entitled to these funds

translated_text:
through fear cast into my enemies’ hearts from a month’s journey away. The earth has been made a place of prayer and a means of purification for me, so let any man of my nation pray when the time for prayer comes. War booty has been made lawful for me, though it was not lawful for anyone before me. I have been granted intercession. Each prophet was sent specifically to his own people, whereas I have been sent to all humanity.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said:

“I have been sent with the sword ahead of the Hour, so that Allah alone is worshipped, without any partner. My provision has been placed beneath the shade of my spear, and humiliation and abasement have been imposed upon whoever opposes my command. Whoever imitates a people is one of them.”

Ahmad narrated this in his Musnad from Ibn ‘Umar, and al-Bukhārī cited it as supporting evidence.

The obligation concerning war booty is to set aside one-fifth, distribute that fifth to those whom Allah Most High has mentioned, and divide the remainder among those who took part in the campaign. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “War booty belongs to those who were present at the battle.” These are those who attended for the purpose of fighting, whether or not they actually fought. It must be divided fairly among them, without favouring anyone because of his leadership, lineage, or merit, just as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his caliphs used to divide it.

Sahīh al-Bukhārī reports that Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās, may Allah be pleased with him, considered himself to have greater merit than those below him. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Are you granted victory and provision except through the weak among you?”

In Ahmad’s Musnad, Sa‘d ibn Abī Waqqās reported:

“I said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, should a man who defends his people receive the same share as anyone else?’ He replied, ‘May your mother be bereaved of you, son of Umm Sa‘d! Are you granted provision and victory

War booty continued to be divided among those who took part in the campaigns under the Umayyad and Abbasid dynasties, when the Muslims fought the Byzantines, Turks, and Berbers.

However, the ruler may grant an additional share to those who distinguish themselves by inflicting greater harm upon the enemy: for example, a detachment sent out from the army, a man who scales a high fortress and captures it, or someone who charges the enemy commander and kills him, thereby routing the enemy, and similar cases. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his caliphs used to grant additional shares for such deeds. He would award a detachment one-quarter after the fifth had been deducted on the outward journey, and one-third after the fifth had been deducted on the return journey.

Regarding this additional award, scholars have said that it is taken from the fifth. Some have said that it is taken from one-fifth of the fifth, so that none of those entitled to the booty receives preferential treatment over the others. The correct view, however, is that it may be taken from the remaining four-fifths, even though this entails favouring some over others, provided this serves a religious interest rather than personal inclination, as the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did on more than one occasion.

This is the position of the jurists of Syria, Abū Hanīfa, Ahmad, and others. On this basis, one view holds that the ruler may award a quarter or a third with or without a prior stipulation, but may award more than that only through a prior stipulation—for example, by saying, “Whoever directs me to a fortress shall receive such-and-such,” or, “Whoever brings me a head shall receive such-and-such,” and similar statements.

Another view holds that he may not award more than a third, nor make an additional award except through a prior stipulation. These are two positions reported from Ahmad and others. Likewise—according to the correct view—

translated_text:
the ruler may say, “Whatever anyone takes is his,” as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said during the Battle of Badr, if he considers the benefit of doing so to outweigh the harm.

If the ruler collects and distributes the spoils, no one may misappropriate anything from them:

“Whoever misappropriates anything will bring what he misappropriated on the Day of Resurrection.”

Misappropriation is a betrayal of trust. Nor is plundering permissible, for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade it.

If the ruler forgoes collecting and distributing the spoils and gives lawful permission to take from them, whatever anyone takes without transgression becomes lawful for him once its fifth has been deducted. Anything that indicates permission constitutes permission.

If, however, the ruler gives no permission, or gives permission that is not lawful, a person may take the equivalent of what he would receive through distribution, taking care to act justly. Whoever forbids Muslims to collect the spoils under these circumstances, yet allows the ruler to do whatever he wishes with them, has adopted two positions at opposite extremes. Allah’s religion follows a middle course.

A just distribution is to allot one share to a foot soldier and three shares to a mounted fighter with an Arabian horse: one for the fighter and two for his horse. This is how the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, distributed the spoils at Khaybar.

Some jurists hold that a mounted fighter receives two shares. The former view, however, is supported by the authentic Sunnah, and also by the fact that a horse requires upkeep for itself and its groom—and a mounted fighter with his horse is of greater benefit than two foot soldiers.

Some of them hold that Arabian and mixed-breed horses are to be treated equally

The early Muslims kept stallions for combat because of their strength and spirit; mares for raids and night attacks, because they do not give a neigh that would alert the enemy and put them on their guard; and geldings for travel, because of their greater endurance on journeys.

There are transmitted reports and scholarly opinions concerning the detailed questions and rulings on spoils. Muslims agree on some of these and disagree on others. This is not the place to discuss them; the purpose here is merely to state the comprehensive principles.

The poor and the needy share a common need for sufficient provision. Zakat is therefore not lawful for a wealthy person or for someone strong and able to earn a living.

(And those employed to administer it) are those who collect it, safeguard it, keep its records, and perform similar duties.

(And those whose hearts are to be reconciled) we shall discuss, if Allah Most High wills, under fay’ revenues.

(And for freeing those in bondage) includes assisting slaves who have contracted to purchase their freedom, ransoming captives, and freeing slaves. This is the strongest opinion concerning this category.

Those in debt are people who have debts they cannot repay. They are given enough to discharge their debts, even if the amount is large, unless they incurred them in disobedience to Allah Most High; in that case, they are not given anything until they repent.

(And in the cause of Allah) refers to fighters who are not given enough from Allah’s funds to meet the needs of their campaigns. They are given what they need to campaign, or enough to make up the shortfall, whether in horses, weapons, expenses, or wages. Hajj also falls within the cause of Allah, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said.

(And the wayfarer) is someone travelling from one land to another.

Section

As for fay’, its basis is what Allah Most High mentioned in Sūrat al-Hashr, which He revealed concerning the expedition against Banū al-Nadīr after Badr, beginning with His words:

“Whatever Allah bestowed upon His Messenger from them—you spurred neither horses nor camels to obtain it, but Allah gives His messengers power

over whom He wills. And Allah has power over all things.”

“Whatever Allah has bestowed upon His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah, the Messenger, his close relatives, orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer, so that wealth may not circulate solely among the rich among you. Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it. And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in punishment.”

“It is for the poor Emigrants who were driven from their homes and possessions, seeking Allah’s bounty and pleasure and supporting Allah and His Messenger. They are the ones who are true.”

“And those who had made their home in the city and embraced the faith before their arrival love those who migrate to them. They feel no resentment in their hearts over what the Emigrants have been given, and they give them preference over themselves, even though they too are in need. Those who are protected from their own souls’ stinginess—it is they who will be successful.”

“And those who come after them say, ‘Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and let there be no rancour in our hearts towards those who believe. Our Lord, You are indeed Most Kind, Most Merciful.’”

Thus Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the Emigrants, the Helpers, and those who came after them with the qualities He described. This third category therefore includes everyone who follows this course until the Day of Resurrection, just as they are included in His words, Most High:

“And those who believe afterwards, emigrate, and strive alongside you—they are of you.”

And in His words:

“And those who follow them in righteousness.”

And in His words:

“And others among them who have not yet joined them. And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

For this reason, the jurists say that fay’ is wealth taken from the disbelievers without fighting, since spurring on horses and camels signifies fighting. It is called fay’ because Allah restored it to the Muslims—that is, returned it to them from the disbelievers. The underlying principle is that Allah Most High created wealth only to assist in His worship, just as He created His creatures only to worship Him. He therefore made lawful for His believing servants who worship Him the lives of the disbelievers, which they did not devote to His worship, and their wealth, which they did not use to assist them in His worship. He restored to the believers what was rightfully theirs, just as a man is given back what was wrongfully taken from his inheritance, even if he had never previously received it.

This includes the jizyah levied on Jews and Christians; money that the enemy agrees to pay under a peace settlement or presents to the Muslim ruler, such as payments sent from Christian lands and the like; the one-tenth levy collected from merchants from enemy territories; and the one-twentieth levy collected from merchants of protected non-Muslim communities when they trade outside their own lands. This was how ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, collected these levies. It also includes wealth taken from those among them who break their covenant, and the land tax originally imposed upon them, even if some of it has since come to be borne by some Muslims.

Furthermore, fay’ encompasses all state funds belonging to the Muslim treasury, such as property with no identifiable owner—for example, the estate of a Muslim who dies without an identifiable heir—and wrongfully seized property, articles lent for use, and deposits held in trust:

Allah Most High mentioned only fay’ in the Quran because, during the Prophet’s lifetime, peace and blessings be upon him, no one died without an identifiable heir, since the lineages of his Companions were well known.

On one occasion, a man from a tribe died, and the Prophet gave his estate to the most senior man of that tribe—that is, the one closest in descent to their common ancestor. A number of scholars adopted this position, including Ahmad, in one expressly recorded opinion, and others. Another man died, leaving only his freedman, and the Prophet gave his estate to that freedman. A number of Ahmad’s followers and other scholars adopted this position. He also gave a man’s estate to someone from the same village. He, peace and blessings be upon him, and his successors took a broad approach to giving a deceased person’s estate to someone related to him by descent, as we have mentioned.

He collected nothing from the Muslims except obligatory alms, and he commanded them to strive in Allah’s cause with their wealth and their lives, as Allah commanded in His Book.

During the time of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, there was no comprehensive register of funds received and distributed. translated_text:
most of it; and that register is the most important of the Muslims’ registers. The provincial centres also had registers for land tax, fay’, and other revenues collected. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and his successors would audit their officials’ accounts of obligatory alms, fay’, and other funds.

Thus, in this period and earlier, revenues came to fall into three categories:

One category consists of funds that the ruler is entitled to collect according to the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus, as we have mentioned. Another consists of funds whose collection is unanimously prohibited, such as levies collected from villagers for the public treasury because someone has been killed among them—even when the deceased has an heir—or payments exacted for an offense someone has committed that incurs a prescribed punishment, which is then waived in return. This also includes tolls whose imposition is unanimously held to be unlawful. A third category is subject to juristic judgment and disagreement, such as the estate of someone who has a blood relative who is neither a fixed-share heir nor a residuary heir, and similar cases.

Rulers and subjects frequently wrong one another in these matters: the former take what is unlawful, while the latter withhold what they are obliged to pay, just as soldiers and farmers may wrong one another. Likewise, some people neglect their obligations of striving in Allah’s cause, while rulers hoard wealth belonging to Allah that they are not permitted to hoard. The same applies to punishments used to enforce payment: punishments that are permissible or obligatory may be neglected, while unlawful punishments may be inflicted.

He may be punished until he produces the property or discloses its whereabouts. If the property’s whereabouts are known and he endures imprisonment, what is due is recovered from that property, and there is no need to beat him. If he refuses both to disclose his property’s whereabouts and to pay, he is beaten until he pays what is due or allows it to be recovered. The same applies if he refuses to provide the maintenance obligatory upon him despite being able to afford it.

This is supported by the report of ‘Amr ibn al-Sharīd, from his father, that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Delay by one who has the means to pay makes it lawful to censure and punish him.”

This was narrated by the compilers of the Sunan. He also said, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Delay in payment by one who can afford it is wrongdoing.”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded this in their Sahīhs. “Delay” here means procrastination, and a wrongdoer deserves punishment and discretionary discipline.

This is an agreed-upon principle: anyone who commits a prohibited act or neglects an obligation deserves punishment. If the punishment is not fixed by Islamic law, it is discretionary, determined by the ruler’s judgment. Thus, a debtor who can afford to pay but procrastinates is punished with imprisonment. If he persists, he is punished by beating until he fulfils his obligation. Jurists among the followers of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others—may Allah be pleased with them—have explicitly stated this, and I know of no disagreement concerning it.

Likewise, preferential treatment shown to governors in transactions such as sales, leases, profit-sharing partnerships, orchard-tending partnerships, sharecropping, and the like is a form of gift. The circumstances called for this, for he was a just ruler who distributed equally. When both ruler and subjects changed, however, each person was obliged to fulfill whatever obligations he could, refrain from what was forbidden to him, and not treat as forbidden what Allah had permitted him.

But if the ruler exacts wealth from his officials intending to reserve it for himself and his relatives, neither side should be assisted, for both are wrongdoers. They are like a thief stealing from another thief, or two factions fighting out of partisan loyalty and rivalry for power. It is unlawful for anyone to assist in wrongdoing.

Cooperation is of two kinds:

The first is cooperation in righteousness and piety, such as jihad, enforcing the prescribed punishments, securing people’s rights, and giving those entitled to receive their due. This is something Allah and His Messenger have commanded. Whoever refrains from it for fear of becoming an accomplice of oppressors has abandoned an individual or communal obligation while imagining himself to be exercising religious scrupulousness. How often cowardice and faintheartedness are mistaken for scrupulousness, since both involve abstaining and holding back!

The second is cooperation in sin and aggression, such as helping to take a protected life, seize protected property, beat someone who does not deserve to be beaten, or the like. This is what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden.  فَهُوَ وَكِيلُ الْمَظْلُومِ؛ لَا وَكِيلُ الظَّالِمِ؛ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الَّذِي يُقْرِضُهُ أَوْ الَّذِي يَتَوَكَّلُ فِي حَمْلِ الْمَالِ لَهُ إلَى الظَّالِمِ. مِثَالُ ذَلِكَ وَلِيُّ الْيَتِيمِ وَالْوَقْفِ إذَا طَلَبَ ظَالِمٌ مِنْهُ مَالًا فَاجْتَهَدَ فِي دَفْعِ ذَلِكَ بِمَالِ أَقَلَّ مِنْهُ إلَيْهِ أَوْ إلَى غَيْرِهِ بَعْدَ الِاجْتِهَادِ التَّامِّ فِي الدَّفْعِ؛ فَهُوَ مُحْسِنٌ وَمَا عَلَى الْمُحْسِنِينَ مِنْ سَبِيلٍ. وَكَذَلِكَ وَكِيلُ الْمَالِكِ مِنْ الْمُنَادِينَ وَالْكُتَّابِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ الَّذِي يَتَوَكَّلُ لَهُمْ فِي الْعَقْدِ وَالْقَبْضِ وَدَفْعِ مَا يُطْلَبُ مِنْهُمْ؛ لَا يَتَوَكَّلُ لِلظَّالِمِينَ فِي الْأَخْذِ.
 كَذَلِكَ لَوْ وُضِعَتْ مَظْلِمَةٌ عَلَى أَهْلِ قَرْيَةٍ أَوْ دَرْبٍ أَوْ سُوقٍ أَوْ مَدِينَةٍ فَتَوَسَّطَ رَجُلٌ مِنْهُمْ مُحْسِنٌ فِي الدَّفْعِ عَنْهُمْ بِغَايَةِ الْإِمْكَانِ وَقَسَّطَهَا بَيْنَهُمْ عَلَى قَدْرِ طَاقَتِهِمْ مِنْ غَيْرِ مُحَابَاةٍ لِنَفْسِهِ وَلَا لِغَيْرِهِ وَلَا ارْتِشَاءٍ بَلْ تَوَكَّلَ لَهُمْ فِي الدَّفْعِ عَنْهُمْ وَالْإِعْطَاءِ:
 كَانَ مُحْسِنًا؛ لَكِنَّ الْغَالِبَ أَنَّ مَنْ يَدْخُلُ فِي ذَلِكَ يَكُونُ وَكِيلُ الظَّالِمِينَ مُحَابِيًا مُرْتَشِيًا مَخْفَرًا لِمَنْ يُرِيدُ وَآخِذًا مِمَّنْ يُرِيدُ. وَهَذَا مِنْ أَكْبَرِ الظَّلَمَةِ الَّذِينَ يُحْشَرُونَ فِي تَوَابِيتَ مِنْ نَارٍ هُمْ وَأَعْوَانُهُمْ وَأَشْبَاهُهُمْ ثُمَّ يُقْذَفُونَ فِي النَّارِ.
translated_text:
helps an oppressed person lessen the injustice inflicted upon him or pay an unjust exaction is acting as the agent of the oppressed, not of the oppressor. He is like someone who lends the oppressed person money or undertakes to carry his money to the oppressor on his behalf.

For example, if an oppressor demands money from the guardian of an orphan or the administrator of an endowment, and, after exhausting his efforts to resist the demand, he strives to avert it by paying a smaller sum to the oppressor or to someone else, then he is doing good:

“There is no blame upon those who do good.”

The same applies to an owner’s agent—whether an auctioneer, a scribe, or someone else—who acts on owners’ behalf in concluding contracts, receiving payments, and paying what is demanded of them, rather than acting for the oppressors in collecting it.

Likewise, if an unjust levy is imposed on the people of a village, street, marketplace, or city, and a well-meaning man from among them intervenes to ward it off as far as possible, apportioning it among them according to their means, without favoring himself or anyone else and without accepting bribes, but instead acting on their behalf in resisting the demand and making payment, then he is doing good.

Usually, however, someone who becomes involved in this acts as an agent of the oppressors, showing favoritism, accepting bribes, shielding whomever he wishes, and taking money from whomever he wishes. Such a person is among the worst oppressors, who will be gathered in coffins of fire, together with their helpers and others like them, and then hurled into the Fire.

فَصْلٌ:
وَأَمَّا الْمَصَارِفُ:
 فَالْوَاجِبُ أَنْ يَبْدَأَ فِي الْقِسْمَةِ بِالْأَهَمِّ فَالْأَهَمِّ مِنْ مَصَالِحِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ الْعَامَّةِ: كَعَطَاءِ مَنْ يَحْصُلُ لِلْمُسْلِمِينَ بِهِ مَنْفَعَةٌ عَامَّةٌ.
 فَمِنْهُمْ الْمُقَاتِلَةُ:
 الَّذِينَ هُمْ أَهْلُ النُّصْرَةِ وَالْجِهَادِ وَهُمْ أَحَقُّ النَّاسِ بِالْفَيْءِ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَحْصُلُ إلَّا بِهِمْ؛
 حَتَّى اخْتَلَفَ الْفُقَهَاءُ فِي مَالِ الْفَيْءِ:
 هَلْ هُوَ مُخْتَصٌّ بِهِمْ أَوْ مُشْتَرَكٌ فِي جَمِيعِ الْمَصَالِحِ؟ وَأَمَّا سَائِرُ الْأَمْوَالِ السُّلْطَانِيَّةِ فَلِجَمِيعِ الْمَصَالِحِ وِفَاقًا إلَّا مَا خُصَّ بِهِ نَوْعٌ كَالصَّدَقَاتِ وَالْمَغْنَمِ.
 وَمِنْ الْمُسْتَحَقِّينَ ذَوُو الْوِلَايَاتِ عَلَيْهِمْ:
 كَالْوُلَاةِ وَالْقُضَاةِ وَالْعُلَمَاءِ وَالسُّعَاةِ عَلَى الْمَالِ: جَمْعًا وَحِفْظًا وَقِسْمَةً وَنَحْوَ ذَلِكَ. حَتَّى أَئِمَّةُ الصَّلَاةِ وَالْمُؤَذِّنِينَ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ.
 وَكَذَا صَرْفُهُ فِي الْأَثْمَانِ وَالْأُجُورِ لِمَا يَعُمُّ نَفْعُهُ:
 مِنْ سَدَادِ الثُّغُورِ بِالْكُرَاعِ وَالسِّلَاحِ وَعِمَارَةِ مَا يَحْتَاجُ إلَى عِمَارَتِهِ مِنْ طُرُقَاتِ النَّاسِ: كَالْجُسُورِ وَالْقَنَاطِرِ وَطُرُقَاتِ الْمِيَاهِ كَالْأَنْهَارِ.
 وَمِنْ الْمُسْتَحَقِّينَ:
 ذَوُو الْحَاجَاتِ؛ فَإِنَّ الْفُقَهَاءَ قَدْ اخْتَلَفُوا هَلْ يُقَدَّمُونَ
translated_text:
Section: Expenditure

In distributing funds, priority must be given to the most important public interests of the Muslims, then to the next most important, such as providing stipends to those whose work benefits Muslims generally.

These include the fighting forces, who provide military support and wage jihad. They have the strongest claim to fay revenues, since these are obtained only through them. Indeed, the jurists have differed over whether fay revenues are reserved exclusively for them or may be allocated to all public interests. As for other state revenues, there is agreement that they serve all public interests, except for funds earmarked for particular categories, such as zakat and spoils of war.

Those entitled to receive funds also include people entrusted with the Muslims’ affairs, such as governors, judges, scholars, and officials responsible for collecting, safeguarding, and distributing funds, and similar duties. This extends to prayer leaders, muezzins, and others in comparable roles.

Funds may likewise be spent on purchases and wages for works of general benefit: securing frontier posts with mounts and weapons, maintaining public thoroughfares that require maintenance—including bridges and arched bridges—and waterways such as rivers.

Those entitled to receive funds also include people in need, for the jurists have differed over whether they should be given priority

original_text:
فِي غَيْرِ الصَّدَقَاتِ مِنْ الْفَيْءِ وَنَحْوِهِ عَلَى غَيْرِهِمْ؟

 فَجَعَلَهُمْ عُمَرُ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ أَرْبَعَةَ أَقْسَامٍ:
 الْأَوَّلُ: ذَوُو السَّوَابِقِ الَّذِينَ بِسَابِقَتِهِمْ حَصَلَ الْمَالُ.

 مَنْ يُغْنِي عَنْ الْمُسْلِمِينَ فِي جَلْبِ الْمَنَافِعِ لَهُمْ كَوُلَاةِ الْأُمُورِ وَالْعُلَمَاءِ الَّذِينَ يَجْتَلِبُونَ لَهُمْ مَنَافِعَ الدِّينِ وَالدُّنْيَا.
 الثَّالِثُ:
 مَنْ يُبْلِي بَلَاءً حَسَنًا فِي دَفْعِ الضَّرَرِ عَنْهُمْ كَالْمُجَاهِدِينَ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ مِنْ الْأَجْنَادِ وَالْعُيُونِ مِنْ الْقُصَّادِ وَالنَّاصِحِينَ وَنَحْوِهِمْ.
 الرَّابِعُ:
 ذَوُو الْحَاجَاتِ. وَإِذَا حَصَلَ مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ مُتَبَرِّعٌ فَقَدْ أَغْنَى اللَّهُ بِهِ؛ وَإِلَّا أُعْطِيَ مَا يَكْفِيهِ أَوْ قَدْرَ عَمَلِهِ. إذَا عَرَفْت أَنَّ الْعَطَاءَ يَكُونُ بِحَسَبِ مَنْفَعَةِ
translated_text:
over others when allocating revenues other than zakat, such as fay and similar funds. There are two views on this in the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. Some hold that they should be given priority; others hold that entitlement to these funds rests on being Muslim, so Muslims share in them just as heirs share in an inheritance. The correct view is that those in need should be given priority, for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to give them priority, as he did when distributing the wealth of Banū al-Nadīr. Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“No one has a greater right to this wealth than anyone else. What matters is a man’s precedence in Islam, the benefit he brings, the efforts he makes, and his need.”

Thus Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, divided them into four categories:

First: those with precedence in Islam, through whose early efforts the funds were acquired.

Second: those who serve the Muslims by securing benefits for them, such as rulers and scholars who bring them religious and worldly benefits.

Third: those who render valuable service in warding off harm from them, such as those who strive in Allah’s cause: soldiers, intelligence agents among emissaries and sincere advisers, and others like them.

Fourth: those in need.

If any of these people serves without payment, Allah has met the need through him. Otherwise, he is given enough to suffice him or an amount commensurate with his work. Once you understand that grants are made according to the benefit

الرَّجُلِ وَبِحَسَبِ حَاجَتِهِ فِي مَالِ الْمَصَالِحِ وَفِي الصَّدَقَاتِ أَيْضًا فَمَا زَادَ عَلَى ذَلِكَ لَا يَسْتَحِقُّهُ الرَّجُلُ إلَّا كَمَا يَسْتَحِقُّهُ نُظَرَاؤُهُ مِثْلَ أَنْ يَكُونَ شَرِيكًا فِي غَنِيمَةٍ أَوْ مِيرَاثٍ.
 وَلَا يَجُوزُ لِلْإِمَامِ أَنْ يُعْطِيَ أَحَدًا مَا لَا يَسْتَحِقُّهُ لِهَوَى نَفْسِهِ:

 فَضْلًا عَنْ أَنْ يُعْطِيَهُ لِأَجْلِ مَنْفَعَةٍ مُحَرَّمَةٍ مِنْهُ كَعَطِيَّةِ الْمُخَنَّثِينَ مِنْ الصِّبْيَانِ المردان:
 الْأَحْرَارِ وَالْمَمَالِيكِ وَنَحْوِهِمْ وَالْبَغَايَا وَالْمُغَنِّينَ وَالْمَسَاخِرِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ؛ أَوْ إعْطَاءِ الْعَرَّافِينَ مِنْ الْكُهَّانِ وَالْمُنَجِّمِينَ وَنَحْوِهِمْ. لَكِنْ يَجُوزُ - بَلْ يَجِبُ -
 الْإِعْطَاءُ لِتَأْلِيفِ مَنْ يَحْتَاجُ إلَى تَأْلِيفِ قَلْبِهِ وَإِنْ كَانَ هُوَ لَا يَحِلُّ لَهُ أَخْذُ ذَلِكَ كَمَا أَبَاحَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى فِي الْقُرْآنِ الْعَطَاءَ لِلْمُؤَلَّفَةِ قُلُوبُهُمْ مِنْ الصَّدَقَاتِ وَكَمَا كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يُعْطِي الْمُؤَلَّفَةَ قُلُوبُهُمْ مِنْ الْفَيْءِ وَنَحْوِهِ وَهُمْ السَّادَةُ الْمُطَاعُونَ فِي عَشَائِرِهِمْ كَمَا كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يُعْطِي الْأَقْرَعَ بْنَ حَابِسٍ سَيِّدَ بَنِي تَمِيمٍ وعُيَيْنَة بْنَ حِصْنٍ سَيِّدَ بَنِي فَزَارَةَ وَزَيْدَ الْخَيْرِ الطَّائِيَّ سَيِّدَ بَنِي نَبْهَانَ وَعَلْقَمَةَ بْنَ عُلَاثَةَ الْعَامِرِيَّ سَيِّدَ بَنِي كِلَابٍ وَمِثْلَ سَادَاتِ قُرَيْشٍ مِنْ الطُّلَقَاءِ:
 كَصَفْوَانَ بْنِ أُمَيَّةَ وَعِكْرِمَةَ بْنِ أَبِي جَهْلٍ وَأَبِي سُفْيَانَ بْنِ حَرْبٍ وَسُهَيْلِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو وَالْحَارِثِ بْنِ هِشَامٍ وَعَدَدٍ كَثِيرٍ.
 فَفِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْ أَبِي سَعِيدٍ الخدري رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَ:
translated_text:
a man brings and his need, from funds for public welfare as well as from zakat, then he is entitled to anything beyond that only on the same basis as his peers—for example, when he shares in war booty or an inheritance.

The ruler may not give anyone something to which he is not entitled merely out of personal inclination, because of kinship, affection or the like. Still less may he give it in return for an unlawful service, as in payments to effeminate, beardless boys, whether free or enslaved, and others like them; to prostitutes, singers, jesters and the like; or to fortune-tellers, such as soothsayers, astrologers and others like them.

However, it is permissible—indeed, obligatory—to give money to win over those whose hearts need to be won over, even if it is not lawful for the recipient to accept it. Thus Allah Most High has permitted in the Quran that zakat be given to those whose hearts are to be won over. Likewise, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to give such people grants from fay and similar revenues. These were leaders whose tribes obeyed them. For example, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to give to al-Aqraʿ ibn Hābis, chief of Banū Tamīm; ʿUyaynah ibn Hisn, chief of Banū Fazārah; Zayd al-Khayr al-Tāʾī, chief of Banū Nabhān; and ʿAlqamah ibn ʿUlāthah al-ʿĀmirī, chief of Banū Kilāb. He also gave to leaders of Quraysh who had been granted amnesty, such as Safwān ibn Umayyah, ʿIkrimah ibn Abī Jahl, Abū Sufyān ibn Harb, Suhayl ibn ʿAmr, al-Hārith ibn Hishām and many others.

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, may Allah be pleased with him, reported:

translated_text:
“While in Yemen, ʿAlī sent the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, a small piece of gold still mixed with its earth. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, divided it among four men: al-Aqraʿ ibn Hābis al-Hanzalī, ʿUyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazārī, ʿAlqamah ibn ʿUlāthah al-ʿĀmirī, chief of Banū Kilāb, and Zayd al-Khayr al-Tāʾī, chief of Banū Nabhān.

He said: “Quraysh and the Ansār became angry and said, ‘He gives to the chiefs of Najd and leaves us out!’ The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said, ‘I did that only to win their hearts.’ Then a man came with a thick beard, prominent cheekbones, deep-set eyes, a protruding forehead and a shaved head. He said, ‘Fear Allah, Muhammad!’ The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, replied, ‘Who would fear Allah if I disobeyed Him? Does He entrust me with the people of the earth, yet you do not trust me?’”

He said: “Then the man turned away, and one of those present asked permission to kill him—they believed it was Khālid ibn al-Walīd. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said, ‘From this man’s stock will come people who recite the Quran, but it will not go beyond their throats. They will kill the people of Islam and leave the idolaters alone. They will pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. If I encounter them, I shall surely slay them as ʿĀd were slain.’”

Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj, may Allah be pleased with him, reported:

“The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, gave Abū Sufyān ibn Harb, Safwān ibn Umayyah, ʿUyaynah ibn Hisn and al-Aqraʿ ibn Hābis one hundred camels each. He gave ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās less than that, whereupon ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās said:

translated_text:
‘Will you divide my share of the spoils and al-ʿUbayd’s
Between ʿUyaynah and al-Aqraʿ?
Neither Hisn nor Hābis
Surpassed Mirdās in the assembly.
Nor was I inferior to either man;
Whoever is lowered today will not be raised.’

He said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, then made his allotment up to one hundred.” Reported by Muslim. Al-ʿUbayd was the name of his horse.

Those whose hearts are to be won over are of two kinds: disbelievers and Muslims. A disbeliever may be given something in the hope of securing a benefit, such as his embracing Islam, or averting his harm if it cannot otherwise be averted. Giving to a Muslim who commands obedience may likewise bring an anticipated benefit: strengthening his commitment to Islam, bringing someone like him to Islam, collecting money from those who will pay only out of fear, inflicting losses on the enemy, or restraining him from harming the Muslims if he cannot otherwise be restrained.

Although this kind of giving may outwardly resemble the practice of kings—giving to leaders while leaving out the weak—deeds are judged by intentions. If the purpose is to serve the interests of the religion and its followers, it belongs to the same category as the giving of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and his caliphs. If the purpose is domination in the land and corruption, it belongs to the same category as Pharaoh’s giving.

It is only those whose religion is corrupt who object to this, such as Dhū al-Khuwaysirah, who objected to the Prophet’s doing so, peace and blessings be upon him, prompting him to say what he said about him. Likewise, his faction, the Khārijites, objected to the actions of the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, through which he sought

Misguided scrupulousness is often confused with cowardice and miserliness, since both involve refraining from something. Thus, avoiding wrongdoing out of fear of Allah Most High may be confused with neglecting the prescribed duties of jihad and spending out of cowardice and miserliness. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The worst qualities in a person are consuming greed and paralyzing cowardice.”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “An authentic hadith.”

Likewise, someone may refrain from acting, believing or pretending that this is scrupulousness, when it is nothing but arrogance and a desire for supremacy. The Prophet’s saying, peace and blessings be upon him,

“Deeds are judged only by intentions,”

is comprehensive and complete. Intention is to a deed what the soul is to the body. After all, both someone prostrating to Allah and someone prostrating to the sun or moon place their foreheads on the ground: their outward forms are identical, yet one is among those nearest to Allah Most High, while the other is among those furthest from Him.

Allah Most High said:

“And urge one another to patience and urge one another to compassion.”

A transmitted report states:

“The best of faith is generosity and patience.”

Caring for people and governing them properly require generosity, meaning giving, and valour, meaning courage. Indeed, neither religious nor worldly affairs can be set right without them. Allah Most High:

“O you who believe, what is the matter with you that, when you are told, ‘Go forth in the cause of Allah,’ you cling heavily to the earth? Are you content with the life of this world rather than the Hereafter? Yet the enjoyment of worldly life is but little compared with the Hereafter.”

“If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and replace you with another people. You will not harm Him at all, and Allah has power over all things.”

Allah Most High also said:

“Here you are, called upon to spend in the cause of Allah, yet some of you are miserly. Whoever is miserly is only miserly at his own expense. Allah is free of all need, while you are the needy. If you turn away, He will replace you with another people, and they will not be like you.”

Allah Most High has also said:

“Those of you who spent and fought before the conquest are not equal to the others. They are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterwards. Yet Allah has promised the finest reward to them all.”

He thus linked the matter to spending, which is generosity, and fighting, which is courage. Likewise, Allah Most High said in more than one place:

“Strive with your wealth and your lives in the cause of Allah.”

He made clear that miserliness is among the major sins in His saying:

“Let not those who withhold what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them. Rather, it is bad for them. On the Day of Resurrection, what they withheld will be fastened around their necks.”

And in His saying:

“Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in the cause of Allah—give them tidings of a painful punishment,”

Hell—an evil destination.” And in His saying, Most High:

“They swear by Allah that they are indeed of you, but they are not of you; rather, they are people who are afraid.”

This is frequently addressed in the Quran and Sunnah, and it is something upon which people everywhere agree. They even say in their popular proverbs:

“He offers neither a spear-thrust nor a bowl of food.”

And they say:

“Neither a horseman nor a notable among the Arabs.”

Yet people have divided into three groups in this regard.

One group is dominated by a love of supremacy in the land and corruption. They give no thought to their ultimate fate in the Hereafter. They consider that authority cannot be maintained without giving, and that giving may be impossible without extracting wealth unlawfully. Thus they become lavish plunderers and lavish givers.

These people say that no one can govern others unless he takes for himself and gives to others. If a scrupulous man assumes office who neither takes nor gives, the leaders become displeased with him and remove him—if they do not also harm him personally or seize his wealth. These people attend to their immediate worldly interests while neglecting the longer-term consequences in both this world and the Hereafter. Their eventual outcome is therefore bad in both worlds, unless repentance or something similar sets their final affairs right.

Another group possesses fear of Allah Most High and religious commitment that restrains them from what they believe to be reprehensible: wronging people and committing forbidden acts. This is good and obligatory. Yet they may also believe that governance cannot be carried out without the forbidden practices of the first group, and so they abstain from it altogether. Their religious commitment may also be accompanied by cowardice, miserliness, or ill temper. Thus they sometimes neglect an obligation whose neglect is

This is the approach of someone who takes nothing for himself and gives nothing to others, and who does not believe in winning over unbelievers and evildoers through money or other benefits. He regards giving to those whose hearts are to be won over as a form of injustice and unlawful giving.

The third group:

The balanced community: those who follow the religion of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and of his successors in authority over people of all ranks until the Day of Resurrection. Their approach is to spend wealth and provide benefits to people—even leaders—as needed to put affairs right, uphold religion, and sustain the worldly affairs necessary for religion. They also exercise personal restraint, refraining from taking even money to which they are entitled. Thus they combine fear of Allah with doing good:

“Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who do good.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Sufyān ibn Harb reported that Heraclius, emperor of the Byzantines, asked him about the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: “What does he command you to do?” He replied: “He commands us to pray, speak truthfully, exercise restraint, and maintain ties of kinship.”

A report states: “Allah revealed to Abraham, His close friend, peace be upon him: ‘Abraham, do you know why I took you as a close friend? Because I saw that giving was dearer to you than taking.’”

What we have discussed concerning provision and giving—generosity and conferring benefits—has its counterpart in patience and anger—courage and warding off harm.

People fall into three groups: those who become angry for their own sake and for their Lord’s sake; those who become angry neither for their own sake nor for their Lord’s sake; and the third, balanced group, who become angry for their Lord’s sake, not their own. Thus, in the two Sahīh collections, ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never struck with his hand any servant of his, any woman, any animal, or anything at all, except when fighting in Allah’s cause; nor

did he ever retaliate for a wrong done to him, unless Allah’s sacred limits were violated. When Allah’s sacred limits were violated, nothing could withstand his anger until he had exacted retribution for Allah’s sake.”

As for those who become angry for their own sake but not their Lord’s, or take for themselves without giving to others, they constitute a fourth group: the worst of creation. Neither religious nor worldly affairs can be set right through them. By contrast, the righteous, who govern in the most complete manner, are those who fulfil their obligations and refrain from what is forbidden. They give whatever serves religion through its giving, take only what is lawful for them, become angry for their Lord’s sake when His prohibitions are violated, and forgo their own rights. Such was the character of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in giving and warding off harm. This is the most perfect conduct, and the closer a person comes to it, the better he is.

Let the Muslim therefore strive to approach it to the best of his ability, then seek Allah’s forgiveness for any shortcoming or negligence, having recognized the perfection of the religion with which Allah Most High sent Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This concerns the words of Allah, Glorified and Exalted:

“Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due.”

And Allah knows best.

Section

As for the words of Allah Most High:

“And when you judge between people, judge with justice.”

Judging between people concerns prescribed punishments and rights, which fall into two categories. The first comprises punishments and rights that do not belong to particular individuals, but benefit Muslims generally or a category of them. All are in need of them.

These are called Allah’s prescribed punishments and Allah’s rights. Examples include the punishments prescribed for highway robbers, thieves, those guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse, and others of their kind, as well as adjudication concerning public funds, charitable endowments, and bequests not designated for particular individuals. These are among the most important responsibilities of governing authorities.

For this reason, ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: “People must have a government, whether righteous or wicked.”

He was asked: “Commander of the Faithful, we understand the righteous kind, but what of the wicked?”

He replied: “Through it, prescribed punishments are enforced, roads are made safe, the enemy is fought, and fay (public revenues) is distributed.”

Rulers must investigate and administer matters in this category without anyone bringing a claim. Likewise, testimony concerning them is given without anyone bringing a claim. The jurists have, however, differed over amputating a thief’s hand: does this require the victim of the theft to claim his property? These punishments must be enforced against the high-born, the lowly, and the weak. It is unlawful to suspend them because of intercession, a gift, or anything else, and interceding to prevent their enforcement is unlawful. Whoever suspends them for such reasons, despite being able to enforce them, incurs the curse of Allah, the angels, and all mankind. Allah will accept neither sarf nor ‘adl from him, and he is among those who have traded Allah’s revelations for a paltry price.

Abū Dāwūd narrated in his Sunan that ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever intercedes to prevent the enforcement of one of Allah’s prescribed punishments has opposed Allah in His command. Whoever knowingly argues in support of falsehood remains under Allah’s wrath until he desists. Whoever falsely attributes something to a devout Muslim will be confined in Radghat al-Khabāl until he clears himself of what he said.”

He was asked: “Messenger of Allah, what is Radghat al-Khabāl?”

He replied: “The discharge from the inhabitants of the Fire.”

Thus, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, mentioned adjudicators, witnesses, and litigants: these are the pillars of adjudication.

There is a lesson in this account. The two noblest clans in Quraysh were Banū Makhzūm and Banū ‘Abd Manāf. This woman’s theft warranted the amputation of her hand—her theft being, according to some scholars, her denial of having borrowed property, or, according to others, a separate act of theft. Although she belonged to one of the greatest tribes and noblest families, when Usāmah, the beloved of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, interceded for her, the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, became angry. He rebuked him for involving himself in something Allah had forbidden: interceding to prevent the enforcement of prescribed punishments. He then gave the example of the foremost of all women—whom Allah had declared innocent of such wrongdoing—saying:

“If Fātimah, the daughter of Muhammad, were to steal, I would cut off her hand.”

It is reported that this woman whose hand was cut off repented, and that she would subsequently visit the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who would attend to her needs.

It is also reported:

“If the thief repents, his hand precedes him into Paradise; if he does not repent, his hand precedes him into the Fire.”

Mālik related in al-Muwatta’ that a group of people seized a thief to bring him before ‘Uthmān, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Zubayr met them and interceded for him. They said, “When he is brought before ‘Uthmān, intercede for him with him.” He replied:

“If cases involving prescribed punishments reach the ruler, may Allah curse both the intercessor and the one who grants the intercession!”

He meant the person who accepts the intercession.

translated_text:
Umayyah was sleeping on a cloak of his in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, when a thief came and stole it. He seized the thief, who was brought before the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. The Prophet ordered that his hand be cut off. Safwān said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, would you cut off his hand over my cloak? I give it to him.’ He replied, ‘Why did you not do that before bringing him to me?’ Then he had his hand cut off.” Reported by the compilers of the Sunan.

He, peace and blessings be upon him, meant that pardoning the thief before bringing him would have been permissible, but not after the matter had been brought before him. Thus, a prescribed punishment may not be set aside through pardon, intercession, a gift, or any other means. For this reason, the scholars agree—as far as I know—that when highway robbers, thieves, and others like them are brought before the ruler and subsequently repent, the prescribed punishment is not waived. Rather, it must be carried out even if they repent. If their repentance is sincere, the punishment serves as an expiation for them, and their submitting to it completes their repentance—just as one must restore people’s rights and submit to legal retribution for violations of human rights.

The basis for this is Allah’s saying:

“Whoever intercedes for a good cause will have a share in it, and whoever intercedes for an evil cause will bear a share of it. Allah is ever a Keeper over all things.”

Intercession means assisting a petitioner, joining him so that they become a pair where previously he stood alone. If someone assists him in righteousness and piety, that is good intercession; if he assists him in sin and aggression, that is evil intercession. Righteousness is what one is commanded to do, and sin is what one is forbidden to do. If, however, they are lying about their repentance, Allah does not bring the schemes of the treacherous to success.

translated_text:
Allah Most High has also said:

“The punishment of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive to spread corruption in the land is that they be killed, crucified, have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be banished from the land. That is their disgrace in this world, and in the Hereafter they will suffer a tremendous punishment.”

“Except those who repent before you apprehend them. Know, then, that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

He thus excepted only those who repent before being apprehended. Anyone who repents after being apprehended remains among those subject to the prescribed punishment, as indicated by the general wording, its implied meaning, and the underlying rationale. This applies when the offence has been established by evidence.

If, however, it is established through a confession, and the person comes forward confessing the sin in repentance, there is a disagreement concerning this, discussed elsewhere. The apparent position of Ahmad’s school is that carrying out the prescribed punishment is not obligatory in such a case. Rather, if the person requests that it be carried out on him, it is carried out; but if he leaves, no prescribed punishment is inflicted on him. This is how the report concerning Mā‘iz ibn Mālik—in which the Prophet said, “Why did you not let him go?”—has been understood, as has the report of the man who said, “I have committed an offence requiring a prescribed punishment, so carry it out on me,” along with other reports.

In the Sunan collections of Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasā’ī, ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Amr reports that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Pardon one another for offences requiring prescribed punishments before bringing them to me. Once such a case reaches me, its punishment becomes obligatory.”

In the Sunan collections of al-Nasā’ī and Ibn Mājah, Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, reports that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“A prescribed punishment carried out on earth is better for its inhabitants than forty mornings of rain.”

This is because sins cause a reduction in provision and fear of the enemy, as the Quran and Sunnah indicate. Thus, when

It is not permissible to take money from someone guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, drinking intoxicants, highway robbery, or similar offences in exchange for suspending the prescribed punishments—whether for the public treasury or anyone else.

Money taken to suspend a prescribed punishment is vile, unlawful gain. If the ruler does this, he combines two grave evils: suspending the prescribed punishment and consuming unlawful gain. He thus neglects an obligation and commits a forbidden act. Allah Most High says:

“Why do the rabbis and religious scholars not forbid them from saying what is sinful and devouring what is unlawful? How wretched is what they have been practicing.”

Allah Most High also says concerning the Jews:

“Avid listeners to falsehood, devourers of unlawful gain.”

This is because they consumed unlawful gains from bribes, known as birtīl and sometimes called gifts or other names. Whenever the ruler consumes unlawful gain, he finds himself needing to listen to lies in the form of false testimony and the like. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, “cursed the giver of a bribe, its recipient, and the go-between—the intermediary between them.” This is reported by the compilers of the Sunan collections.

 مِنْ الْأَعْرَابِ وَالتُّرْكُمَانِ وَالْأَكْرَادِ وَالْفَلَّاحِينَ وَأَهْلِ الْأَهْوَاءِ كَقَيْسِ وَيَمَنَ وَأَهْلِ الْحَاضِرَةِ مِنْ رُؤَسَاءِ النَّاسِ وَأَغْنِيَائِهِمْ وَفُقَرَائِهِمْ وَأُمَرَاءِ النَّاسِ وَمُقَدِّمِيهِمْ وَجُنْدِهِمْ وَهُوَ سَبَبُ سُقُوطِ حُرْمَةِ الْمُتَوَلِّي وَسُقُوطِ قَدْرِهِ مِنْ الْقُلُوبِ وَانْحِلَالِ أَمْرِهِ فَإِذَا ارْتَشَى وَتَبَرْطَلَ عَلَى تَعْطِيلِ حَدٍّ ضَعُفَتْ نَفْسُهُ أَنْ يُقِيمَ حَدًّا آخَرَ
translated_text:
this man—meaning a hired worker—and he had unlawful intercourse with his wife. I ransomed him with a hundred sheep and a servant. I asked some men of learning, and they told me that my son was liable to a hundred lashes and banishment for a year, and that this man’s wife was liable to stoning.’

He said, ‘By Him in whose hand is my soul, I shall certainly judge between you according to the Book of Allah. The hundred sheep and the servant must be returned to you. Your son shall receive a hundred lashes and be banished for a year. Go in the morning, O Unays, to this man’s wife and question her. If she confesses, stone her.’ He questioned her, and she confessed, so he stoned her.”

This hadith shows that when this money was paid on the offender’s behalf to spare him the prescribed punishment, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, ordered that the money be returned to its owner and that the prescribed punishment be carried out. He did not take the money for the Muslims, whether those fighting in Allah’s cause, the poor, or others. The Muslims unanimously agree that suspending a prescribed punishment in exchange for money or otherwise is impermissible. They also unanimously agree that money taken from those guilty of unlawful sexual intercourse, theft, drinking intoxicants, armed aggression, highway robbery, or similar offences in exchange for suspending the prescribed punishment is vile, unlawful gain.

Much of the corruption in people’s affairs arises from suspending prescribed punishments in exchange for money or through influence. This is one of the chief causes of corruption among the inhabitants of the deserts, villages, and cities: the Bedouins, Turkomans, Kurds, peasants, and partisans such as Qays and Yaman; and among urban people, including their leaders, rich and poor, rulers, commanders, and soldiers. It causes the official in authority to lose people’s respect, diminishes his standing in their hearts, and undermines his authority. When he accepts bribes and payments to suspend one prescribed punishment, his resolve to enforce another is weakened

translated_text:
and he becomes like the accursed Jews.

The word birtīl originally means an elongated stone. A bribe was given this name because it stops the recipient’s mouth from speaking the truth, just as a long stone would. As a report states:

“When bribery enters through the door, trustworthiness leaves through the window.”

The same applies when money is taken for the state in exchange for suspending a prescribed punishment, such as these unlawful payments called “disciplinary fines.” Do you not see how, when troublemaking Bedouins take people’s property and then come to the ruler, leading horses to present to him, or bringing other gifts, their eagerness to spread corruption grows, respect for the governing authority and its power is undermined, and the subjects become corrupt?

The same applies to peasants and others. Likewise, when someone who drinks intoxicants is caught and pays some of his money, see how emboldened the wine dealers become! They hope that, if caught, they too can buy their release with some of their wealth. That governor then takes it as unlawful gain, devoid of blessing, while the corruption continues.

The same applies to influential people who protect someone from having a prescribed punishment carried out against him. For example, a peasant may commit an offence and then seek refuge in a village belonging to the sultan’s deputy or one of his commanders, where he is protected in defiance of Allah and His Messenger. The person who protects him is then among those whom Allah and His Messenger have cursed. Muslim narrated in his Sahīh from ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“May Allah curse whoever commits an offence or shelters an offender.”

Thus, whoever shelters any of these offenders

translated_text:
has been cursed by Allah and His Messenger.

If the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever intercedes to prevent one of Allah’s prescribed punishments from being carried out has opposed Allah’s command,”

then what of someone who prevents these punishments through his power and direct intervention, accepting unlawful money in exchange for shielding criminals? This applies especially to prescribed punishments against desert dwellers. Among the greatest causes of corruption among them is protecting their transgressors through influence or money. Whether the money is taken for the public treasury or for the governor, secretly or openly, all of this is forbidden by Muslim consensus. It is akin to tadmīn (financial arrangements) involving taverns and wine. Anyone who is enabled to do this, or who helps another do it in return for money he receives, falls into the same category.

Money taken in this way resembles a prostitute’s earnings, a soothsayer’s fee, the price paid for a dog, and the payment received by someone who facilitates unlawful sexual relations—the person called a procurer. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The price paid for a dog is foul, a prostitute’s earnings are foul, and a soothsayer’s fee is foul.”

Narrated by al-Bukhārī. A prostitute’s earnings are what is called hudūr al-qihāb. The same applies to money given to effeminate boys, whether enslaved or free, in return for committing sexual immorality with them. A soothsayer’s fee includes such things as the gratuity given to an astrologer or someone similar for what he claims to be good news, and other such reports.

When a ruler refrains from opposing wrongdoing and enforcing the prescribed punishments for it in return for money he receives, he becomes like a bandit chief who shares the plunder with highway robbers, or a procurer who takes his payment to bring two people together for an act of sexual immorality,

and his conduct resembles that of the wicked old woman, Lot’s wife, who directed evildoers to his guests. Concerning her, Allah Most High said:

“So We saved him and his family, except his wife; she was among those who remained behind.”

And He said:

“So set out with your family during a portion of the night, and let none of you look back, except your wife; she will indeed suffer what they suffer.”

Thus Allah punished that wicked old woman, who acted as a procuress, with the same punishment He inflicted upon the wicked people who perpetrated vile deeds. This is because all such conduct amounts to taking money to assist in sin and transgression. A ruler is appointed only to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong: this is the purpose of authority. If a governor enables wrongdoing in return for money he receives, he acts in direct opposition to that purpose. He is like someone you appoint to help you against your enemy, only for him to help your enemy against you, or someone who takes money to wage jihad in Allah’s cause, then uses it to fight the Muslims.

This becomes clear when we consider that people’s well-being depends on enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. For the well-being of people and their livelihoods lies in obedience to Allah and His Messenger, and this cannot be fully achieved without enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. It is through this that this community became the best community brought forth for humanity. Allah Most High said:

“You are the best community brought forth for humanity: you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.”

And He said:

“Let there be among you a group who call to goodness, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong.”

And He said:

“The believing men and believing women are allies of one another: they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.”

And He said concerning the Children of Israel:

“They would not forbid one another

from the wrongdoing they committed. Evil indeed was what they used to do.”

And Allah Most High said:

“When they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil and seized the wrongdoers with a terrible punishment for their defiance.”

Allah Most High thus tells us that when the punishment descended, He saved those who forbade evil and subjected the wrongdoers to severe punishment.

An authentic hadith relates that Abū Bakr al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, addressed the people from the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, saying:

“O people, you recite this verse but apply it incorrectly: ‘O you who believe, take care of yourselves. Those who go astray will not harm you if you are rightly guided.’ Yet I heard the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, say: ‘When people see wrongdoing and do not change it, Allah may soon encompass them all with a punishment from Him.’”

Another hadith states:

“When a sin is committed secretly, it harms only the one who commits it. But when it becomes public and is not condemned, it harms the community at large.”

The foremost purpose of this category of adjudication concerning Allah’s prescribed limits and His rights, which we have discussed, is to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.

Enjoining what is right includes enjoining prayer, zakāh, fasting, pilgrimage, truthfulness, trustworthiness, dutifulness to parents, maintaining ties of kinship, treating one’s family and neighbours well, and similar matters. The ruler must therefore command everyone under his authority to perform the obligatory prayers and punish anyone who neglects them, according to the consensus of the Muslims.

translated_text:
If those who neglect the prayers form a group that resists enforcement, they are to be fought for abandoning them, by the consensus of the Muslims. Likewise, they are to be fought for abandoning zakāh, fasting and other obligations, and for declaring lawful manifest prohibitions agreed upon by consensus, such as marrying women within the prohibited degrees of kinship, spreading corruption in the land, and similar acts. Every group that collectively resists compliance with any of Islam’s manifest ordinances established by mass transmission must be fought until religion is wholly for Allah, according to the agreement of the scholars.

If the person who neglects prayer is an individual, one view holds that he is to be punished by beating and imprisonment until he prays. The majority of scholars, however, hold that he must be executed if he refuses to pray after being called upon to repent. If he repents and prays, he is spared; otherwise, he is executed. Is he executed as a disbeliever or as a sinful Muslim? There are two views on this. Most of the early Muslim generations held that he is executed as a disbeliever. All of this concerns someone who acknowledges that prayer is obligatory. If, however, he denies its obligation, he is a disbeliever by the consensus of the Muslims. The same applies to anyone who denies the other obligations mentioned above or denies the prohibitions over which fighting is required.

Punishment for abandoning obligations and committing prohibited acts is thus the purpose of jihad in Allah’s cause. Jihad is obligatory upon the Muslim community by agreement, as indicated by the Quran and Sunnah, and it is among the best deeds.

A man said:

“O Messenger of Allah, direct me to a deed equal to jihad in Allah’s cause.”

He replied:

“You cannot do it,” or, “You would not be able to bear it.”

The man said:

“Tell me what it is.”

He replied:

“Can you, when the fighter sets out, fast without breaking your fast

and pray without flagging?”

The man said:

“Who could do that?”

He replied:

“That, then, is what equals jihad in Allah’s cause.”

He also said:

“In Paradise there are indeed a hundred ranks, with a distance like that between heaven and earth between each rank and the next. Allah has prepared them for those who wage jihad for His cause.”

Both hadiths are recorded in the two Sahīh collections. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The foundation of the matter is Islam, its pillar is prayer, and its pinnacle is jihad in Allah’s cause.”

Allah Most High said:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then never doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in Allah’s cause. It is they who are truthful.”

He Most High also said:

“Do you consider providing water to pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque equal to believing in Allah and the Last Day and striving in Allah’s cause? They are not equal in Allah’s sight, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.”

“Those who believe, emigrate, and strive in Allah’s cause with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank with Allah. It is they who are successful.”

“Their Lord gives them good news of mercy from Him, His pleasure, and gardens in which they will have lasting bliss.”

“They will remain there forever. Indeed, with Allah is a great reward.”

“The penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and strive to spread corruption in the land is that they be executed or crucified, or have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be banished from the land. Al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah have mercy on him, narrated in his Musnad that Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said concerning highway robbers:

“If they kill and seize property, they are executed and crucified. If they kill without seizing property, they are executed but not crucified. This is the view of many scholars, including al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, and it is close to the view of Abū Hanīfah, may Allah have mercy on him.

Some scholars hold that the ruler may exercise his judgment concerning them: he may execute anyone whose execution he considers beneficial, even if that person has not killed anyone—for example, a leader whose orders are obeyed in such activities. He may likewise order amputation for anyone whose amputation he considers beneficial, even if that person has not taken any property—for example, someone with the stamina and strength to seize property. Some scholars also hold that when they seize property, they are executed, subjected to amputation, and crucified. The first view is that of the majority.

If an armed aggressor has killed someone, the ruler must execute him as a prescribed punishment. By scholarly consensus, he may under no circumstances be pardoned. Ibn al-Mundhir reported this consensus. Nor is the decision in his case left to the heirs of the person killed. In that case, the decision concerning the killer’s life rests with the victim’s legal heirs: they may have him executed, pardon him, or accept blood money, because he killed for a personal purpose. Armed robbers, however, kill in order to seize people’s property, so their harm affects the public, like that of thieves. Their execution is therefore a prescribed punishment owed to Allah. This is agreed upon among the jurists. They have differed, however, over whether a person is to be executed for armed robbery even when the victim is not of equivalent legal status to the killer—for example, when the killer is free and the victim enslaved, or the killer is Muslim and the victim a non-Muslim under a covenant of protection or someone granted safe-conduct. The stronger view is that he is to be executed as a prescribed punishment because his killing spreads harm throughout society, just as he is subject to amputation for taking their property and imprisonment to enforce their rights.

When armed robbers form a group, and one of them personally commits the killing while the others assist and support him, one view holds that only the actual killer is executed. The majority, however, hold that all of them are executed, even if they number a hundred, and that those providing support and the actual killer are treated alike. This is what has been transmitted from the Rightly Guided Caliphs: ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, executed the lookout of a band of armed robbers. The lookout is the observer who sits in an elevated position to watch for anyone approaching them. Moreover, the actual killer was only able to commit the killing through the strength and assistance of those supporting him. When members of a group reinforce one another until they can resist being subdued, they share in both reward and punishment, as do those who fight in Allah’s cause. {الْمُسْلِمُونَ تَتَكَافَأُ دِمَاؤُهُمْ وَيَسْعَى بِذِمَّتِهِمْ أَدْنَاهُمْ وَهُمْ يَدٌ عَلَى مَنْ سِوَاهُمْ وَيَرُدُّ مُتَسَرِّيهِمْ عَلَى قَاعِدِهِمْ}
 . يَعْنِي أَنَّ جَيْشَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ إذَا تَسَرَّتْ مِنْهُ سَرِيَّةٌ فَغَنِمَتْ مَالًا فَإِنَّ الْجَيْشَ يُشَارِكُهَا فِيمَا غَنِمَتْ؛ لِأَنَّهَا بِظَهْرِهِ وَقُوَّتِهِ تَمَكَّنَتْ؛ لَكِنْ تُنَفَّلُ عَنْهُ نَفْلًا؛ فَإِنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَانَ يُنَفِّلُ السَّرِيَّةَ إذَا كَانُوا فِي بِدَايَتِهِمْ الرُّبُعُ بَعْدَ الْخُمُسِ فَإِذَا رَجَعُوا إلَى أَوْطَانِهِمْ وَتَسَرَّتْ سَرِيَّةٌ نَفَّلَهُمْ الثُّلُثَ بَعْدَ الْخُمُسِ وَكَذَلِكَ لَوْ غَنِمَ الْجَيْشُ غَنِيمَةً شَارَكَتْهُ السَّرِيَّةُ لِأَنَّهَا فِي مَصْلَحَةِ الْجَيْشِ كَمَا قَسَمَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لِطَلْحَةِ وَالزُّبَيْرِ يَوْمَ بَدْرٍ؛ لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ قَدْ بَعَثَهُمَا فِي مَصْلَحَةِ الْجَيْشِ فَأَعْوَانُ الطَّائِفَةِ الْمُمْتَنِعَةِ وَأَنْصَارِهَا مِنْهَا فِيمَا لَهُمْ وَعَلَيْهِمْ. وَهَكَذَا الْمُقْتَتِلُونَ عَلَى بَاطِلٍ لَا تَأْوِيلَ فِيهِ؛ مِثْلَ الْمُقْتَتِلِينَ عَلَى عَصَبِيَّةِ وَدَعْوَى جَاهِلِيَّةٍ؛ كَقَيْسِ وَيُمَنِّ وَنَحْوِهِمَا؛ هُمَا ظَالِمَتَانِ. كَمَا قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{إذَا الْتَقَى الْمُسْلِمَانِ بِسَيْفَيْهِمَا فَالْقَاتِلُ وَالْمَقْتُولُ فِي النَّارِ.
 قِيلَ:
 يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ هَذَا الْقَاتِلُ فَمَا بَالُ الْمَقْتُولِ؟
 قَالَ:
 إنَّهُ أَرَادَ قَتْلَ صَاحِبِهِ}
 . أَخْرَجَاهُ فِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ. وَتَضَمَّنَ كُلُّ طَائِفَةٍ مَا أَتْلَفَتْهُ لِلْأُخْرَى مِنْ نَفْسٍ وَمَالٍ. وَإِنْ لَمْ يَعْرِفْ عَيْنَ الْقَاتِلِ؛ لِأَنَّ الطَّائِفَةَ الْوَاحِدَةَ الْمُمْتَنِعَ بَعْضُهَا بِبَعْضِ كَالشَّخْصِ الْوَاحِدِ وَفِي ذَلِكَ قَوْله تَعَالَى 
{كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْقِصَاصُ فِي الْقَتْلَى}
 .
translated_text:
said:

“Muslims’ lives are equally inviolable; protection granted by the lowest in status among them is binding upon them all; they stand united against others; and their raiding detachments share their spoils with those who remain behind.”

This means that when a detachment goes out from the Muslim army and captures spoils, the army shares in those spoils, because the detachment succeeded through its backing and strength. The detachment, however, receives an additional allotment beyond that of the rest of the army. When a detachment went out at the beginning of a campaign, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would award it an additional quarter after the fifth had been set aside. On their return to their homelands, if a detachment went out, he would award it an additional third after the fifth had been set aside.

Likewise, if the army captured spoils, the detachment would share in them, because it was serving the army’s interests. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, allotted shares to Talha and al-Zubayr at Badr because he had sent them on a mission serving the army’s interests. The helpers and supporters of a group able to resist being subdued therefore belong to it, sharing its rights and liabilities.

The same applies to those who fight on wrongful grounds without any interpretive justification, such as those fighting out of tribal partisanship and rallying to the calls of pre-Islamic ignorance—Qays and Yaman, for example, and similar groups: both sides are wrongdoers. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When two Muslims confront one another with their swords, both the killer and the one killed are in the Fire.”

He was asked, “O Messenger of Allah, that is the killer, but why the one killed?”

He replied, “He intended to kill his companion.”

Al-Bukhārī and Muslim both recorded it in their Sahīh collections. Each faction is liable for the lives and property it has destroyed belonging to the other, even if the individual killer is not identified, because a faction whose members strengthen one another to resist being subdued is like a single person. Concerning this, Allah Most High says:

“Prescribed for you is legal retribution for those murdered.”

وَأَمَّا إذَا أَخَذُوا الْمَالَ فَقَطْ وَلَمْ يَقْتُلُوا - كَمَا قَدْ يَفْعَلُهُ الْأَعْرَابُ كَثِيرًا -
