 وَقِيلَ:
 هُوَ حَبْسُهُمْ.
 وَقِيلَ:
 هُوَ مَا يَرَاهُ الْإِمَامُ أَصْلَحَ مِنْ نَفْيٍ أَوْ حَبْسٍ أَوْ نَحْوِ ذَلِكَ.
 وَالْقَتْلُ الْمَشْرُوعُ:
 هُوَ ضَرْبُ الرَّقَبَةِ بِالسَّيْفِ وَنَحْوِهِ لِأَنَّ ذَلِكَ أَرْوَحُ أَنْوَاعِ الْقَتْلِ وَكَذَلِكَ شَرَعَ اللَّهُ قَتْلَ مَا يُبَاحُ قَتْلُهُ مِنْ الْآدَمِيِّينَ وَالْبَهَائِمِ
translated_text:
If, however, they take property without killing anyone—as Bedouins often do—then, according to most scholars, including Abū Hanīfa, Ahmad and others, each offender’s right hand and left foot are to be amputated. This is the meaning of Allah Most High’s words:

“Or that their hands and feet be cut off on opposite sides.”

The hand with which he strikes and the foot on which he walks are amputated. The wounds are cauterized with boiling oil or the like to stop the bleeding, lest continued blood loss cause his death. Likewise, a thief’s amputated hand is cauterized with oil.

This punishment may be a stronger deterrent than execution. When Bedouins, lawless soldiers and others continually see someone among them whose hand and foot have been amputated, they are reminded of his crime and are deterred. An execution, by contrast, may be forgotten. Some proud individuals may prefer being killed to having their hand and foot amputated on opposite sides; thus, this punishment is more severe as an exemplary punishment for them and others like them.

If, however, they brandish weapons without killing anyone or taking any property, then sheathe them or flee and abandon armed aggression, they are to be banished. One view is that banishment means driving them from place to place, without allowing them to settle in any locality. Another is that it means imprisoning them. A third is that the ruler should adopt whichever measure he considers most beneficial, whether banishment, imprisonment or something similar.

The prescribed method of execution is to strike the neck with a sword or a similar implement, because this is the least painful manner of killing. Likewise, Allah has prescribed the killing of those humans and animals that may lawfully be killed

in this manner when one has power over them. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah has prescribed excellence in all things. So when you kill, kill well; and when you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each of you sharpen his blade and spare his animal suffering.”

Narrated by Muslim. He also said:

“The believers are the most restrained of all people in killing.”

As for the crucifixion mentioned, it means raising them up in an elevated place so that people may see them and their case become widely known. According to the majority of scholars, this takes place after execution. Some scholars, however, say that they are crucified and then killed while crucified. Some scholars have permitted killing them by means other than the sword, even saying that they may be left in that elevated place until they die of their own accord, without being killed.

Mutilation in killing, however, is not permissible except as retaliation in kind. ‘Imrān ibn Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never delivered a sermon to us without commanding us to give charity and forbidding us to mutilate. Even when we kill disbelievers, we do not mutilate them after death, cut off their ears and noses, or slit open their bellies—unless they have done that to us, in which case we may do to them as they did to us.”

Yet refraining is better, as Allah Most High says:

“If you retaliate, then retaliate only to the extent that you have suffered. But if you are patient, that is certainly better for those who are patient.”

“And be patient; your patience is only through Allah.”

It is said that this was revealed when the polytheists mutilated Hamza and other martyrs of Uhud, may Allah be pleased with them. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“If Allah grants me victory over them, I will surely inflict twice as much mutilation as they inflicted on us.”

Allah then revealed this verse—although it had already been revealed earlier in Mecca

translated_text:
as with His words:

“And they ask you about the spirit. Say, ‘The spirit is of my Lord’s command.’”

And His words:

“And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds do away with misdeeds.”

The same applies to other verses revealed in Mecca: an occasion subsequently arose in Medina that called for the same address, so they were revealed a second time—the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then said:

“Rather, we shall be patient.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Burayda ibn al-Husayb, may Allah be pleased with him, reported:

“Whenever the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent a commander at the head of a detachment or an army, or on an errand of his own, he would instruct him personally to fear Allah Most High and to treat the Muslims accompanying him well. Then he would say: ‘Go forth in Allah’s name, in Allah’s cause. Fight those who disbelieve in Allah. Do not misappropriate the spoils, act treacherously, mutilate, or kill a child.’”

If they brandish weapons to seize property in a built-up area rather than in the open country, some scholars have said that they are not classed as brigands, but rather as snatch-thieves and plunderers, because help can reach the victim if he calls upon people for assistance.

Most scholars, however, hold that the same ruling applies to them in built-up areas and in the open country. This is the well-known position reported from Mālik, and the position of al-Shāfi‘ī, most of Ahmad’s followers, and some of Abū Hanīfa’s followers. Indeed, they deserve punishment even more in built-up areas than in the open country, because built-up areas are places of safety and tranquillity, where people support and help one another. translated_text:
usually carries only part of his wealth. This is the correct view, particularly in the case of these organized gangs whom ordinary people in Syria and Egypt call al-minsar and who were known in Baghdad as al-ayyārīn. Even if they fight with sticks or stones thrown by hand or with slings and the like, they are still brigands.

Some jurists are reported to have held that brigandage can only be committed with edged weapons. Others have reported a consensus that it can be committed with either edged or blunt weapons. Whether or not there is disagreement on this, the correct view, held by the overwhelming majority of Muslims, is that anyone who fights to seize property, by whatever means of fighting, is a brigand and highway robber. Likewise, any disbeliever who fights Muslims, by whatever means of fighting, is a belligerent; and any Muslim who fights the disbelievers with a sword, spear, arrow, stones, or a stick is fighting in Allah’s cause.

As for someone who kills people secretly to seize their property—for example, someone who rents out an inn to travellers, then kills some of them and takes their property when he is alone with them; or someone who invites into his home a person he has hired for tailoring, medical treatment, or the like, then kills him and takes his property—this is called murder by treachery. Some ordinary people call such killers al-mu‘arrijīn. If their purpose is to seize property, are they treated as brigands, or are they subject to the law of retribution? The jurists hold two views on this.

The first is that they are treated as brigands, because killing through deception is like killing by force: neither can be guarded against. Indeed, the harm of the former may be greater, because one does not

The second view is that a brigand is someone who fights openly, whereas the fate of someone who murders by stealth is left to the victim’s next of kin. The first view is more consistent with the principles of Islamic law. Indeed, the harm of such murder may be greater, because one does not see it coming.

The jurists also differed concerning those who kill the ruler, such as the murderers of ʿUthmān and the murderer of ʿAlī—may Allah be pleased with them both. Are they treated like brigands and executed as a prescribed punishment, or is their fate left to the victims’ next of kin? There are two views within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere, for killing the ruler causes harm to society at large.

Section

All of this applies when they have been brought under control. But if the ruler or his deputies seek to apprehend them to carry out the prescribed punishment without committing any injustice, and they resist him, then the Muslims must fight them, by scholarly consensus, until all of them have been brought under control. If they will submit only through fighting that leads to all of them being killed, they must be fought even if it leads to that outcome, whether or not they have killed anyone.

During the fighting, they may be killed by whatever means are possible, whether by striking the neck or elsewhere. Those who fight alongside them, protecting and assisting them, must also be fought. This is combat, whereas the former is the enforcement of a prescribed punishment. Fighting these people is even more imperative than killing groups that refuse to submit to the laws of Islam.

For these people have banded together to destroy lives and property and ruin crops and offspring; their aim is neither to uphold a religion nor to establish a kingdom.

They are like brigands who take refuge in a fortress, a cave, a mountaintop, a valley bottom, or somewhere similar, robbing those who pass their way. When the ruler’s troops come to bring them into obedience to the Muslims and their collective authority so that the prescribed punishments may be enforced, they fight and repel them. Such are the Bedouins who rob pilgrims or other travellers along the roads, or the mountain dwellers who shelter on mountaintops or in caves to engage in highway robbery. Likewise are the confederates who have allied themselves to rob travellers between Syria and Iraq, calling this “al-nahīda.”

They are to be fought as we have explained. However, fighting them is not equivalent to fighting disbelievers if they are not themselves disbelievers. Nor may their property be seized unless they have wrongfully taken other people’s property. In that case, they are liable to compensate for it, and an amount equal to what they took is recovered from them, even if we do not know the identity of the actual taker. The same applies if his identity is known, for the supporting accomplice and the direct perpetrator are treated alike, as we have stated. When the actual taker is identified, however, ultimate liability rests with him.

Whatever is recovered from them is returned to its rightful owners. If returning it to them proves impossible, it is used for the public interests of the Muslims, including providing for the force fighting them and other such purposes.

Rather, the purpose of fighting them is to bring them under control so that the prescribed punishments may be enforced and they may be prevented from spreading corruption. Thus, if one of them is severely wounded, he must not be finished off and killed

unless he has already incurred the death penalty. If he flees and no longer poses a threat to us, we do not pursue him unless he is liable to a prescribed punishment or we fear the consequences of letting him go. Anyone taken captive among them is subject to the same prescribed punishment as anyone else. Some jurists take a stricter position regarding them, even permitting their property to be taken as spoils of war, with one-fifth set aside; most, however, reject this. But if they join the realm of a group that has departed from the law of Islam and assist that group against the Muslims, they are fought in the same manner as that group.

As for someone who does not commit highway robbery but exacts a protection fee or levy from travellers for each person, animal, load, or the like, he is an unlawful toll collector and is subject to the punishment applicable to such collectors. The jurists have differed over whether he may be put to death. He is not a highway robber, since his activity does not cut off passage along the road, even though he will be among those most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said concerning the woman from Ghāmid:

“She has repented so sincerely that, had an unlawful toll collector repented in this way, he would have been forgiven.”

By the consensus of the Muslims, those subjected to aggression—whose property is being sought—may fight their attackers. They are not obliged to surrender any property to them, whether little or much, if they are able to fight them. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever is killed defending his property is a martyr; whoever is killed defending his life is a martyr; whoever is killed defending his religion is a martyr; and whoever is killed defending his honour is a martyr.”

This is the person whom the jurists call an “assailant”: one who commits aggression without any interpretive justification

or lawful authority. If the assailant seeks property, he may be repelled by whatever means are possible. If he can only be repelled by fighting, he is to be fought. If, instead, the person refrains from fighting and gives the attackers some property, that is permissible.

If, however, the assailant seeks to violate someone’s honour—for example, by seeking illicit intercourse with a person’s female relatives, or seeking to commit a sexual act with a woman, an enslaved boy, or anyone else—the person targeted must defend himself by whatever means possible, even by fighting. Under no circumstances is it permissible to submit to this. Property is different: one may allow it to be taken, because giving up property is permissible, whereas submitting oneself or those under one’s protection to sexual immorality is not.

If the assailant intends to kill someone, the intended victim may defend himself. But is he obliged to do so? Scholars within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere hold two views on this. This applies when the people have an established ruler. But if there is civil strife—Allah forbid—such as when two Muslim rulers dispute sovereignty and fight over it, may a person defend himself during that strife when one ruler enters the other’s territory and bloodshed ensues? Or should he surrender and refrain from fighting in it? Scholars within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere hold two views on this.

When the ruler captures highway robbers who have taken people’s property, he must recover that property from them and restore it to its owners, while also carrying out the prescribed punishment upon them. The same applies to a thief. If they refuse to produce the property after their liability for it has been established, he must punish them with imprisonment and beating until they make its recovery possible, whether by producing it, appointing someone to bring it, or disclosing its whereabouts, just as punishment is imposed on anyone who refuses

translated_text:
to discharge an obligation incumbent upon him. For Allah has permitted a man in His Book to strike his wife if she is defiant and refuses to fulfil the duty incumbent upon her, until she fulfils it. These offenders are all the more deserving of such treatment. The right to demand restitution and to have this punishment imposed belongs to the owner of the property. If he wishes to give them the property, reach a settlement over it, or waive their punishment, he may do so. This differs from carrying out the prescribed punishment upon them, which cannot be waived under any circumstances. Nor may the ruler compel the owner to relinquish any part of his right.

If the property has been consumed or otherwise destroyed while in their possession, or in the thief’s possession, one view is that they must compensate its owners, just as other debtors are liable. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with them both. If they are insolvent, the debt remains their liability until they have the means to pay.

Another view is that compensation and amputation cannot both be imposed. This is the view of Abū Hanīfah, may Allah have mercy on him.

A third view is that they are liable for compensation only if they have the means, not if they are insolvent. This is the view of Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him.

It is not permissible for the ruler to charge property owners a fee for pursuing highway robbers, carrying out the prescribed punishment, and recovering people’s property from them, or for pursuing thieves—whether for himself or for the soldiers he sends after them. Rather, pursuing these offenders is a form of jihad in Allah’s cause. The Muslim troops therefore go forth for this purpose just as they do on other military campaigns, known as baykār. Those fighting in this undertaking are to be supported from the same funds used to support other military expeditions. If their assigned revenue or stipend suffices, that is enough; otherwise, they are to be given whatever additional amount is needed for their campaign from charitable funds devoted to public interests;

for this is in Allah’s cause. If the wayfarers who have been robbed—such as merchants who may fall victim to robbery—owe zakat, the ruler may collect the zakat on their wealth and spend it in Allah’s cause, such as on supporting those who pursue highway robbers. If the robbers possess considerable strength that makes it necessary to win them over, the ruler may give some of their chiefs payments from fay’ (revenues acquired without fighting), public-interest funds, and zakat, to help bring in the others, or to induce a chief to cease his wrongdoing, thereby weakening the rest, or for similar purposes. These recipients would fall among those whose hearts are to be won over. More than one imam, including Ahmad and others, has stated this, and it accords with the apparent meaning of the Book and the Sunnah and the fundamental principles of Islamic law.

The ruler must not send anyone too weak to confront the robbers, nor anyone who takes money from their victims—merchants and other wayfarers. Rather, he must send strong, trustworthy soldiers. If that is impossible, he must send the most suitable available, then the next most suitable.

If any of the ruler’s deputies, village chiefs, or others secretly or openly direct the robbers to plunder, then take a share of whatever they seize, shield them, and either appease the victims by returning some of their wealth or leave them unappeased, such an official’s crime is graver than that of the robbers’ chief. For the latter can be checked by lesser means than are needed to check the former. Such an official must be subject to the same ruling as those who provide the robbers with backing and assistance.  وَإِذَا ظَفَرَ بِهَذَا الَّذِي آوَى الْمُحْدِثَ فَإِنَّهُ طَلَبَ مِنْهُ إحْضَارَهُ أَوْ الْإِعْلَامَ بِهِ فَإِنْ امْتَنَعَ عُوقِبَ بِالْحَبْسِ وَالضَّرْبِ مَرَّةً بَعْدَ مَرَّةٍ حَتَّى يُمَكَّنَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْحَدَثِ كَمَا ذَكَرْنَا أَنَّهُ يُعَاقِبُ الْمُمْتَنِعَ مِنْ أَدَاءِ الْمَالِ الْوَاجِبِ. فَمَنْ وَجَبَ حُضُورُهُ مِنْ النُّفُوسِ وَالْأَمْوَالِ يُعَاقِبُ مَنْ مَنَعَ حُضُورَهَا. وَلَوْ كَانَ رَجُلًا يَعْرِفُ مَكَانَ الْمَالِ الْمَطْلُوبِ بِحَقِّ أَوْ الرَّجُلَ الْمَطْلُوبَ بِحَقِّ وَهُوَ الَّذِي يَمْنَعُهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ الْإِعْلَامُ بِهِ وَالدَّلَالَةُ عَلَيْهِ. وَلَا يَجُوزُ كِتْمَانُهُ. فَإِنَّ هَذَا مِنْ بَابِ التَّعَاوُنِ عَلَى الْبِرِّ وَالتَّقْوَى وَذَلِكَ وَاجِبٌ؛ بِخِلَافِ مَا لَوْ كَانَ النَّفْسُ أَوْ الْمَالُ مَطْلُوبًا بِبَاطِلِ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَحِلُّ الْإِعْلَامُ بِهِ لِأَنَّهُ مِنْ التَّعَاوُنِ عَلَى الْإِثْمِ وَالْعُدْوَانِ؛ بَلْ يَجِبُ الدَّفْعُ عَنْهُ؛ لِأَنَّ
translated_text:
knowledge. If they seize property, his hand and foot are to be cut off. If they kill and seize property, he is to be put to death and crucified. According to a group of scholars, he is to undergo amputation, be put to death, and be crucified. It has also been said that a choice may be made between these two penalties. This applies even if he had not authorized them, but, upon gaining power over them, shared in the wealth they had taken and left some claims and prescribed punishments unenforced.

Anyone who shelters a highway robber, thief, murderer, or someone else liable to a prescribed punishment or an obligation owed to Allah Most High or to another person, and prevents its lawful enforcement against him without transgression, is his accomplice in the crime. Allah and His Messenger have cursed him.

Muslim narrated in his Sahīh that ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Allah has cursed anyone who commits an offense or shelters an offender.”

Once the person sheltering the offender is apprehended, he is to be required to produce him or disclose his whereabouts. If he refuses, he is to be punished with imprisonment and repeated beatings until the offender can be apprehended, just as we have explained that someone who refuses to pay money he owes is to be punished. Whoever prevents a person or property from being brought forward when this is required is to be punished. Even if a man knows the whereabouts of property rightfully sought, or of a person rightfully sought, and is himself preventing access to it or him, he must disclose that information and indicate the location. He may not conceal it. This constitutes cooperation in righteousness and piety, which is obligatory.

By contrast, if the person or property is being sought unjustly, it is not permissible to disclose the whereabouts, for that constitutes cooperation in sin and aggression. Rather, one must protect that person or property, because

supporting the oppressed is obligatory.

In the two Sahīhs, Anas ibn Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Help your brother, whether he is an oppressor or is oppressed.”

I said, “O Messenger of Allah, I would help him if he were oppressed, but how should I help him if he is an oppressor?”

He said, “By preventing him from committing oppression; that is how you help him.”

Muslim narrated a similar report from Jābir. In the two Sahīhs, al-Barā’ ibn ‘Āzib, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded us to do seven things and forbade us seven things. He commanded us to visit the sick, follow funeral processions, invoke Allah’s mercy upon one who sneezes, help someone fulfill his oath, accept invitations, support the oppressed, and spread greetings of peace. He forbade us gold rings, drinking from silver vessels, saddle cushions, and wearing silk, qassī cloth, brocade, and heavy brocade.”

If someone who knows his whereabouts refuses to disclose them, he may be punished with imprisonment or otherwise until he provides that information. This is because he has refused to fulfill an obligation incumbent upon him that cannot be discharged by a proxy, and so he is punished as explained above. He may not, however, be punished for this unless it is known that he possesses the information. This principle applies consistently to matters handled by governors, judges, and others, whenever someone refuses to fulfill an obligation, whether in word or deed.

This does not amount to demanding that a man fulfill an obligation incumbent upon someone else, nor to punishing him for another person’s offense, such that it would fall under the words of Allah Most High:

“No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another,”

or the words of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him:

“Take heed! An offender’s guilt falls only upon himself.”

Rather, that would be the case, for example, if a man were required to pay money that

That is what is unlawful.

In the case under discussion, however, he is punished only for his own offense: he knows the whereabouts of the wrongdoer whose presence is required to secure the fulfillment of a rightful claim, or he knows the whereabouts of property to which others have rightful claims, yet refuses to provide the assistance and support incumbent upon him according to the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus. He may do so out of favoritism or partisan zeal for that wrongdoer, as people bound by partisan loyalties sometimes do for one another, or out of hostility or hatred toward the oppressed.

Allah Most High has said:

“Do not let hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”

Or he may do so out of an unwillingness to stand up for Allah and uphold the justice Allah has enjoined, and out of cowardice, weakness, and failure to support His religion—like those who fail to support Allah, His Messenger, His religion, and His Book, and who, when told to go forth in Allah’s cause, cling heavily to the earth. Whatever the motive, a person of this kind deserves punishment by agreement of the scholars. Whoever does not adopt these measures leaves the prescribed punishments unenforced and rights unprotected, allowing the strong to prey upon the weak.

refused to surrender it to a just judge who would use it to repay his debt or provide the maintenance he owes his family, relatives, slaves, or animals. An obligation often falls upon a man on account of someone else, just as he must provide maintenance because of a relative’s need, and just as blood money is payable by the killer’s ʿāqilah (the group collectively liable for his blood money).

This form of discretionary punishment applies to someone known to have in his keeping property or a person that must be produced, yet who fails to produce it or him—such as highway robbers, thieves, and those who shelter them—or someone known to have information about their whereabouts, yet who refuses to disclose it. If, however, he refuses to disclose their whereabouts or produce them to prevent the person seeking them from committing aggression or injustice against them, then he is doing good. These two situations are often confused, and uncertainty becomes entangled with personal desire. What is required is to distinguish right from wrong.

This frequently occurs among chiefs in both nomadic and settled communities when someone seeks their protection or is related to them by kinship or friendship. With the partisan zeal of pre-Islamic ignorance, pride in sin, and concern for their reputation among the rabble, they consider it a point of honor to support him—even when he is an unjust wrongdoer—against the wronged party who is in the right. This is especially so if the wronged party is a chief who vies with them and opposes them: they regard surrendering someone under their protection to an opponent as humiliation or weakness. Such an unqualified stance is pure pre-Islamic ignorance. It is among the greatest causes of corruption in both religious and worldly affairs.

It has been related that many wars among the Bedouin, such as the War of al-Basūs between Banū Bakr and Taghlib, arose from things of this kind. Likewise, the reason for the Turks and Mongols entering the lands of Islam

and their subjugation of the rulers of Transoxiana and Khurāsān lay in something of this kind.

Whoever humbles himself before Allah has truly honored himself, and whoever willingly renders what is due from him has ennobled himself. For the noblest of people in Allah’s sight are those most mindful of Him. Whoever seeks honor through wrongdoing—by withholding others’ rights and committing sins—has degraded and debased himself. Allah Most High says:

“Whoever desires honor—all honor belongs to Allah.”

He also says of the hypocrites:

“They say, ‘If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the lowlier from it.’ Yet honor belongs to Allah, His Messenger, and the believers, but the hypocrites do not know.”

Describing people of this kind, Allah Most High says:

“Among people is one whose words about worldly life please you, and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the fiercest of adversaries.”

“When he turns away, he strives throughout the land to spread corruption in it and destroy crops and livestock. And Allah does not love corruption.”

“When he is told, ‘Fear Allah,’ pride drives him to sin. Hell is enough for him—what an evil resting place!”

Rather, anyone whose protection is sought must support the person seeking it if he has been wronged. His having been wronged is not established merely by his own claim: many a man complains when he himself is the wrongdoer. Instead, the person offering protection must investigate his case by hearing from his adversary and others. If he is the wrongdoer, he must restrain him from wrongdoing gently if possible, whether through reconciliation or a just judgment; otherwise, by force. If each of them is both a wrongdoer and a victim of wrongdoing, as with those driven by partisan passions among Qays and Yaman

Section

As for the thief, his right hand must be cut off, according to the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus. Allah Most High says:

“As for male and female thieves, cut off their hands as punishment for what they have done—a deterrent from Allah. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”

“But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, Allah will surely turn to him in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”

Once liability for the prescribed punishment has been established against him through evidence or confession, its execution may not be deferred—whether by imprisonment, a payment to ransom himself, or any other means. Rather, his hand is to be cut off during sacred times as well as at other times, for enforcing the prescribed punishment is an act of worship, like fighting in Allah’s cause.

It should be understood that enforcing the prescribed punishments is a mercy from Allah toward His servants. The ruler should therefore be firm in enforcing the punishment, not allowing pity to lead him to suspend what Allah’s religion requires. His aim should be mercy toward people by restraining them from wrongdoing, not to vent his anger or seek supremacy over them. He is like a father disciplining his child: if he refrained from disciplining him—as the mother urges out of tenderness and compassion—the child would become corrupt. He disciplines him only out of mercy and to reform him, although he would much prefer that the child never made discipline necessary. He is also like a physician who gives a patient bitter medicine, or like amputating a decaying limb, cupping, and cutting

This is why the prescribed punishments were instituted, and this should be the ruler’s intention when enforcing them. Whenever his aim is to reform his subjects and prevent wrongdoing by securing benefits for them and warding off harm, seeking thereby the Face of Allah Most High and obedience to His command, Allah will soften people’s hearts toward him, facilitate the means of goodness for him, and spare him human punishment. It is related that before becoming caliph, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—may Allah be pleased with him—served as al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik’s governor over the city of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. “How much awe does he inspire among you?”

They replied, “We cannot bring ourselves to look at him.”

He asked, “How much do you love him?”

They replied, “He is dearer to us than our own families.”

He asked, “How does he discipline you?”

They replied, “With between three and ten lashes.”

He said, “Such awe, such love, and such discipline—this is something from heaven.”

His hand is cut off only if the stolen property reaches the prescribed minimum value: a quarter of a dinar or three dirhams, according to the majority of scholars among the people of the Hijaz, the hadith scholars, and others, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad. Some scholars hold that it is one dinar or ten dirhams. Whoever steals that amount is subject to amputation by scholarly agreement.

In the two Sahih collections, Ibn ʿUmar—may Allah be pleased with them both—reported:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, cut off a hand for the theft of a shield whose price was three dirhams.”

In Muslim’s wording:

“He cut off a thief’s hand for stealing a shield worth three dirhams.”

A mijann is a shield.

In the two Sahih collections, ʿĀ’ishah—may Allah be pleased with her—reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The hand is to be cut off for stealing a quarter of a dinar or more.”

In a version recorded by Muslim:

“A thief’s hand is not to be cut off except for stealing a quarter of a dinar or more.”

In a version recorded by al-Bukhārī, he said:

“Cut off the hand for stealing a quarter of a dinar, but do not cut it off for anything less than that.”

Kathar means the tender core of a date palm. This was reported by the compilers of the Sunan.

ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb narrated from his father, from his grandfather—may Allah be pleased with him—who said:

“I heard a man from Muzaynah questioning the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, I have come to ask you about stray camels.’

“He replied, ‘A camel has its footwear and water supply with it. It feeds on trees and goes to water, so leave it until its owner comes looking for it.’

“The man asked, ‘What about stray sheep?’

“He replied, ‘It is for you, your brother, or the wolf. Take it in until its owner comes looking for it.’

“The man asked, ‘What about livestock stolen from their grazing grounds?’

“He replied, ‘The penalty is twice their value and a deterrent beating. For livestock taken from their enclosure, amputation is prescribed if the value of what is taken reaches the price of a shield.’

“The man asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, what about fruit and what is taken from its sheaths?’

“He replied, ‘Whoever eats some directly, without gathering any in the fold of his garment, bears no liability. Whoever carries any away must pay twice its value and receive a deterrent beating. For fruit taken from its drying floors, amputation is prescribed if the value of what is taken reaches the price of a shield. If it does not reach the price of a shield, the penalty is compensation of twice its value and deterrent lashes.’”

“No amputation is prescribed for a plunderer, a snatcher, or one who betrays a trust.”

A plunderer takes property openly while people are watching. A snatcher grabs an object and is noticed before taking it. As for the cutpurse—the thief who slits open pockets, kerchiefs, sleeves, and the like—amputation is prescribed according to the correct view.

Section

As for one who commits unlawful sexual intercourse, if he is muhsan (has the legal status conferred by consummating a valid marriage), he is stoned until he dies. Thus the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stoned Māʿiz ibn Mālik al-Aslamī, the woman of Ghāmid, the two Jews, and others. The Muslims continued to carry out stoning after him.

Scholars have differed over whether he should receive one hundred lashes before being stoned. There are two views on this within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. If he is not muhsan, he receives one hundred lashes in accordance with the Book of Allah and is banished for a year in accordance with the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, although some scholars consider banishment obligatory.

some scholars hold that the prescribed punishment is waived, while others hold that it is not.

A muhsan is a man who, while free and legally accountable, has had vaginal intercourse, even once, with a woman whom he married under a valid marriage contract. Must the woman share these qualifications with the man? Scholars hold two views on this. Does a girl approaching puberty confer this status upon an adult man, and vice versa?

Non-Muslims living under Muslim protection may also have muhsan status according to most scholars, including al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad, because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, stoned two Jews at the entrance to his mosque. This was the first stoning in Islam.

Scholars differ concerning a woman who is found to be pregnant, has neither husband nor master, and alleges no legally excusing circumstance surrounding her pregnancy. There are two views within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. One holds that she is not subject to the prescribed punishment, since she may have conceived through forced intercourse, the introduction of semen without intercourse, or intercourse involving a legal uncertainty. The other holds that she is subject to the prescribed punishment. This is the position transmitted from the Rightly Guided Caliphs, accords more closely with the principles of Islamic law, and is the position of the scholars of Medina. Rare possibilities are disregarded, just as the possibility that she or the witnesses may be lying is disregarded.

As for anal intercourse between men, some scholars hold that its prescribed punishment is the same as that for unlawful sexual intercourse. It has also been said that its punishment is less severe. The correct view, upon which the Companions agreed, is that both men—the active and the passive partner—are to be put to death, whether they are muhsan or not. translated_text:
Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever you find committing the act of the people of Lot, put to death both the active and the passive partner.”

Abū Dāwūd also narrated that Ibn Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said concerning a man who was not muhsan and was found engaging in anal intercourse with another man: “He is to be stoned.” Something similar is related from Alī ibn Abī Tālib, may Allah be pleased with him. The Companions did not differ over putting him to death, but they differed over the manner of execution.

It is related that al-Siddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, ordered that he be burned, while others prescribed killing him. Some held that a wall should be toppled onto him so that he dies beneath the rubble. It was also said that both men should be confined in the foulest place until they die. Others held that he should be taken to the top of the highest wall in the town, thrown from it, and have stones hurled after him, just as Allah did to the people of Lot. This is one report from Ibn Abbās. In the other report, he said: “He is to be stoned.”

This was the position of most of the early generations. They argued that Allah stoned the people of Lot and prescribed stoning for the adulterer as a punishment corresponding to His stoning of the people of Lot. Both men are therefore to be stoned, whether both are free, both are slaves, or one is a slave and the other free, provided that both have reached puberty. If one has not reached puberty, he is to receive a punishment short of death, and only the one who has reached puberty is to be stoned.

translated_text:
Section

As for the prescribed punishment for drinking intoxicants, it is established by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the consensus of the Muslims. The compilers of the Sunan collections narrated through several routes that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever drinks intoxicants, flog him. If he drinks again, flog him. If he drinks again, flog him. Then, if he drinks a fourth time, put him to death.”

It is established that he flogged those who drank on several occasions, as did his caliphs and the Muslims after him. Most scholars hold that the ruling prescribing execution was abrogated. Others hold that it remains in force. It is also said that it is a discretionary punishment which the ruler may impose when necessary.

The following is also established:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, administered forty strokes with palm stalks and sandals for drinking intoxicants. Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, administered forty strokes, while Umar administered eighty during his caliphate. Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, would sometimes administer forty strokes and sometimes eighty.”

Some scholars therefore hold that eighty strokes are obligatory. Others hold that forty are obligatory, and that the ruler may add more when necessary—for example, when people become addicted to intoxicants, when the drinker cannot be deterred by fewer strokes, or in similar circumstances.

translated_text:
When drinkers are few and the drinker’s case is relatively mild, forty strokes suffice. This is the stronger of the two views. It is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and, according to one of the two reports from him, Ahmad—may Allah have mercy on them both.

When drinking became widespread, Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, added banishment and shaving the head as further deterrents. Thus, it would be appropriate to banish the drinker in addition to administering forty strokes, so that he is no longer heard of, or to remove him from his position of authority. Indeed, when Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, heard that one of his deputies had recited verses about intoxicating drink, he dismissed him.

The intoxicants which Allah and His Messenger prohibited, and for drinking which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribed flogging, include every intoxicating beverage, whatever its source: fruits such as grapes, fresh dates and figs; grains such as wheat and barley; dews such as honey; or animal products such as mares’ milk.

Indeed, when Allah, glorified and exalted is He, revealed the prohibition of intoxicants to His Prophet Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the people of Medina had no grape wine. There were no grapevines in Medina; grape wine was brought in from Syria. Most of their drink was made from dates. Reports transmitted through numerous independent chains from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, his rightly guided caliphs and his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, establish that he prohibited every intoxicating drink and made clear that every such drink is khamr.

They also used to drink sweet nabīdh, prepared by placing dates and raisins in water

 فَاخْتَلَفَ الصَّحَابَةُ وَمَنْ بَعْدَهُمْ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ. مِنْهُمْ مَنْ لَمْ يَبْلُغْهُ النَّسْخُ أَوْ لَمْ يُثْبِتْهُ فَنَهَى عَنْ الِانْتِبَاذِ فِي الْأَوْعِيَةِ. وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ اعْتَقَدَ ثُبُوتَهُ وَأَنَّهُ نَاسِخٌ فَرَخَّصَ فِي الِانْتِبَاذِ فِي الْأَوْعِيَةِ فَسَمِعَ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ الْفُقَهَاءِ أَنَّ بَعْضَ الصَّحَابَةِ كَانُوا يَشْرَبُونَ النَّبِيذَ فَاعْتَقَدُوا أَنَّهُ الْمُسْكِرُ فَتَرَخَّصُوا فِي شُرْبِ أَنْوَاعٍ مِنْ الْأَشْرِبَةِ الَّتِي لَيْسَتْ مِنْ الْعِنَبِ وَالتَّمْرِ. وَتَرَخَّصُوا فِي الْمَطْبُوخِ مِنْ نَبِيذِ التَّمْرِ وَالزَّبِيبِ إذَا لَمْ يُسْكِرْ الشَّارِبَ.
translated_text:
—that is, casting them into it, since nabdh means “casting in”—to sweeten the water, especially since much of the water in the Hijaz is salty. This nabīdh is permissible by the consensus of the Muslims because it does not intoxicate, just as grape juice is permissible to drink before it becomes intoxicating.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had forbidden them to prepare this nabīdh in wooden vessels, earthenware vessels made of clay, gourds, or pitch-coated containers. He instructed them instead to prepare it in containers whose mouths were tied shut with cords. This was because intoxicating strength develops gradually and imperceptibly in nabīdh, so a person might unknowingly drink something that had already acquired an intoxicating, exhilarating potency. If a waterskin was tied shut, it would split when the nabīdh fermented inside it, thus preventing a person from falling into what was forbidden. Those other vessels, however, would not split.

It is reported that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, subsequently permitted preparing nabīdh in those vessels, saying:

“I had forbidden you to prepare nabīdh in those vessels. Now prepare it, but do not drink anything intoxicating.”

The Companions and the scholars who came after them differed. Some had not learned of the abrogation or did not consider it established, and therefore prohibited preparing nabīdh in those vessels. Others accepted the later report as authentic and as abrogating the earlier prohibition, and therefore permitted preparing nabīdh in them.

Some jurists heard that certain Companions used to drink nabīdh and assumed that it was intoxicating. They consequently considered it permissible to drink certain kinds of beverages not made from grapes or dates. They also permitted boiled nabīdh made from dates and raisins, provided it did not intoxicate the drinker.

translated_text:
The correct view, however, is that held by the great majority of Muslims: every intoxicant is khamr (wine), and whoever drinks it is to be flogged, even if he drinks only a single drop, whether for medicinal purposes or otherwise. For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about using wine medicinally and replied:

“It is a disease, not a remedy. Allah has not placed the healing of my community in what has been forbidden to them.”

The prescribed punishment must be imposed when the offence is established by evidence or the drinker confesses. If, however, the smell of wine is detected on him, or he is seen vomiting it, or something similar occurs, one view holds that the prescribed punishment is not to be imposed, since he may have drunk something other than wine, or drunk wine without knowing what it was, or under compulsion, or in similar circumstances.

Another view holds that he is indeed to be flogged if he knew that it was intoxicating. This is what has been transmitted from the Rightly Guided Caliphs and other Companions, including 'Uthmān, 'Alī and Ibn Mas'ūd. It is supported by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and it is the position conducive to people's upright conduct. It is also the position of Mālik, of Ahmad in most of his recorded statements, and of others.

Hashish made from grape leaves is likewise forbidden, and whoever consumes it is to be flogged just as a wine drinker is flogged. It is more pernicious than wine in that it corrupts the mind and constitution, inducing effeminacy, indifference to sexual misconduct within one's family, and other forms of corruption. Wine is more pernicious in that it leads to quarrelling and fighting. Both turn people away from the remembrance of Allah Most High and from prayer.

should receive a discretionary punishment less severe than the prescribed punishment, since they supposed that it altered the mind without producing euphoria, like the plant banj. We have found no discussion of it by the earlier scholars. Yet that supposition is incorrect: those who consume it experience euphoria and crave it just as wine drinkers crave wine, or even more. When they consume it excessively, it turns them away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer, besides its other harmful effects: indifference to sexual misconduct within one’s family, effeminacy, corruption of the constitution and mind, and so forth.

However, because it is a solid substance that is eaten rather than drunk, jurists within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere have differed over its ritual impurity, expressing three views. One holds that it is ritually impure, like wine that is drunk; this is the sound analogy. Another holds that it is not, because it is solid. A third distinguishes between its solid and liquid forms. In any event, both the wording and the meaning of Allah’s and His Messenger’s prohibition of wine and intoxicants encompass it.

Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“O Messenger of Allah, give us a ruling on two drinks we used to make in Yemen: bitʿ, made from honey left to ferment until it becomes strong, and mizr, made from sorghum and barley left to ferment until it becomes strong.”

He continued: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had been endowed with comprehensive and conclusive speech. He said: ‘Every intoxicant is forbidden.’”

Reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim in their Sahīh collections.

Al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Wine can be made from wheat, from barley, from raisins, from dates, and from honey. I forbid every intoxicant.”

Abū Dāwūd and others; however, in the two Sahīh collections this is reported as a statement of ʿUmar himself. He delivered it in a sermon from the pulpit of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saying:

“Wine is whatever clouds the mind.”

Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every intoxicant is wine, and every intoxicant is forbidden.”

Another version reads:

“Every intoxicant is wine, and every wine is forbidden.”

Muslim reported both versions in his Sahīh.

ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every intoxicant is forbidden. Whatever causes intoxication when consumed in a faraq (a measure of volume) is forbidden even in a palmful.”

Al-Tirmidhī graded this hadith sound.

The compilers of the Sunan collections reported through several chains that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whatever intoxicates in large quantities is forbidden in small quantities.”

Leading hadith scholars graded it authentic.

Jābir, may Allah be pleased with him, reported:

“A man asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about a drink made from sorghum that they drank in their land, called mizr. He asked, ‘Does it intoxicate?’

“The man replied, ‘Yes.’

“He said, ‘Every intoxicant is forbidden. Allah has pledged that whoever drinks an intoxicant will be given tīnat al-khabāl to drink.’

“They asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, what is tīnat al-khabāl?’

“He replied, ‘The sweat of the people of Hell, or the discharge of the people of Hell.’”

Muslim reported it in his Sahīh.

Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Everything that clouds the mind is wine; every intoxicant is forbidden.”

He made no distinction between one kind and another. Whether a substance is eaten or drunk makes no difference. Indeed, wine is sometimes used as a condiment, while hashish may be dissolved in water and drunk. Thus every kind of wine can be drunk or eaten, and hashish can be eaten or drunk; all of this is forbidden. The earlier scholars did not discuss hashish specifically only because eating it became a practice relatively recently, towards the end of the sixth century AH or thereabouts. Likewise, intoxicating drinks were introduced after the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and all fall within the comprehensive statements of the Quran and Sunnah.

Section

Among the prescribed punishments established by the Quran and Sunnah, and unanimously agreed upon by the Muslims, is the punishment for accusations of unlawful sexual intercourse. If a man accuses a muhsan of unlawful sexual intercourse or sodomy, he incurs the prescribed punishment of eighty lashes. Here, muhsan means a free, chaste person; in the discussion of the prescribed punishment for unlawful sexual intercourse, it means someone who has had full sexual intercourse within a fully valid marriage.

Section

As for sins for which there is neither a fixed prescribed punishment nor an expiation, examples include kissing a boy or a woman who is neither one’s wife nor unmarriageable kin; engaging in physical intimacy without intercourse; eating forbidden things, such as blood or carrion; making accusations against people other than accusations of unlawful sexual intercourse; stealing something not kept in a secure place, even something of little value; betraying a trust—as when administrators of public treasury funds, endowments, or orphans’ property and the like betray their trust, or when agents and partners do so; acting fraudulently in one’s dealings, as those who cheat in food, clothing, and similar goods do; giving short measure or weight; bearing false witness or coaching others to do so; accepting bribes when passing judgment; judging by other than what Allah has revealed; oppressing one’s subjects; raising the rallying cries of pre-Islamic ignorance or answering its call; and other kinds of forbidden acts.

Such offenders receive discretionary punishment to deter and discipline them, to the extent the ruler deems appropriate, taking into account how widespread or rare the particular sin is among the people. If it is widespread, he increases the punishment, unlike when it is rare. He also considers the offender’s circumstances: someone habitually engaged in wickedness receives a greater punishment than someone who seldom commits such acts. He likewise considers the gravity of the sin: someone who harasses other people’s women and children receives a greater punishment than someone who has harassed only a woman

or a single boy. There is no fixed minimum for discretionary punishment. It may take any form that causes a person distress, whether through words, actions, withholding words, or withholding actions. A man may be disciplined by admonition, rebuke, or stern words. He may also be disciplined by shunning him and withholding greetings until he repents, when this serves the best interest, just as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and his Companions shunned “the three who were left behind.”

He may be disciplined by removal from office, as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and his Companions used to do. He may also be disciplined by no longer being employed in the Muslim army, as in the case of a soldier who flees the battlefield. Fleeing the battlefield is a major sin, and cutting off his pay is a form of discretionary punishment. Likewise, if a commander commits a grave offense, he may be removed from his command as a disciplinary punishment.

Discretionary punishment may also take the form of imprisonment, beating, blackening the offender’s face, or making him ride an animal backwards. It is reported that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb (may Allah be pleased with him) ordered such treatment for a false witness. For the liar has blackened his own reputation, so his face is blackened; he has turned the account upside down, so he is made to ride backwards.

As for its maximum, one view states: “No more than ten lashes may be administered.” Many scholars hold that discretionary punishment must fall short of a fixed prescribed punishment. They then differ between two views. Some say: “It must fall short of the least prescribed punishment.” Thus, for a free person, it must fall short of the least prescribed punishment applicable to a free person, which is forty or eighty lashes; and for a slave, it must fall short of the least prescribed punishment applicable to a slave, which is

twenty or forty lashes. Another view holds that, for either, it must fall short of the prescribed punishment for a slave.

Some scholars say that the punishment for each offense must fall short of the prescribed punishment for its category, even if it exceeds the prescribed punishment for another category. Thus, someone who steals property not kept in a secure place must not have his hand amputated, even if he is given more lashes than the prescribed punishment for falsely accusing someone of unlawful sexual intercourse. Likewise, someone who commits acts short of unlawful sexual intercourse must not receive the prescribed punishment for that intercourse, even if his punishment exceeds that for a false accusation.

It is reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb (may Allah be pleased with him) that a man made an engraving on his seal ring and used it to obtain money from the public treasury. ʿUmar ordered that he be given a hundred strokes, then had him given a hundred strokes on the second day and a hundred on the third.

It is also reported from the Rightly Guided Caliphs concerning a man and woman found together under one blanket:

“They are each to be given a hundred lashes.”

It is reported from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), concerning a man who has intercourse with his wife’s slave woman, that if his wife had given him permission, he is to be given a hundred lashes; if she had not given him permission, he is to be stoned to death.

These views are found in the school of Ahmad and others. The first two views are found in the school of al-Shāfiʿī and others.

As for Mālik and others, it is reported that they held that certain crimes may warrant execution. Some scholars of Ahmad’s school agreed with him in cases such as that of a Muslim spy who spies on the Muslims for the enemy. Ahmad withheld judgment on whether such a person should be executed. Mālik and some Hanbalī scholars, such as Ibn ʿAqīl, permitted his execution, while Abū Hanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, and some Hanbalī scholars, such as Judge Abū Yaʿlā, prohibited it.

A group of scholars from the schools of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad, and others, also permitted the execution of anyone who advocates religious innovations contrary to the Quran and Sunnah. Many scholars of Mālik’s school held the same view. They said that Mālik and others permitted the execution of the Qadariyya only for spreading corruption in the land, not for apostasy.

The same explanation has also been given for executing a sorcerer. Most scholars hold that he is to be executed. It has been narrated from Jundub (may Allah be pleased with him), both as his own statement and as a report traced back to the Prophet:

“The prescribed punishment for a sorcerer is a stroke of the sword.”

This was reported by al-Tirmidhī. The execution of sorcerers has also been reported from Umar, Uthmān, Hafsa, Abd Allāh ibn Umar, and other Companions (may Allah be pleased with them). Some scholars said that this is on account of disbelief, while others said that it is for spreading corruption in the land. Most of these scholars, however, regard his execution as a prescribed punishment.

Abū Hanīfa likewise allows execution as a discretionary punishment for repeated crimes when crimes of that kind warrant execution, as in the case of someone who repeatedly commits sodomy or treacherously murders people to seize their wealth, and similar offenses.

Evidence that someone who spreads corruption is to be executed if his evil cannot otherwise be stopped may be drawn from the report narrated by Muslim in his Sahīh, from Arfaja al-Ashja'ī (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: “I heard the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) say:

‘If someone comes to you while you are united under one man, seeking to break your unity or divide your community, kill him.’”

Another version states:

“There will be disturbances and more disturbances. Whoever seeks to divide this community while it is united, strike him with the sword, whoever he may be.”

The same explanation may also be given for his command to execute a wine-drinker on the fourth occasion, as supported by what Ahmad narrated in his Musnad from Daylam al-Himyarī (may Allah be pleased with him), who said:

“I asked the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), saying: ‘O Messenger of Allah, we live in a land where we perform strenuous work, and we make a drink from wheat to strengthen us for our work and against the cold of our land.’

“He asked: ‘Does it intoxicate?’ I replied: ‘Yes.’ He said: ‘Then avoid it.’ I said: ‘The people will not give it up.’ He said: ‘If they do not give it up, kill them.’”

This is because someone who spreads corruption is like an aggressor: if the aggressor cannot be repelled except by killing him, he is killed.

In sum, punishment is of two kinds. The first is punishment for a past offense, as recompense for what the offender has done and an exemplary punishment from Allah, such as flogging a wine-drinker or someone who makes an accusation of unlawful sexual intercourse, and the amputation imposed on armed robbers and thieves.

The second is punishment intended to secure the fulfillment of an obligation and abstention from what is forbidden in the future. Thus, an apostate is called upon to repent and embrace Islam: if he repents, he is spared; otherwise, he is executed. Likewise, someone who neglects prayer, zakat, or the rights of others is punished until he fulfills them. Discretionary punishment in this second category is more severe than in the first. Hence, he may be beaten repeatedly until he performs the obligatory prayer or fulfills the duty incumbent upon him.

In the Quran and Sunnah, “limits” denotes the boundary between the lawful and the unlawful: the furthest extent of what is lawful and the point at which the unlawful begins. Concerning the former, Allah says:

Concerning the latter, He says:

Calling a prescribed punishment a hadd, however, is a later terminological convention. The hadith means that someone administering a beating to enforce a personal right—such as a man striking his wife for marital defiance—must not exceed ten lashes.

The flogging prescribed by Islamic law consists of moderate strokes with a whip, for the best course is the middle one. ‘Alī (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

“Moderation in the stroke, and moderation in the whip.”

Flogging is not to be administered with sticks or scourges, nor does a light whip suffice. Rather, a light whip is used for discretionary punishment, whereas prescribed punishments require flogging with a whip. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb (may Allah be pleased with him) used to administer discipline with a light whip, but when a prescribed punishment was to be carried out, he would call for a whip.

The person being flogged is not to be stripped of all his clothing. Only what prevents him from feeling the pain of the blows—such as padded garments, furs, and the like—is to be removed. He is not to be bound unless necessary, nor is his face to be struck, for the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said:

Section

The punishments prescribed by Islamic law for those who disobey Allah and His Messenger are of two kinds:

The first is punishment of those who are under control, whether one person or several, as discussed above.

The second is punishment of a group that resists enforcement, such as one that can only be brought under control through fighting. The foundation of this is jihad against the disbelievers, the enemies of Allah and His Messenger. Anyone whom the Messenger of Allah’s call to the religion with which Allah sent him reaches, but who does not respond to it, must be fought:

“Until there is no more persecution and worship is devoted entirely to Allah.”

For when Allah sent His Prophet and commanded him to call people to His religion, He did not permit him to kill or fight anyone on that account until he emigrated to Medina. Then He granted permission to him and the Muslims, saying:

“Permission to fight is granted to those who are being fought, because they have been wronged. And Allah is certainly able to grant them victory.”

“Those who have been driven from their homes unjustly, merely for saying, ‘Our Lord is Allah.’ Were it not for Allah restraining some people by means of others, destruction would surely have befallen monasteries and churches

, synagogues, and mosques in which Allah’s name is often mentioned. Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is All-Powerful, Almighty.”

“Those who, if We establish them in the land, maintain prayer, give zakah, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And to Allah belongs the outcome of all matters.”

Then, after that, He made fighting obligatory for them, saying, Most High:

“Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate something that is good for you, and perhaps you love something that is bad for you. Allah knows, while you do not know.”

He reaffirmed this obligation and emphasized the importance of jihad in most of the Medinan surahs. He censured those who abandoned it, describing them as having hypocrisy and sickness in their hearts. He, Most High, said:

“Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your relatives, the wealth you have acquired, the trade whose decline you fear, and the homes you cherish are dearer to you than Allah, His Messenger, and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings about His decree. Allah does not guide defiantly disobedient people.”

He, Most High, also said:

“The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, then do not doubt, and strive with their wealth and their lives in Allah’s cause. It is they who are truthful.”

He, Most High, also said:

“But when an unambiguous surah is revealed and fighting is mentioned in it, you see those in whose hearts is sickness looking at you like someone overcome by the throes of death. Yet better for them would be obedience and fitting words. Then, when the matter is resolved, if they were true to Allah, it would be better for them. If you turn away, would you then spread corruption on earth and sever your ties of kinship?”

There are many such passages

in the Quran. Likewise, jihad and those who undertake it are exalted in Surah al-Saff, in which He says:

“O you who believe, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?

“Believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in Allah’s cause with your wealth and your lives. That is better for you, if only you knew.

“He will forgive your sins and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in Gardens of everlasting residence. That is the great triumph.

“And another blessing that you love: help from Allah and a victory near at hand. So give good tidings to the believers.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Do you regard providing water to the pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque as equal to the deeds of one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in Allah’s cause? They are not equal before Allah. Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.

“Those who believe, emigrate, and strive in Allah’s cause with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank before Allah. It is they who are successful.

“Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him, His pleasure, and gardens in which they will have lasting bliss,

“Remaining there forever. Indeed, with Allah is a great reward.”

And He, Most High, says:

“Whoever among you turns back from his religion, Allah will bring forth a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers and firm toward the disbelievers. They strive in Allah’s cause and do not fear the reproach of any critic. That is Allah’s bounty, which He grants to whom He wills. Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.”

He, Most High, also says:

“That is because no thirst, fatigue, or hunger afflicts them in Allah’s cause, nor do they tread any ground that enrages the disbelievers, nor inflict any loss on an enemy, without there being recorded for them

a righteous deed on that account. Indeed, Allah does not allow the reward of those who do good to be lost.”

“Nor do they spend any amount, small or large, or cross any valley without it being recorded for them, so that Allah may reward them according to the best of what they used to do.”

Thus, He mentions both the effects of their deeds and the deeds they perform directly.

The commands to undertake jihad and the accounts of its virtues in the Quran and Sunnah are too numerous to enumerate. For this reason, it is the best voluntary deed a person can undertake. By scholarly agreement, it is superior to Hajj and ‘umrah, voluntary prayer, and voluntary fasting, as indicated by the Quran and Sunnah. Indeed, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The foundation of the matter is Islam, its pillar is prayer, and its highest peak is jihad.”

He also said:

“In Paradise there are a hundred degrees which Allah has prepared for those who strive in His cause. The distance between one degree and the next is like the distance between heaven and earth.”

Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

He also said:

“Whoever’s feet become dusty in Allah’s cause, Allah forbids the Fire from touching him.”

Reported by al-Bukhārī.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also said:

“Keeping guard for a day and a night in Allah’s cause is better than fasting for a month and spending its nights in prayer. If he dies, the reward for the deeds he used to perform continues, his provision continues, and he is spared the trial of the grave.”

Reported by Muslim. The Sunan collections also contain the following:

“Keeping guard for one day in Allah’s cause is better than a thousand days spent in any other station.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also said:

“Two eyes will not be touched by the Fire: an eye that wept out of fear of Allah, and an eye that spent the night intent on Allah’s cause.”

This is a vast subject. Nothing comparable to what has been reported concerning its reward and virtue has been reported concerning other deeds.

This is because Allah Most High has permitted taking life to the extent necessary for the welfare of His creation. As He Most High says:

“Persecution is worse than killing.”

That is, although killing involves evil and corruption, the persecution perpetrated by the unbelievers involves greater evil and corruption. Whoever does not prevent Muslims from upholding religion for Allah harms only himself through his unbelief.

For this reason, the jurists have stated that someone who promotes innovations contrary to the Quran and Sunnah is subject to punishments not imposed on someone who remains silent.

It is related in a hadith:

“When a sin is concealed, it harms only its perpetrator; but when it becomes public and is not denounced, it harms the community at large.”

For this reason, Islamic law has made fighting the unbelievers obligatory, but has not made it obligatory to kill those of them who have been subdued. Rather, if one of their men is captured, whether in battle or otherwise—for example, if a ship casts him onto our shores, he loses his way, or he is captured through a ruse—the ruler is to choose whichever course best serves the public interest: killing him, enslaving him, releasing him without ransom, or ransoming him for money or in exchange for another person. This is the position of most jurists, as indicated by the Quran and Sunnah, although some jurists hold that the permission to release him without ransom or to ransom him has been abrogated.

As for the People of the Book and the Magians, they are to be fought until they embrace Islam or pay the jizya directly, in a state of submission.

The jurists have differed over whether it is permissible to fight a group that refuses compliance if it abandons a regular sunnah prayer, such as the two rakahs before the dawn prayer. There are two opinions on this.

As for manifest and widely known obligations and prohibitions, there is agreement that such people are to be fought until they commit themselves to performing the prescribed prayers, paying zakat, fasting the month of Ramadan, making pilgrimage to the House, and refraining from prohibited acts, such as marrying sisters, consuming impure things, attacking Muslims’ lives and property, and similar acts. It is obligatory to initiate fighting against such people once the call of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has reached them concerning the requirements over which they are fought. If, however, they attack the Muslims first, the obligation to fight them becomes more emphatic, as we explained when discussing fighting aggressors who resist enforcement, namely highway robbers.

The most far-reaching form of obligatory jihad—against unbelievers and those who refuse to observe certain religious laws, such as those who withhold zakat, the Khawārij, and others like them—is required both offensively and defensively.

When undertaken offensively, it is a communal obligation: if some fulfil it, the obligation is lifted from the rest, while the merit belongs to those who undertake it. As Allah Most High says:

“Not equal are those believers who remain behind, other than those with disabilities…”

And so the verse continues. But if the enemy intends to attack the Muslims, repelling them becomes obligatory upon all those targeted, and upon those not targeted as well, to assist them. As Allah Most High says:

“And if they seek your help in matters of religion, you must help them, except against a people with whom you have a treaty.”

Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded that a Muslim be supported, whether or not one is a salaried soldier. This is obligatory upon everyone according to their ability, through their person and wealth, whether their numbers are few or many, and whether on foot or mounted. Thus, when the enemy attacked the Muslims in the year of the Trench, Allah did not permit anyone to refrain from defending them, whereas He had permitted some to refrain from initiating jihad in pursuit of the enemy, distinguishing between those who remained behind and those who went forth. Rather, He censured those who sought the Prophet’s permission to leave, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Saying, ‘Our homes are exposed,’ though they were not exposed. They wanted nothing but to flee.”

This is the defence of religion, inviolable rights, and lives: fighting undertaken out of necessity. The other is fighting undertaken by choice to advance and exalt the religion and to deter the enemy, as in the expedition to Tabūk and similar campaigns. This form of punishment applies to groups that resist enforcement.

As for inhabitants of Muslim lands and others like them who do not resist enforcement, they must be compelled to fulfil their obligations: the five pillars of Islam and other duties, such as discharging trusts, honouring agreements in dealings, and so forth.

Anyone who does not pray, whether male or female, must be commanded to pray. If they refuse, they are to be punished until they pray, by scholarly consensus. Moreover, most scholars hold that such a person must be executed if they do not pray. They are first called upon to repent; if they repent, they are spared, but otherwise they are executed. Is such a person executed as an unbeliever or

an apostate, or a sinner? There are two well-known positions on this in the school of Ahmad and among other scholars. What is transmitted from most of the early generations implies that he is an unbeliever. This concerns someone who acknowledges that prayer is obligatory. As for someone who denies its obligation, he is an unbeliever by consensus.

Indeed, guardians must instruct a child to pray upon reaching seven years of age and strike him for failing to pray at ten, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded when he said:

“Instruct them to pray at seven, strike them for failing to pray at ten, and give them separate sleeping places.”

The same applies to the obligatory purification and other requirements of prayer.

Completing this duty entails attending to the Muslims’ mosques and their imams, and instructing the imams to lead them in prayer as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed. He said:

“Pray as you have seen me pray.”

Narrated by al-Bukhārī.

“He once led his Companions in prayer on the edge of the pulpit and said: ‘I have done this only so that you may follow me and learn how I pray.’”

Whoever leads the people, in prayer or otherwise, must look to their welfare, ensuring that they do not miss out on anything that completes their religious practice and depends upon his actions. Indeed, every prayer leader must lead them in a complete prayer, rather than confining himself to the minimum sufficient for validity that someone praying alone may observe, unless there is a valid excuse. The same applies to their leader during Hajj and their commander in war.

Whenever rulers attend to setting people’s religious affairs right, both rulers and subjects prosper in their religious and worldly affairs; otherwise, their affairs fall into disorder. The foundation of all this is sincere concern for the subjects, complete sincerity in devotion to Allah, and reliance upon Him.

Sincerity and reliance upon Allah together encompass what sets right the affairs of both the elite and the general populace, just as He commanded us to say in our prayers:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.”

It has been said that these two statements encompass the meanings of the Books revealed from heaven. It has also been reported:

“Once, during one of his military expeditions, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘O Master of the Day of Judgment, You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.’ Then heads began falling from shoulders.”

Allah has mentioned this in several places in His Book, as in His words:

“So worship Him and rely upon Him.”

And His words, Exalted is He:

“Upon Him I rely, and to Him I turn.”

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, slaughtered his sacrificial animal, he would say: ‘O Allah, this is from You and for You.’”

Three things provide the greatest assistance to those in authority in particular, and to everyone else in general:

First: sincerity towards Allah and reliance upon Him through supplication and other means. The foundation of this is diligently observing the prayers with both heart and body.

Second: doing good to people by benefiting them and giving wealth in zakah.

Third: patiently enduring the harm people cause and other adversities.
