 وَلَا يَقُولُونَ إنَّ أَمْوَالَهُمْ مَعْصُومَةٌ كَمَا كَانَتْ وَمَا كَانَ ثَابِتًا بِعَيْنِهِ رَدٌّ إلَى صَاحِبِهِ وَمَا أُتْلِفَ فِي حَالِ الْقِتَالِ لَمْ يَضْمَنْ حَتَّى أَنَّ جُمْهُورَ الْعُلَمَاءِ يَقُولُونَ:
 لَا يَضْمَنُ لَا هَؤُلَاءِ وَلَا هَؤُلَاءِ كَمَا قَالَ الزُّهْرِيُّ: وَقَعَتْ الْفِتْنَةُ وَأَصْحَابُ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مُتَوَافِرُونَ فَأَجْمَعُوا أَنَّ كُلَّ مَالٍ أَوْ دَمٍ أُصِيبَ بِتَأْوِيلِ الْقُرْآنِ فَإِنَّهُ هَدَرٌ. وَهَلْ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُسْتَعَانَ بِسِلَاحِهِمْ فِي حَرْبِهِمْ إذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ إلَى ذَلِكَ ضَرُورَةٌ؟
 عَلَى وَجْهَيْنِ:
 فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد يَجُوزُ وَالْمَنْعُ قَوْلُ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَالرُّخْصَةُ قَوْلُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ. وَاخْتَلَفُوا فِي قَتْلِ أَسِيرِهِمْ وَاتِّبَاعِ مُدْبِرَهُمْ وَالتَّذْفِيفِ عَلَى جَرِيحِهِمْ
translated_text:
among the followers of Abū Hanīfa and al-Shāfi‘ī, and those followers of Ahmad and others who agreed with them. They all agree that the Companions are not morally corrupt but upright.

They therefore maintain that rebels remain upright despite their fighting, and that their error is like that of scholars exercising independent legal judgment in subsidiary matters. A group, including Ibn ‘Aqīl and others, disagreed and held that rebels are morally corrupt. These scholars considered those whom they counted as rebels in their own time and judged them morally corrupt. Undoubtedly, they do not include the Companions in this judgment. Only some adherents of deviant doctrines among the Mu‘tazila and similar groups declare the Companions morally corrupt, just as some adherents of deviant doctrines among the Khawārij and the Rāfida declare them unbelievers. This is not the position of the imams and jurists of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah.

Nor do they say that their property retains the same inviolability as before. Whatever property remains in its original form is returned to its owner, while no compensation is due for what was destroyed during the fighting. Indeed, the majority of scholars hold that neither side is liable for compensation. As al-Zuhrī said: “Civil strife broke out while the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, were still numerous. They unanimously agreed that no compensation was due for any loss of property or bloodshed occasioned by an interpretation of the Quran.”

Is it permissible to use their weapons in fighting them when there is no necessity to do so? There are two views within Ahmad’s school. One permits it; prohibition is al-Shāfi‘ī’s position, while permission is Abū Hanīfa’s position.

They disagreed over killing their captives, pursuing their retreating fighters, and finishing off their wounded

original_text:
إذَا كَانَ لَهُمْ فِئَةٌ يَلْجَئُونَ إلَيْهَا.
 فَجَوَّزَ ذَلِكَ أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ وَمَنَعَهُ الشَّافِعِيُّ وَهُوَ الْمَشْهُورُ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَفِي مَذْهَبِهِ وَجْهٌ:
 أَنَّهُ يَتْبَعُ مُدْبَرَهُمْ فِي أَوَّلِ الْقِتَالِ.
 وَأَمَّا إذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُمْ فِئَةٌ فَلَا يُقْتَلُ أَسِيرٌ وَلَا يُذَفَّفُ عَلَى جَرِيحٍ كَمَا رَوَاهُ سَعِيدٌ وَغَيْرُهُ عَنْ مَرْوَانَ بْنِ الْحَكَمِ قَالَ:
 خَرَجَ صَارِخٌ لِعَلِيِّ يَوْمَ الْجَمَلِ لَا يُقْتَلَنَّ مُدْبِرٌ وَلَا يُذَفَّفُ عَلَى جَرِيحٍ وَمَنْ أَغْلَقَ بَابَهُ فَهُوَ آمِنٌ وَمَنْ أَلْقَى السِّلَاحَ فَهُوَ آمِنٌ. فَمَنْ سَلَكَ هَذِهِ الطَّرِيقَةَ فَقَدْ يَتَوَهَّمُ أَنَّ هَؤُلَاءِ التَّتَارَ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْبَغْيِ الْمُتَأَوِّلِينَ وَيُحْكَمُ فِيهِمْ بِمِثْلِ هَذِهِ الْأَحْكَامِ كَمَا أَدْخَلَ مَنْ أَدْخَلَ فِي هَذَا الْحُكْمِ مَانِعِي الزَّكَاةِ وَالْخَوَارِجَ. وَسَنُبَيِّنُ فَسَادَ هَذَا التَّوَهُّمِ إنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى.
 وَالطَّرِيقَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ:
 إنَّ قِتَالَ مَانِعِي الزَّكَاةِ وَالْخَوَارِجِ وَنَحْوِهِمْ لَيْسَ كَقِتَالِ أَهْلِ الْجَمَلِ وصفين وَهَذَا هُوَ الْمَنْصُوصُ عَنْ جُمْهُورِ الْأَئِمَّةِ الْمُتَقَدِّمِينَ وَهُوَ الَّذِي يَذْكُرُونَهُ فِي اعْتِقَادِ أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ وَالْجَمَاعَةِ وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ أَهْلِ الْمَدِينَةِ كَمَالِكِ وَغَيْرِهِ وَمَذْهَبِ أَئِمَّةِ الْحَدِيثِ كَأَحْمَدَ وَغَيْرِهِ. وَقَدْ نَصُّوا عَلَى الْفَرْقِ بَيْنَ هَذَا وَهَذَا فِي غَيْرِ مَوْضِعٍ حَتَّى فِي الْأَمْوَالِ. فَإِنَّ مِنْهُمْ مَنْ أَبَاحَ غَنِيمَةَ أَمْوَالِ الْخَوَارِجِ وَقَدْ نَصَّ أَحْمَد فِي رِوَايَةِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ فِي حرورية كَانَ لَهُمْ سَهْمٌ فِي قَرْيَةٍ فَخَرَجُوا
translated_text:
if they have a force to which they can retreat.

Abū Hanīfa permitted this, while al-Shāfi‘ī prohibited it; the latter is also the well-known position within Ahmad’s school. Another view within his school permits pursuing their retreating fighters at the outset of the fighting.

If, however, they have no such force, their captives are not to be killed, nor their wounded finished off. Sa‘īd and others narrated that Marwān ibn al-Hakam said: “On the day of the Battle of the Camel, a herald went out on ‘Alī’s behalf, proclaiming: ‘No retreating fighter is to be killed, nor any wounded man finished off. Whoever closes his door is safe, and whoever lays down his weapons is safe.’”

Someone following this approach might mistakenly suppose that these Tatars are rebels acting on an interpretive judgment and should be subject to these same rulings, just as some have included those who withheld zakat and the Khawārij under this ruling. We shall explain the error of this supposition, if Allah Most High wills.

The second approach is that fighting those who withhold zakat, the Khawārij, and others like them is not the same as fighting the participants in the Battles of the Camel and Siffīn. This is the position explicitly transmitted from the majority of the early imams, and it is what they mention when setting out the creed of Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamā‘ah. It is the position of the scholars of Medina, such as Mālik and others, and of the imams of hadith, such as Ahmad and others. They explicitly distinguished between the two in several places, even regarding property. Some of them permitted taking the property of the Khawārij as spoils. In the report transmitted by Abū Tālib, Ahmad gave an explicit ruling concerning some Harūriyya who held a share in a village and then went out

original_text:
يُقَاتِلُونَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ فَقَتَلَهُمْ الْمُسْلِمُونَ فَأَرْضُهُمْ فَيْءٌ لِلْمُسْلِمِينَ فَيُقْسَمُ خُمُسُهُ عَلَى خَمْسَةٍ وَأَرْبَعَةُ أَخْمَاسِهِ لِلَّذِينَ قَاتَلُوا يُقْسَمُ بَيْنَهُمْ أَوْ يَجْعَلُ الْأَمِيرُ الْخَرَاجَ عَلَى الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَلَا يُقْسَمُ مِثْلُ مَا أَخَذَ عُمَرُ السَّوَادَ عَنْوَةً وَوَقَفَهُ عَلَى الْمُسْلِمِينَ. فَجَعَلَ أَحْمَد الْأَرْضَ الَّتِي لِلْخَوَارِجِ إذَا غُنِمَتْ بِمَنْزِلَةِ مَا غُنِمَ مِنْ أَمْوَالِ الْكُفَّارِ. وَبِالْجُمْلَةِ فَهَذِهِ الطَّرِيقَةُ هِيَ الصَّوَابُ الْمَقْطُوعُ بِهِ. فَإِنَّ النَّصَّ وَالْإِجْمَاعَ فَرْقٌ بَيْنَ هَذَا وَهَذَا وَسِيرَةُ عَلِيٍّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ تَفَرُّقٌ بَيْنَ هَذَا وَهَذَا. فَإِنَّهُ قَاتَلَ الْخَوَارِجَ بِنَصِّ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ وَفَرِحَ بِذَلِكَ وَلَمْ يُنَازِعْهُ فِيهِ أَحَدٌ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ. وَأَمَّا الْقِتَالُ يَوْمَ صفين فَقَدْ ظَهَرَ مِنْهُ مِنْ كَرَاهَتِهِ وَالذَّمِّ عَلَيْهِ مَا ظَهَرَ.
 وَقَالَ فِي أَهْلِ الْجَمَلِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ:
 إخْوَانُنَا بَغَوْا عَلَيْنَا طَهَّرَهُمْ السَّيْفُ وَصَلَّى عَلَى قَتْلَى الطَّائِفَتَيْنِ. وَأَمَّا الْخَوَارِجُ فَفِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْ عَلِيِّ بْنِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ. قَالَ سَمِعْت رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَقُولُ 
{سَيَخْرُجُ قَوْمٌ فِي آخِرِ الزَّمَانِ حِدَاثُ الْأَسْنَانِ سُفَهَاءُ الْأَحْلَامِ يَقُولُونَ مِنْ خَيْرِ قَوْلِ الْبَرِّيَّةِ لَا يُجَاوِزُ إيمَانُهُمْ حَنَاجِرَهُمْ: يَمْرُقُونَ مِنْ الدِّينِ كَمَا يَمْرُقُ السَّهْمُ مِنْ الرَّمِيَّةِ. فَأَيْنَمَا لَقِيتُمُوهُمْ فَاقْتُلُوهُمْ فَإِنَّ فِي قَتْلِهِمْ أَجْرًا لِمَنْ قَتَلَهُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ}
 . وَفِي صَحِيحِ مُسْلِمٍ عَنْ زَيْدِ بْنِ وَهْبٍ أَنَّهُ كَانَ فِي الْجَيْشِ الَّذِي
translated_text:
to fight the Muslims and were killed by the Muslims. Their land then becomes booty for the Muslims: one fifth is divided into five shares, while the remaining four fifths belong to those who fought and are divided among them. Alternatively, the ruler may levy land tax on the Muslims and leave the land undivided, just as ‘Umar conquered the Sawād by force and made it an endowment for the Muslims. Thus, Ahmad treated land captured from the Khawārij in the same way as property captured from the disbelievers.

In short, this approach is unquestionably correct. Both the scriptural evidence and scholarly consensus distinguish between these two cases, as does the conduct of ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him. He fought the Khawārij on the explicit instruction of the Messenger of Allah, rejoiced in doing so, and was opposed in this by none of the Companions. As for the fighting at Siffīn, his aversion to it and his condemnation of it were manifest.

Concerning those who fought at the Battle of the Camel and others, he said: “They are our brothers who rebelled against us; the sword has purified them.” He offered funeral prayers for the slain of both sides.

As for the Khawārij, the two Sahīh collections report that ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib said: “I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say:

‘Near the end of time, a people will emerge, young in years and foolish in judgment, who utter some of the finest words spoken by mankind. Their faith will not go beyond their throats. They will pass out of the religion as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will be rewarded on the Day of Resurrection.’”

Sahīh Muslim also reports from Zayd ibn Wahb that he was in the army that

original_text:
كَانُوا مَعَ عَلِيٍّ الَّذِينَ سَارُوا إلَى الْخَوَارِجِ فَقَالَ عَلِيٌّ:

{يَخْرُجُ قَوْمٌ مِنْ أُمَّتِي يَقْرَءُونَ الْقُرْآنَ لَيْسَ قِرَاءَتُكُمْ إلَى قِرَاءَتِهِمْ بِشَيْءِ وَلَا صَلَاتُكُمْ إلَى صَلَاتِهِمْ بِشَيْءِ وَلَا صِيَامُكُمْ إلَى صِيَامِهِمْ بِشَيْءِ يَقْرَءُونَ الْقُرْآنَ يَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّهُ لَهُمْ وَهُوَ عَلَيْهِمْ لَا تُجَاوِزُ صَلَاتُهُمْ تَرَاقِيَهُمْ. يَمْرُقُونَ مِنْ الْإِسْلَامِ كَمَا يَمْرُقُ السَّهْمُ مِنْ الرَّمِيَّةِ. لَوْ يَعْلَمُ الْجَيْشُ الَّذِينَ يُصِيبُونَهُمْ مَا قُضِيَ لَهُمْ عَلَى لِسَانِ مُحَمَّدٍ نَبِيِّهِمْ لَنَكَلُوا عَنْ الْعَمَلِ وَآيَةُ ذَلِكَ أَنَّ فِيهِمْ رَجُلًا لَهُ عَضُدٌ لَيْسَ لَهُ ذِرَاعٌ عَلَى عَضُدِهِ مِثْلُ حَلَمَةِ الثَّدْيِ عَلَيْهِ شَعَرَاتٌ بِيضٌ}
 . قَالَ فَيَذْهَبُونَ إلَى مُعَاوِيَةَ وَأَهْلِ الشَّامِ وَيَتْرُكُونَ هَؤُلَاءِ يَخْلُفُونَكُمْ فِي ذَرَارِيِّكُمْ وَأَمْوَالِكُمْ. وَاَللَّهِ إنِّي لَأَرْجُو أَنْ يَكُونُوا هَؤُلَاءِ الْقَوْمَ فَإِنَّهُمْ قَدْ سَفَكُوا الدَّمَ الْحَرَامَ وَأَغَارُوا فِي سَرْحِ النَّاسِ فَسِيرُوا عَلَى اسْمِ اللَّهِ.
 قَالَ:
 فَلَمَّا الْتَقَيْنَا وَعَلَى الْخَوَارِجِ يَوْمئِذٍ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ وَهْبٍ رَئِيسًا.
 فَقَالَ لَهُمْ:
 أَلْقُوا الرِّمَاحَ وَسُلُّوا سُيُوفَكُمْ مِنْ حَقْوَتِهَا فَإِنِّي أُنَاشِدُكُمْ كَمَا نَاشَدُوكُمْ يَوْمَ حَرُورَاءَ. فَرَجَعُوا فَوَحَّشُوا بِرِمَاحِهِمْ وَسَلُّوا السُّيُوفَ وَسَحَرَهُمْ النَّاسُ بِرِمَاحِهِمْ.
 قَالَ:
 وَأَقْبَلَ بَعْضُهُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ وَمَا أُصِيبَ مِنْ النَّاسِ يَوْمئِذٍ إلَّا رَجُلَانِ.
 فَقَالَ عَلِيٌّ:

accompanied ‘Alī on the march against the Khawārij. ‘Alī said:

“O people, I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say:

‘A people will emerge from my nation who recite the Quran. Your recitation will be nothing compared with theirs, your prayer nothing compared with theirs, and your fasting nothing compared with theirs. They recite the Quran, thinking that it supports them, whereas it stands against them. Their prayer does not go beyond their collarbones. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. If the army that encounters them knew what had been decreed for them through the words of Muhammad, their Prophet, they would cease striving. Their distinguishing sign is that among them is a man with an upper arm but no forearm. On his upper arm is something like a nipple, bearing a few white hairs.’”

He said: “Are they, then, to march against Mu‘āwiyah and the people of Syria, leaving these men behind among your children and possessions? By Allah, I certainly hope that these are the people described, for they have shed blood forbidden to them and raided people’s grazing livestock. So march in the name of Allah.”

He said: “When we met in battle, the Khawārij were led that day by ‘Abd Allah ibn Wahb. He said to them: ‘Cast down your spears and draw your swords from your belts. I adjure you as they adjured you on the day of Harūrā’.’ They turned back, threw away their spears, and drew their swords, while our men thrust at them with their spears.”

He said: “They closed in on one another, and only two of our men were killed that day.”

‘Alī said: “Search among them for the man with the malformed arm.” They searched but did not find him. He rose, leaning on his sword, and came to some men pressed against one another.

He said: “Move them aside.” They found him underneath, next to the ground. ‘Alī proclaimed Allah’s greatness and then said: “Allah has spoken the truth, and His Messenger has delivered the message.”

Him, did you hear this hadith from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace?’

He replied: ‘Yes, by Allah, besides whom there is no god but Him.’ He made him swear three times, and each time he swore to him.”

The Muslim community is agreed on condemning the Khawārij and judging them misguided. Their disagreement concerns only whether they are disbelievers. There are two well-known positions on this in the schools of Mālik and Ahmad, and there is also disagreement within al-Shāfi‘ī’s school regarding their disbelief.

Thus, under the first approach, there are two opinions concerning them in Ahmad’s school and elsewhere. The first is that they are rebels. The second is that they are disbelievers, like apostates: it is permissible to initiate fighting against them, kill their captives, and pursue those who flee. Anyone among them who is apprehended is called upon to repent, like an apostate; if he repents, he is spared, otherwise he is killed.

Likewise, two positions are transmitted from Ahmad concerning those who withhold zakat and fight the ruler over it: do they become disbelievers despite acknowledging that it is obligatory?

All of this demonstrates that al-Siddīq’s fighting against those who withheld zakat and ‘Alī’s fighting against the Khawārij were not like the fighting at the Battles of the Camel and Siffīn. The statements of ‘Alī and others concerning the Khawārij imply that they are not disbelievers like those who apostatize from Islam itself. This is the position explicitly transmitted from the imams, such as Ahmad and others. Nevertheless, the rulings concerning them are not the same as those concerning the participants in the Battles of the Camel and Siffīn. Rather, they constitute a third category. This is the soundest of the three positions concerning them.

Among those whom the Companions fought—despite their acknowledgment of the two testimonies of faith, prayer, and other matters—were those who withheld zakat. As reported in the two Sahīh collections:

“Abu Hurayrah reported that ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb said to Abū Bakr: ‘O successor to the Messenger of Allah, how can you fight the people when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that I am the Messenger of Allah. Once they say this, their lives and property are protected from me, except as its rightful requirements demand”?’

“Abū Bakr replied: ‘Did he not tell you, “except as its rightful requirements demand”? Zakat is one of its rightful requirements. By Allah, if they withheld from me even a young female goat that they used to give to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, I would fight them for withholding it.’

“‘Umar said: ‘As soon as I saw that Allah had opened Abū Bakr’s heart to fighting, I knew that this was right.’”

The Companions and the imams after them agreed that those who withhold zakat are to be fought, even if they perform the five daily prayers and fast the month of Ramadan. These people had no plausible grounds for doubt, and were therefore apostates. They are to be fought for withholding it, even if they acknowledge its obligation, as Allah has commanded.

It is reported that they said: ‘Allah commanded His Prophet to collect zakat in His words, “Take charity from their wealth,” but this obligation lapsed with his death.’ Likewise, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded that those who would not desist from drinking wine be fought.

Those associated with their rule were none but the worst of creation: either a heretical hypocrite who did not inwardly believe in Islam; one of the worst adherents of religious innovation, such as the Rāfidah, Jahmiyyah, Ittihādiyyah, and their like; or one of the most wicked and openly sinful people.

In their own lands, despite having the means, they do not perform pilgrimage to the Ancient House. an ally, even if he is an unbeliever; whoever rejects their authority, they regard as an enemy, even if he is among the finest Muslims. They do not fight for Islam, nor do they impose jizyah and subjection. Indeed, many of the Muslims among them, including their highest-ranking emirs and ministers, aspire to no more than for a Muslim to enjoy the same standing among them as the polytheists among the Jews and Christians whom they revere. Thus, their foremost commander among those who came to Syria, while addressing the Muslim envoys and seeking their goodwill by declaring, “We are Muslims,” said: “These are two great signs that came from Allah: Muhammad and Genghis Khan.”

This, then, is the furthest their foremost commander goes in seeking the Muslims’ goodwill: equating the Messenger of Allah—the noblest of creation in His sight, the master of the children of Adam, and the Seal of the Messengers—with an unbelieving, polytheistic king, among the worst polytheists in unbelief, corruption, and aggression, of the same kind as Nebuchadnezzar and his like.

These Tatars held an exalted belief concerning Genghis Khan: they believed him to be the son of Allah, much as the Christians believe concerning the Messiah. They say that the sun impregnated his mother: she was in a tent, and the sun descended through an opening in the tent and entered her, causing her to conceive. Everyone who professes a religion knows that this is a lie. This is evidence that he was born of fornication, and that his mother committed fornication, concealed it, and made this claim to ward off its disgrace.

Despite this, they regard him as the greatest messenger in Allah’s sight, venerating what he instituted and prescribed for them according to his own conjecture and desire, to the point that

they say of the wealth they possess, “This is provision from Genghis Khan,” and thank him for their food and drink. They consider it lawful to kill anyone who opposes what this accursed unbeliever instituted for them—this enemy of Allah, His prophets, His Messenger, and His believing servants.

Thus, this man and others like him among their commanders, even after embracing Islam, aspired to no more than placing Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on the same level as this accursed man. It is well known that Musaylimah the Liar caused the Muslims less harm than this man did, yet he claimed to share Muhammad’s messengership. On that account, the Companions deemed it lawful to fight him and his apostate followers. What, then, of someone who, in his outward profession of Islam, places Muhammad on a par with Genghis Khan?

In reality, despite their outward profession of Islam, they exalt the cause of Genghis Khan above that of the Muslims who follow the law of the Quran. They do not fight those who follow what Genghis Khan instituted as they fight the Muslims; rather, they fight the Muslims still more fiercely. Those unbelievers offer him obedience and submission, bring him wealth, and acknowledge his authority as deputy. They disobey his commands only as someone who rebels against a ruler disobeys that ruler.

Yet they wage war against the Muslims and show them the utmost enmity. They demand that the Muslims obey them, surrender their wealth, and submit to what that unbelieving, polytheistic king laid down for them—a king resembling Pharaoh, Nimrod, and their like. Indeed, he wrought even greater corruption on earth than either of them.

Allah Most High said:

This unbeliever likewise exalted himself in the land, oppressing the adherents of all faiths—Muslims, Jews, Christians, and those polytheists who opposed him—by killing the men, taking the women captive, seizing wealth, and destroying crops and offspring. Allah does not love corruption. He turns people away from the ways of the prophets and messengers that they had followed until they embrace the pagan way and unbelieving law he devised.

Thus, they profess Islam while exalting the religion of those unbelievers above the religion of the Muslims. Their obedience and allegiance to them far exceed their obedience to Allah and His Messenger and their allegiance to the believers. Disputes among their leading men are adjudicated according to the judgment of pagan ignorance, not the judgment of Allah and His Messenger.

Likewise, their senior ministers and other leading figures place Islam on a par with Judaism and Christianity, holding that all these are paths to Allah, comparable to the four schools of law among the Muslims. Some prefer Judaism or Christianity, while others prefer Islam. This view is widespread and predominant among them, even among their jurists and worshippers, particularly the Jahmiyyah among the Pharaonic monists and others like them, for philosophy has come to dominate their thinking. Thus, they include in this category untold numbers of polytheists, People of the Book, and followers of religious innovations, and treat the people of knowledge and faith as just one category.

Indeed, they make the Qarmatians—godless esotericists, heretics, and hypocrites such as al-Tūsī and his like—the rulers over everyone associated with learning or religion among the Muslims, Jews, and Christians. Likewise, their foolish minister, given the title al-Rashīd, exercises authority over these groups and gives precedence to the worst of the Muslims, such as the Rāfidīs and the godless, over the best of the Muslims—the people of knowledge and faith. Thus, His words,

“For you is your religion, and for me is my religion,”

are like His words,

“To us are our deeds, and to you are yours.”

He followed this with its necessary implication and consequence, saying:

The affair of Ibn al-ʿAlqamī and others like him with the caliph, and their affair in Aleppo with its ruler, are widely known.

Likewise, those familiar with the wars between the Muslims and the Christians along the Syrian coast know that the Rāfidah side with the Christians against the Muslims, and that they helped them seize the lands when the Tatars came. The conquest of Acre and other coastal towns grieved the Rāfidah. When the Muslims defeat the Christians and polytheists, this causes the Rāfidah bitter distress; when the polytheists and Christians defeat the Muslims, it is an occasion of celebration and joy for them.

Adherents of heresy and godlessness also joined the Rāfidah, including the “Nusayriyyah,” the “Ismāʿīliyyah,” and others like them among the godless “Qarāmitah” and others in Khurāsān, Iraq, Syria, and elsewhere. The Rāfidah are Jahmīs and Qadarīs. Their lying, religious innovations, and fabrications against Allah and His Messenger exceed those of the Kharijites who departed from the religion, whom the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī, and the other Companions fought at the command of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Indeed, their apostasy from the laws of the religion is greater than that of those who withheld zakah, whom Abū Bakr al-Siddīq and the Companions fought.

Among the gravest grounds on which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, condemned the Kharijites was his statement about them:

“They kill the people of Islam and leave the idolaters alone.”

Abū Sa‘īd said: “I testify that I heard this hadith from Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and I testify that Alī ibn Abī Tālib fought them while I was with him. He ordered a search for that man, who was brought to him, and I saw that he matched the description given by Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

Among the gravest grounds on which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, condemned these Khārijites, who pass out of the religion, was that they kill the people of Islam and leave the idolaters alone. He also mentioned that they would emerge at a time of division among the people. Yet even these Khārijites did not assist the disbelievers in fighting the Muslims, whereas the Rāfidah assist the disbelievers in fighting the Muslims. They were not content merely to refrain from fighting the disbelievers alongside the Muslims; they went so far as to fight the Muslims alongside the disbelievers. Thus, their departure from the religion was far, far greater than that of those who passed out of it.

The Muslims have unanimously agreed that the Khārijites, the Rāfidah and others like them must be fought if they break away from the Muslim community, just as Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, fought them. What, then, if they also adopt provisions from the laws of the polytheists—kanā’isā—and Genghis Khan, king of the polytheists, that are among the gravest contradictions of the religion of Islam?

Anyone who defects to them, whether a military commander or otherwise, is subject to the same ruling as they are. The extent of their apostasy from the laws of Islam corresponds to the extent to which each has renounced those laws. And if the early generations

“A group of my ummah will continue to uphold the truth and prevail, unharmed by those who oppose them or abandon them, until the Hour comes.”

In one narration recorded by Muslim:

“The people of the West will continue…”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, spoke these words in his city, Medina. Thus, the west, from his perspective, was whatever lay west of it, and the east was whatever lay east of it. East and west are relative directions, for every land has its east and west. Another hadith describes the victorious group as follows:

This group is the one that is in and around Jerusalem today.

The Sunnah has firmly established that the punishment of an apostate is more severe than that of someone who has never been Muslim, in several respects.

One is that an apostate is put to death in all circumstances: no jizya tax is levied on him, nor is a covenant of protection concluded with him, unlike someone who has never been Muslim. Another is that an apostate is put to death even if incapable of fighting, whereas someone who has never been Muslim and is not a combatant is not put to death according to most scholars, including Abū Hanīfah, Mālik and Ahmad. Thus, the majority hold that an apostate is put to death, as is the position of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. Another is that an apostate may neither inherit nor marry, and meat from an animal he slaughters may not be eaten, unlike someone who has never been Muslim. There are other such rulings as well.

Yet after professing the two testimonies of faith, those Turks—even though they neglect many of the religion’s laws—are better than the apostates among the Persians, Arabs, and others. This makes it clear that those in their ranks who were Muslim to begin with are worse than the Turks who were formerly unbelievers. For someone who was originally Muslim and then abandons some of its laws in apostasy is in a worse position than someone who has not yet embraced those laws. Such were those who withheld zakat and others whom al-Siddīq fought.

Even if someone who apostatizes from some of these laws is versed in jurisprudence, a Sufi, a merchant, a scribe, or something else, such people are worse than the Turks who have not embraced those laws but have persisted in Islam. Thus, Muslims suffer harm to their religion from these people that they do not suffer from those Turks. Those Turks also submit more fully to Islam and its laws, and to obedience to Allah and His Messenger, than these people who have apostatized from part of the religion and practised hypocrisy in another part, even though they outwardly claim an affiliation with religious learning and devotion.

At their most extreme, such people are heretics: Nusayrīs, Ismāʿīlīs, or Rāfidīs. Even the best of them is a Jahmī Ittihādī or the like. For no one who outwardly professes Islam joins them voluntarily unless he is a hypocrite, a secret unbeliever, or a wicked evildoer. Whoever they compel to accompany them will be resurrected according to his intention. We, however, must fight the entire army, since those under compulsion cannot be distinguished from the others.

“An army of people will attack this House. While they are on an open plain, the earth will swallow them up.” He was asked, “O Messenger of Allah, among them will be people who were compelled to join them.” He replied, “They will be resurrected according to their intentions.”

This hadith has been widely transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through several chains. The compilers of the Sahīh collections recorded it on the authority of ‘Ā’ishah, Hafsah, and Umm Salamah.

In Sahīh Muslim, Umm Salamah reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Someone will seek refuge in the House, and a military force will be sent against him. When they reach an open plain, the earth will swallow them up.”

I asked, “O Messenger of Allah, what about someone who was unwilling to accompany them?” He replied, “He will be swallowed up along with them, but on the Day of Resurrection he will be resurrected according to his intention.”

In the two Sahīh collections, ‘Ā’ishah reported:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, moved restlessly in his sleep. We said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, you did something in your sleep that you had not done before.’ He replied, ‘What is astonishing is that some people from my community will head towards this House because of a man of Quraysh who has sought refuge in it. When they reach the open plain, the earth will swallow them up.’

“We said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, the road may bring all kinds of people together.’ He replied, ‘Yes. Among them will be those seeking support, the insane, and wayfarers. They will all perish together, but their ultimate fates will differ: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will resurrect them according to their intentions.’”

In a version recorded by al-Bukhārī, ‘Ā’ishah reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“An army will attack the Kaaba. When they reach an open plain, the earth will swallow them up, from the first of them to the last.”

She said: “I asked, ‘O Messenger, how will they be swallowed up, from the first of them to the last, when among them are people in their markets and others who do not belong to them?’ He replied, ‘They will be swallowed up, from the first of them to the last, and then resurrected according to their intentions.’”

translated_text:
In Sahīh Muslim, Hafsah reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A people lacking defensive strength, numbers, and equipment will seek refuge in this House—meaning the Kaaba. An army will be sent against them at that time, and when they reach an open plain, the earth will swallow them up.”

Yūsuf ibn Māhik said, “At that time, the people of Syria were marching towards Mecca.” ‘Abd Allāh ibn Safwān said, “By Allah, it is not this army.”

Allah Most High thus destroyed the army that intended to violate what He had made sacred—including both those compelled to join it and those who were not—despite His ability to distinguish between them, though He will resurrect them according to their intentions. How, then, can the believers engaged in jihad be required to distinguish between those acting under compulsion and others, when they have no knowledge of this? Indeed, even if someone claimed that he had gone out under compulsion, his mere claim would not avail him. As it is reported:

“When the Muslims captured al-‘Abbās ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib on the day of Badr, he said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ‘O Messenger of Allah, I was compelled.’ He replied, ‘Outwardly, you were against us; as for what was in your heart, that is for Allah to judge.’”

Indeed, even if there were righteous people among them, among the best of people, and fighting them were impossible without killing these righteous people, they too would be killed. For the imams agree that if the disbelievers used Muslims as shields, and harm to the Muslims were feared if the disbelievers were not fought, it would be permissible to shoot at them while aiming at the disbelievers. {إنَّهَا سَتَكُونُ فِتَنٌ أَلَا ثَمَّ تَكُونُ فِتَنٌ أَلَا ثَمَّ تَكُونُ فِتَنٌ: الْقَاعِدُ فِيهَا خَيْرٌ مِنْ الْمَاشِي وَالْمَاشِي فِيهَا خَيْرٌ مِنْ السَّاعِي. أَلَا فَإِذَا نَزَلَتْ - أَوْ وَقَعَتْ -
 فَمَنْ كَانَ لَهُ إبِلٌ فَلْيَلْحَقْ بِإِبِلِهِ وَمَنْ كَانَتْ لَهُ غَنَمٌ فَلْيَلْحَقْ بِغَنَمِهِ وَمَنْ كَانَتْ لَهُ أَرْضٌ فَلْيَلْحَقْ بِأَرْضِهِ قَالَ فَقَالَ رَجُلٌ:
 يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ أَرَأَيْت مَنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ إبِلٌ وَلَا غَنَمٌ وَلَا أَرْضٌ؟
 قَالَ:
 يَعْمِدُ إلَى سَيْفِهِ فَيَدُقُّ عَلَى حَدِّهِ بِحَجَرِ ثُمَّ لِيَنْجُ إنْ اسْتَطَاعَ النَّجَاةَ. اللَّهُمَّ هَلْ بَلَّغْت. اللَّهُمَّ هَلْ بَلَّغْت. اللَّهُمَّ هَلْ بَلَّغْت.
 فَقَالَ رَجُلٌ:
 يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ. أَرَأَيْت إنْ أُكْرِهْت حَتَّى يُنْطَلَقَ بِي إلَى إحْدَى الصَّفَّيْنِ أَوْ - إحْدَى الْفِئَتَيْنِ - فَيَضْرِبُنِي رَجُلٌ بِسَيْفِهِ أَوْ بِسَهْمِهِ فَيَقْتُلُنِي؟
 قَالَ:
 يَبُوءُ بِإِثْمِهِ وَإِثْمِك وَيَكُونُ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ النَّارِ}
 .
translated_text:
Allah and His Messenger have commanded—though he is in truth wrongfully killed—is a martyr and will be resurrected according to his intention. His killing entails no greater harm than the killing of believers engaged in jihad. If jihad is obligatory even though as many Muslims as Allah wills may be killed, then the killing of Muslims in their ranks out of the necessity of jihad is no graver than this. Indeed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded anyone compelled to fight in times of strife to break his sword. He is not permitted to fight, even if he is killed, as reported in Sahīh Muslim from Abū Bakrah, who said:

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There will surely be times of strife. Then, take heed, more times of strife will come; then, take heed, still more times of strife will come. The one who sits during them is better than the one who walks, and the one who walks is better than the one who runs. Take heed: when it comes—or occurs—let whoever has camels go to his camels, whoever has sheep go to his sheep, and whoever has land go to his land.”

He said: A man asked, “O Messenger of Allah, what about someone who has neither camels, nor sheep, nor land?”

He replied, “Let him take his sword and strike its edge with a stone, then escape if he can. O Allah, have I conveyed the message? O Allah, have I conveyed the message? O Allah, have I conveyed the message?”

A man asked, “O Messenger of Allah, what if I am compelled and taken to one of the two battle lines—or one of the two factions—and a man strikes me with his sword or his arrow and kills me?”

He replied, “He will bear his own sin and yours, and he will be among the people of the Fire.”

translated_text:
This hadith shows that he prohibited fighting in times of strife. Indeed, he commanded measures that make fighting impossible: withdrawing or rendering one’s weapons unusable. This applies both to those compelled to fight and to others.

He then explained that if someone compelled to fight is wrongfully killed, the killer will bear his own sin and that of the person killed. Likewise, in the account of Adam’s two sons, Allah Most High relates the words of the wronged brother:

“I want you to bear my sin and yours, and so become one of the people of the Fire. Such is the recompense of the wrongdoers.”

It is well established by the Sunnah and scholarly consensus that a person whose life is threatened by an assailant may defend himself. The scholars differed only over whether he is obliged to defend himself by fighting. There are two views, both reported from Ahmad. According to the first, he must defend himself, even if he has not joined the battle line. According to the second, he may refrain from defending himself. As for initiating combat in times of strife, this is undoubtedly impermissible.

The point is that someone compelled to fight in times of strife is not permitted to fight. Rather, he must render his weapons unusable and patiently endure, even until he is wrongfully killed. How much more, then, does this apply to someone compelled to fight against the Muslims alongside a faction that has departed from the laws of Islam, such as those who withhold zakah, apostates, and others like them? There is no doubt that if he is compelled to join their ranks, he must refrain from fighting, even if the Muslims kill him. This is just as if the disbelievers compelled him to join their battle line to fight against the Muslims, or as if one man compelled another to kill a Muslim whose life is inviolable. By the consensus of the Muslims, he is not permitted to kill that person, even if compelled under threat of death. For saving his own life by killing that person whose life is inviolable has no greater claim than the reverse.

فَلَيْسَ لَهُ أَنْ يَظْلِمَ غَيْرَهُ فَيَقْتُلُهُ لِئَلَّا يُقْتَلَ هُوَ؛ بَلْ إذَا فَعَلَ ذَلِكَ كَانَ الْقَوَدُ عَلَى الْمُكْرَهِ وَالْمُكْرَهِ جَمِيعًا عِنْدَ أَكْثَرِ الْعُلَمَاءِ كَأَحْمَدَ وَمَالِكٍ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ فِي أَحَدِ قَوْلَيْهِ وَفِي الْآخَرِ يَجِبُ الْقَوَدُ عَلَى الْمُكْرَهِ فَقَطْ كَقَوْلِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَمُحَمَّدٍ.

 كَمَا قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ الصَّحِيحِ:
 
{مَنْ قُتِلَ دُونَ مَالِهِ فَهُوَ شَهِيدٌ وَمَنْ قُتِلَ دُونَ دَمِهِ فَهُوَ شَهِيدٌ وَمَنْ قُتِلَ دُونَ حَرَمِهِ فَهُوَ شَهِيدٌ}
 فَكَيْفَ
translated_text:
Thus, he may not wrong another person by killing him to avoid being killed himself. Indeed, if he does so, both the coercer and the person coerced are liable to execution in retaliation according to most scholars, including Ahmad, Mālik, and al-Shāfi‘ī in one of his two opinions. According to his other opinion, only the coercer is liable to execution in retaliation, as also held by Abū Hanīfah and Muhammad.

Another view holds that liability falls upon the coerced person who directly committed the killing, as reported from Zufar. Abū Yūsuf requires compensation through blood money instead of execution in retaliation, which he does not impose.

Muslim narrated in his Sahīh, from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), the account of the people of the trench, which includes the following:

“The boy was instructed to bring about his own death so that the religion might prevail.”

For this reason, the four imams permitted a Muslim to plunge into the ranks of the disbelievers, even if he considers it most likely that they will kill him, provided this benefits the Muslims. We have discussed this issue at length elsewhere.

If a man may undertake an action that he believes will lead to his death for the benefit of jihad—even though killing oneself is graver than killing another—then it is all the more permissible to undertake an action leading to another’s death for a benefit to the religion that cannot otherwise be attained, and to avert the harm of an enemy who corrupts religious and worldly affairs and whose harm cannot otherwise be repelled.

And if the Sunnah and scholarly consensus agree that a Muslim assailant may be killed when his assault cannot otherwise be repelled, even if the property he seeks to take amounts to only a qīrāt—a small fraction of a dinar—as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said in the authentic hadith:

“Whoever is killed defending his property is a martyr; whoever is killed defending his life is a martyr; and whoever is killed defending his family is a martyr,”

then how much more

 إنَّ الْإِمَامَ يُرَاسِلُهُمْ فَإِنْ ذَكَرُوا شُبْهَةً بَيَّنَهَا وَإِنْ ذَكَرُوا مَظْلِمَةً أَزَالَهَا. فَأَيُّ شُبْهَةٍ لِهَؤُلَاءِ الْمُحَارِبِينَ لِلَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ السَّاعِينَ فِي الْأَرْضِ فَسَادًا الْخَارِجِينَ عَنْ شَرَائِعِ الدِّينِ. وَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّهُمْ لَا يَقُولُونَ إنَّهُمْ أَقْوَمُ بِدِينِ الْإِسْلَامِ عِلْمًا وَعَمَلًا مِنْ هَذِهِ الطَّائِفَةِ؛ بَلْ هُمْ مَعَ دَعْوَاهُمْ الْإِسْلَامَ يَعْلَمُونَ أَنَّ هَذِهِ الطَّائِفَةَ أَعْلَمُ بِالْإِسْلَامِ مِنْهُمْ وَأَتْبَعُ لَهُ مِنْهُمْ. وَكُلُّ مَنْ تَحْتَ أَدِيمِ السَّمَاءِ مِنْ مُسْلِمٍ وَكَافِرٍ يَعْلَمُ ذَلِكَ وَهُمْ مَعَ ذَلِكَ يُنْذِرُونَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ بِالْقِتَالِ فَامْتَنَعَ أَنْ يَكُونَ لَهُمْ شُبْهَةٌ بَيِّنَةٌ يَسْتَحِلُّونَ بِهَا قِتَالَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ كَيْفَ وَهَمَ قَدْ سَبُّوا غَالِبَ حَرِيمِ الرَّعِيَّةِ الَّذِينَ لَمْ يُقَاتِلُوهُمْ حَتَّى أَنَّ النَّاسَ قَدْ رَأَوْهُمْ يُعَظِّمُونَ الْبُقْعَةَ وَيَأْخُذُونَ مَا فِيهَا مِنْ الْأَمْوَالِ وَيُعَظِّمُونَ الرَّجُلَ
translated_text:
justified is it to fight these people who have forsaken the laws of Islam and wage war against Allah and His Messenger, whose aggression and rebellion are the least of their evils?

Fighting aggressive assailants is established by the Sunnah and scholarly consensus. These people are aggressors attacking the Muslims’ lives, property, families, and religion. Each of these provides grounds for fighting an assailant who attacks it, and whoever is killed defending it is a martyr. What, then, of someone who fights to defend them all? These people are among the worst of the unjust rebels who invoke a religious interpretation. Yet anyone who claims that they should be fought in the same manner as rebels acting on a religious interpretation has committed a grievous error and strayed far astray. For the minimum requirement in the latter case is that they have a defensible interpretation on whose basis they have rebelled.

For this reason, the scholars said that the ruler should correspond with them: if they raise a doubt, he should clarify it; and if they mention a grievance, he should redress it. What doubt can these people raise, when they wage war against Allah and His Messenger, spread corruption throughout the land, and forsake the laws of the religion?

Undoubtedly, they do not claim to uphold the religion of Islam more faithfully, in knowledge and practice, than this group. Rather, despite professing Islam, they know that this group is more knowledgeable about Islam and follows it more faithfully than they do. Everyone beneath the sky, Muslim and disbeliever alike, knows this. Nevertheless, they threaten the Muslims with war. They therefore cannot have any clear misconception on whose basis they deem fighting the Muslims lawful. How could they, when they have reviled the womenfolk of most of the subjects who never fought them? Indeed, people have seen them venerating a place while seizing the wealth it contains, and venerating a man

translated_text:
and seeking blessings through him, while stripping him of his clothes, reviling his womenfolk, and subjecting him to punishments inflicted only upon the most unjust and wicked of people. Someone acting on a religious interpretation punishes only those whom he considers disobedient to the religion. Yet these people venerate those they punish for their religious devotion and say that they are more obedient to Allah than themselves. What interpretation, then, remains for them? Even supposing that they were acting on an interpretation, it would not be defensible. Indeed, the interpretation of the Khawārij and those who withheld zakat was more plausible than theirs. The Khawārij claimed to follow the Quran and maintained that any Sunnah that contradicted it could not be followed.

As for those who withheld zakat, it is reported that they said: “Allah said to His Prophet:

‘Take charity from their wealth.’

This addresses His Prophet alone, so we are not obliged to pay it to anyone else.” Thus, they would neither pay it to Abū Bakr nor hand it over to him. The Khawārij possess knowledge and engage in worship, and scholars have debated them, just as they have debated the Rāfidah and the Jahmiyyah. As for these people, there is no debating their grounds for fighting the Muslims. Even if they were acting on an interpretation, theirs would not be one that any rational person would advance.

One of them addressed me, saying: “Our king is a king, son of a king, son of a king, going back through seven forefathers, whereas your king is the son of a mawlā (a freedman or client).”

I told him: “That king’s forefathers were all disbelievers, and there is no cause for pride in a disbeliever. Indeed, a Muslim slave is better than a disbelieving king. Allah Most High says:

‘A believing slave is better than a polytheist, even though he may please you.’”

Such are their arguments. It is well known that a Muslim is obliged

to obey a Muslim, even if he is a slave, and not to obey a disbeliever. It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Listen and obey, even if an Abyssinian slave whose head is like a raisin is appointed over you, so long as he upholds among you the Book of Allah and the religion of Islam.”

A person’s superiority lies only in his faith and piety, not in his forefathers—even if they belonged to Banū Hāshim, the household of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Allah created Paradise for whoever obeys Him, even if he is an Abyssinian slave, and created Hell for whoever disobeys Him, even if he is a nobleman of Quraysh. Allah Most High says:

“O mankind, We created you from a male and a female and made you into peoples and tribes so that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”

It is reported in the Sunan collections that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, nor a black person over a white person, nor a white person over a black person, except through piety. People are descended from Adam, and Adam was made from dust.”

It is reported in the two Sahīh collections that he said concerning a tribe closely related to him:

“The family of Abū so-and-so are not my allies. My allies are only Allah and the righteous believers.”

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, thus explained that his allegiance was not based on kinship and lineage, but on faith and piety. If this applies to the relatives of the Messenger, then what of the relatives of Genghis Khan, the disbeliever and polytheist? The Muslims unanimously agree that whoever has greater faith and piety is superior to someone whose faith and piety are lesser, even if the former is a black Abyssinian and the latter a descendant of ‘Alī or al-‘Abbās.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him and be pleased with him—was asked about soldiers who refuse to fight the Tatars, saying, “Some among them are compelled to go out with them,” and whether, if one of them flees, he should be pursued.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. Fighting the Tatars who have come to the lands of Syria is obligatory according to the Quran and the Sunnah. Allah says in the Quran:

“Fight them until there is no more persecution and religion is entirely for Allah.”

Religion means obedience. Thus, if some obedience is devoted to Allah and some to others besides Him, fighting becomes obligatory until all obedience is devoted to Allah. For this reason, Allah Most High says:

“O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains of usury, if you are believers.”

“If you do not, then be informed of war from Allah and His Messenger.”

This verse was revealed concerning the people of al-Tā’if when they embraced Islam and committed themselves to prayer and fasting but refused to give up usury. Allah therefore made clear that they were at war with Him and His Messenger if they did not desist from usury. Usury was the last thing Allah prohibited, and it is money taken with its owner’s consent. If such people are at war with Allah and His Messenger and must be fought, then what of those who abandon many—or most—of the prescribed duties and laws of Islam, as the Tatars do?

translated_text:
The Muslim scholars have agreed that a group resisting compliance must be fought if it refuses to observe some of Islam’s manifest obligations established by mass transmission. If they profess the two testimonies of faith but refuse to perform prayer and pay zakah, fast the month of Ramadan, make pilgrimage to the Ancient House, judge among themselves according to the Quran and Sunnah, prohibit sexual immorality, wine, or marriage to women within the prohibited degrees of kinship, or [prohibit] treating lives and property as lawful to violate without right, usury, or gambling, or wage jihad against the unbelievers, or impose jizyah on the People of the Book, or observe other such laws of Islam, then they are to be fought over these matters until religion is entirely for Allah.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that when ʿUmar debated with Abū Bakr concerning those who withheld zakah, Abū Bakr said to him:

“How could I not fight those who abandon the dues that Allah and His Messenger have made obligatory, such as zakah, even if they have embraced Islam?” He also told him: “Zakah is among its rightful dues. By Allah, if they withheld from me a young she-goat that they used to give to the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—I would fight them for withholding it.”

ʿUmar said:

“As soon as I saw that Allah had opened Abū Bakr’s heart to fighting, I knew that it was right.”

It is also recorded in the Sahīh through several routes of transmission that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—mentioned the Kharijites and said of them:

“Any one of you would consider his prayer insignificant beside theirs, his fasting beside theirs, and his recitation beside theirs. They recite the Quran, but it does not go beyond their throats. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them,

The early generations and the leading scholars agreed that these people must be fought. The first to fight them was the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib—may Allah be pleased with him. The Muslims continued fighting them during the early Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates alongside the rulers, even when those rulers were unjust. Al-Hajjāj and his deputies were among those who fought them. All the leading Muslim scholars therefore enjoin fighting them.

The Tatars and those like them depart further from the law of Islam than those who withheld zakah and the Kharijites among the people of Tā’if who refused to abandon usury. Whoever doubts that they must be fought is among the most ignorant of the religion of Islam. Whenever fighting them is obligatory, they are to be fought even if some among them are acting under compulsion, by agreement of the Muslims.

When al-ʿAbbās was captured on the day of Badr, he said:

“O Messenger of Allah, I went out under compulsion.”

The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—replied:

“Outwardly, you were against us; as for what was within you, that rests with Allah.”

If these Muslims are killed, they are martyrs, and obligatory jihad is not to be abandoned because some may be killed as martyrs. When Muslims fight unbelievers, any Muslim killed is a martyr. Likewise, anyone killed for the welfare of Islam, despite not inwardly deserving to be killed, is a martyr.

It is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“An army will march against this House, and while they are on an open plain, the earth will swallow them up.”

He was asked, “O Messenger of Allah, there will be people among them acting under compulsion.”

He replied, “They will be resurrected according to their intentions.”

If the punishment Allah sends upon an army attacking the Muslims falls upon both those acting under compulsion and those acting willingly, then what of the punishment Allah inflicts upon them Himself or at the hands of the believers? As the Most High says:

“Say, ‘Are you awaiting anything for us other than one of the two good outcomes? We, for our part, await Allah’s afflicting you with punishment from Himself or at our hands.’”

We do not know who is acting under compulsion, nor can we distinguish them from the others. If we kill them at Allah’s command, we are rewarded and excused, while they are judged according to their intentions. Whoever is compelled and unable to refrain will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection according to his intention. If he is killed so that the religion may be upheld, that is no graver than the killing of someone in the Muslim army. As for when one of them flees, some people regard fighting them as equivalent to fighting rebels acting on an interpretation of religion.

And if these rebels have a group capable of resistance, may their retreating fighters be pursued, their prisoners killed, and their wounded finished off? Scholars hold two well-known views on this.

One view is that this is not to be done, because the herald of ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib proclaimed on the day of the Battle of the Camel: “No retreating fighter is to be pursued, no wounded man finished off, and no prisoner killed.”

The other view is that this may indeed be done, because at the Battle of the Camel they had no group capable of resistance. The purpose of fighting was to repel them; once they had been repelled, there was no need for such measures, just as when repelling an aggressor.

It has also been reported that at the battles of the Camel and Siffīn, their practice was otherwise. Those who place them in the same category as rebels acting on an interpretation of religion apply these two views to them. The correct position, however, is that these people are not rebels acting on an interpretation of religion, for they have no defensible interpretation whatsoever. Rather, they belong to the same category as the renegade Khawārij, those who withheld zakat, the people of Tā’if, the Khurramiyya, and others who were fought because of the prescriptions of Islam they had abandoned.

This is a point that has confused many jurists. Those who have written on “Fighting Rebels” have classified the fighting against those who withheld zakat, the fighting against the Khawārij, ʿAlī’s fighting against the people of Basra, and his fighting against Muʿāwiya and his followers as fighting rebels, regarding all of it as commanded. They developed the detailed rulings accordingly, following this view of fighting among people. But they were mistaken. Rather, the correct position is that held by the leading scholars of hadith and the Sunnah and the people of the Prophet’s city, such as al-Awzāʿī, al-Thawrī, Mālik, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal

 وَنَحْوِهِ فَلَمْ يَتَّفِقْ عَلَيْهِ الصَّحَابَةُ؛ بَلْ صَدَّ عَنْهُ أَكَابِرُ الصَّحَابَةِ؛ مِثْلَ سَعْدِ بْنِ أَبِي وَقَّاصٍ وَمُحَمَّدِ بْنِ مسلمة وَأُسَامَةَ بْنِ زَيْدٍ وَعَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عُمَرَ وَغَيْرِهِمْ. وَلَمْ يَكُنْ بَعْدَ عَلِيِّ بْنِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ فِي الْعَسْكَرَيْنِ مِثْلَ سَعْدِ بْنِ أَبِي وَقَّاصٍ. وَالْأَحَادِيثُ الصَّحِيحَةُ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ تَقْتَضِي أَنَّهُ كَانَ يَجِبُ الْإِصْلَاحُ بَيْنَ تينك الطَّائِفَتَيْنِ؛
 لَا الِاقْتِتَالُ بَيْنَهُمَا كَمَا ثَبَتَ عَنْهُ فِي صَحِيحِ الْبُخَارِيِّ أَنَّهُ خَطَبَ النَّاسَ وَالْجَيْشَ مَعَهُ فَقَالَ:
 
{إنَّ ابْنِي هَذَا سَيِّدٌ وَسَيُصْلِحُ اللَّهُ بِهِ بَيْنَ طَائِفَتَيْنِ عَظِيمَتَيْنِ مِنْ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ}
 فَأَصْلَحَ اللَّهُ بِالْحَسَنِ بَيْنَ أَهْلِ الْعِرَاقِ وَأَهْلِ الشَّامِ: فَجَعَلَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ الْإِصْلَاحَ بِهِ مِنْ فَضَائِلِ الْحَسَنِ مَعَ أَنَّ الْحَسَنَ نَزَلَ عَنْ الْأَمْرِ وَسَلَّمَ الْأَمْرَ إلَى مُعَاوِيَةَ. فَلَوْ كَانَ الْقِتَالُ هُوَ الْمَأْمُورُ بِهِ دُونَ تَرْكِ الْخِلَافَةِ وَمُصَالَحَةِ مُعَاوِيَةَ لَمْ يَمْدَحْهُ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ عَلَى تَرْكِ مَا أَمَرَ بِهِ وَفَعَلَ مَا لَمْ يُؤْمَرْ بِهِ وَلَا مَدَحَهُ عَلَى تَرْكِ الْأَوْلَى وَفَعَلَ الْأَدْنَى. فَعُلِمَ أَنَّ الَّذِي فَعَلَهُ الْحَسَنُ هُوَ الَّذِي كَانَ يُحِبُّهُ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ؛ لَا الْقِتَالَ.
 وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ فِي الصَّحِيحِ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ كَانَ يَضَعُهُ وَأُسَامَةَ عَلَى فَخِذَيْهِ وَيَقُولُ:
 {اللَّهُمَّ إنِّي أُحِبُّهُمَا فَأَحِبَّهُمَا وَأَحِبَّ
translated_text:
and others: a distinction must be drawn between these two cases. ʿAlī’s fighting against the Khawārij is established by explicit texts from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, by the agreement of the Muslims. As for the fighting “on the day of Siffīn” and similar occasions, the Companions did not agree on it. Rather, eminent Companions discouraged it, including Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās, Muhammad ibn Maslama, Usāma ibn Zayd, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, and others. Apart from ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib, no one in either army was the equal of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās.

The authentic hadiths from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, indicate that reconciliation between those two groups was obligatory, not fighting between them. It is established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī that he addressed the people, with the army beside him, saying:

“This son of mine is a leader, and through him Allah will reconcile two great groups of believers.”

Thus Allah brought about reconciliation through al-Hasan between the people of Iraq and the people of Syria. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, therefore counted this reconciliation among al-Hasan’s virtues, even though al-Hasan relinquished authority and handed it over to Muʿāwiya. Had fighting been what was commanded, rather than relinquishing the caliphate and making peace with Muʿāwiya, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would not have praised him for abandoning what he had commanded and doing what he had not been commanded to do. Nor would he have praised him for abandoning the better course and taking the lesser one. It is therefore clear that what al-Hasan did was what Allah and His Messenger loved—not fighting.

It is also established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would seat him and Usāma on his thighs and say:

“O Allah, I love them both, so love them both, and love

those who love them.”

The effect of the Messenger of Allah’s love for them both, peace and blessings be upon him, became evident in their aversion to fighting during the civil strife. Usāma refused to fight alongside either group. Likewise, al-Hasan constantly advised ʿAlī not to fight, and when authority passed to him, he did what he had advised his father to do. May Allah be pleased with them all.

It is also authentically established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“A faction will break away at a time of division among the Muslims; of the two groups, the one closer to the truth will kill them.”

This breakaway faction was the Khawārij, whom ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib fought. This is corroborated by the other hadiths commanding that the Khawārij be fought. They make clear that killing them is something Allah and His Messenger love, and that those who fought them alongside ʿAlī were closer to the truth than Muʿāwiya and his companions. Yet despite their being closer to the truth, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, did not command either group to fight as he commanded fighting the Khawārij. Rather, he praised reconciliation between them.

Many authentic hadiths establish the Prophet’s aversion to fighting during times of strife and his warnings against such strife, though this is not the place to recount them all. Among them is his saying:

“There will be times of strife in which the one sitting will be better than the one standing, the one standing better than the one walking, and the one walking better than the one running.”

He also said:

“Soon the best wealth a Muslim possesses will be sheep that he takes to the mountaintops and places where rain falls, fleeing strife to preserve his religion.”

translated_text:
Civil strife includes wars between Muslim rulers and Muslim groups when both sides remain committed to the laws of Islam, as was the case with those who fought at the Battles of the Camel and Siffīn. They fought one another only because of misconceptions and circumstances that arose.

As for fighting the Khawārij, those who withhold zakat, and the people of Tā’if who did not regard usury as forbidden, these are fought until they submit to the laws established by the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. If they have a group that maintains resistance, there is no doubt that it is permissible to kill their captives, pursue those fleeing, and finish off their wounded. For if they remain in their lands persisting in their ways, the Muslims must go to their lands to fight them until all religion is for Allah alone.

These Tatars are not fought on account of the religion of Islam; rather, they fight people until they submit to their rule. Whoever submits to their rule is left alone, even if he is a polytheist, a Christian, or a Jew. Whoever does not submit is their enemy, even if he is among the prophets and the righteous. Allah has commanded the Muslims to fight His disbelieving enemies and to maintain allegiance to His believing servants.

Thus, all Muslims serving in the armies of Syria, Egypt, Yemen, and the Maghrib must cooperate in fighting the disbelievers. They may not fight one another merely for leadership and personal desires. The very least required of these Tatars is that they fight the disbelievers nearest them, refrain from fighting the Muslims nearest them, and cooperate with those Muslims in

fighting the disbelievers. Moreover, no one fights alongside them without being coerced unless he is an evildoer, an adherent of religious innovation, or a heretic—such as the heretical Qarmatian esotericists, the Rāfidah who engage in reviling, and the attribute-denying Jahmiyyah among the negationists who profess divine indwelling. Among those with them whom they follow—people claiming learning and religious devotion—are some who are worse than they are. For the Tatars are ignorant people who blindly follow those of whom they think well. In their error and waywardness, they follow them in misguidance whereby they fabricate lies about Allah and His Messenger, alter Allah’s religion, do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and do not adhere to the religion of truth. Were I to describe what I know of their affairs, the discussion would be lengthy.

In short, their doctrine and the religion of Islam are incompatible. Were they to openly uphold the upright religion of Islam with which Allah sent His Messenger, they would be rightly guided and obedient, like the group granted victory. For it is authentically reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“A group of my community will continue to prevail upon the truth, unharmed by those who oppose them or abandon them, until the Hour comes.”

It is also authentically reported from him in the Sahīh that he said:

“The people of the west will continue to prevail.”

The west begins with the region lying in line with al-Bīrah and similar places. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, spoke these words while in the Prophet’s city, Medina. Whatever lies west of it is therefore west, such as Syria and Egypt, and whatever lies east of it is east, such as al-Jazīrah and Iraq. The early generations used to call the people of Syria “the people of the west” and the people of Iraq “the people of the east.” This summary I have given is supported by

عَنْ طَائِفَةٍ مِنْ رَعِيَّةِ الْبِلَادِ كَانُوا يَرَوْنَ مَذْهَبَ الْنُصَيْرِيَّة ثُمَّ أَجْمَعُوا عَلَى رَجُلٍ وَاخْتَلَفَتْ أَقْوَالُهُمْ فِيهِ. فَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَزْعُمُ أَنَّهُ إلَهٌ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَزْعُمُ أَنَّهُ نَبِيٌّ مُرْسَلٌ وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ ادَّعَى أَنَّهُ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ الْحَسَنِ - يَعْنُونَ الْمَهْدِيَّ - وَأَمَرُوا مَنْ وَجَدَهُ بِالسُّجُودِ لَهُ وَأَعْلَنُوا بِالْكُفْرِ بِذَلِكَ وَسَبِّ الصَّحَابَةِ وَأَظْهَرُوا الْخُرُوجَ عَنْ الطَّاعَةِ وَعَزَمُوا عَلَى الْمُحَارَبَةِ. فَهَلْ يَجِبُ قِتَالُهُمْ وَقَتْلُ مُقَاتَلَتِهِمْ؟ وَهَلْ تُبَاحُ ذَرَارِيُّهُمْ وَأَمْوَالُهُمْ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، هَؤُلَاءِ يَجِبُ قِتَالُهُمْ مَا دَامُوا مُمْتَنِعِينَ حَتَّى يَلْتَزِمُوا شَرَائِعَ الْإِسْلَامِ؛ فَإِنَّ الْنُصَيْرِيَّة مِنْ أَعْظَمِ النَّاسِ كُفْرًا بِدُونِ اتِّبَاعِهِمْ لِمِثْلِ هَذَا الدَّجَّالِ فَكَيْفَ إذَا اتَّبَعُوا مِثْلَ هَذَا الدَّجَّالِ.
 وَهُمْ مُرْتَدُّونَ مِنْ أَسْوَأِ النَّاسِ رِدَّةً:
 تُقْتَلُ مُقَاتِلَتُهُمْ وَتَغْنَمُ أَمْوَالُهُمْ. وَسَبْيُ الذَّرِّيَّةِ فِيهِ نِزَاعٌ؛ لَكِنَّ أَكْثَرَ الْعُلَمَاءِ عَلَى أَنَّهُ تُسْبَى الصِّغَارُ مِنْ أَوْلَادِ الْمُرْتَدِّينَ وَهَذَا هُوَ الَّذِي دَلَّتْ عَلَيْهِ سِيرَةُ الصِّدِّيقِ فِي قِتَالِ الْمُرْتَدِّينَ.
 وَكَذَلِكَ قَدْ تَنَازَعَ الْعُلَمَاءُ فِي اسْتِرْقَاقِ الْمُرْتَدِّةِ:
 فَطَائِفَةٌ تَقُولُ: إنَّهَا تُسْتَرَقُّ
translated_text:
reports from the early generations and evidence from Islamic law discussed elsewhere. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A group of the country’s inhabitants formerly held the doctrines of the Nusayriyyah. They then rallied around a man, although their claims about him differed. Some claim that he is a god; others claim that he is a prophet sent by Allah; and others claim that he is Muhammad ibn al-Hasan—meaning the Mahdī. They ordered anyone who encountered him to prostrate before him. Through this and their reviling of the Companions, they openly proclaimed unbelief. They openly renounced obedience to the authorities and resolved to wage war. Is it obligatory to fight them and kill their combatants? May their offspring be taken captive and their property seized, or not?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. These people must be fought as long as they continue to resist, until they commit themselves to the laws of Islam. The Nusayriyyah are among the most extreme unbelievers even without following such an impostor; how much more so when they follow such an impostor!

They are apostates whose apostasy is among the worst. Their combatants are to be killed, and their property taken as spoils. There is disagreement over taking their offspring captive. Most scholars, however, hold that the young children of apostates may be taken captive. This is what is indicated by the conduct of Abū Bakr al-Siddīq in fighting the apostates.

The scholars have likewise disagreed over the enslavement of an apostate woman. One group says that she may be enslaved

وَلَا حِجَابَ عَلَيْهِ إلَّا … مُحَمَّدٌ الصَّادِقُ الْأَمِينُ
وَلَا طَرِيقَ إلَيْهِ إلَّا … سَلْمَانُ ذُو الْقُوَّةِ الْمَتِينُ
وَأَمَّا إذَا لَمْ يُظْهِرُوا الرَّفْضَ وَأَنَّ هَذَا الْكَذَّابَ هُوَ الْمَهْدِيُّ الْمُنْتَظَرُ وَامْتَنَعُوا؛ فَإِنَّهُمْ يُقَاتَلُونَ أَيْضًا؛ لَكِنْ يُقَاتَلُونَ كَمَا يُقَاتَلُ الْخَوَارِجُ الْمَارِقُونَ الَّذِينَ قَاتَلَهُمْ عَلِيُّ بْنُ أَبِي طَالِبٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ بِأَمْرِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ

صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَكَمَا يُقَاتَلُ الْمُرْتَدُّونَ الَّذِينَ قَاتَلَهُمْ أَبُو بَكْرٍ الصِّدِّيقُ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ. فَهَؤُلَاءِ يُقَاتَلُونَ مَا دَامُوا مُمْتَنِعِينَ وَلَا تُسْبَى ذَرَارِيُّهُمْ وَلَا تُغْنَمُ أَمْوَالُهُمْ الَّتِي لَمْ يَسْتَعِينُوا بِهَا عَلَى الْقِتَالِ. وَأَمَّا مَا اسْتَعَانُوا بِهِ عَلَى قِتَالِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ مِنْ خَيْلٍ وَسِلَاحٍ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ فَفِي أَخْذِهِ نِزَاعٌ بَيْنَ الْعُلَمَاءِ. وَقَدْ رُوِيَ عَنْ عَلِيِّ بْنِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ أَنَّهُ نَهَبَ عَسْكَرُهُ مَا فِي عَسْكَرِ الْخَوَارِجِ. فَإِنْ رَأَى وَلِيُّ الْأَمْرِ أَنْ يَسْتَبِيحَ مَا فِي عَسْكَرِهِمْ مِنْ الْمَالِ كَانَ هَذَا سَائِغًا. هَذَا مَا دَامُوا مُمْتَنِعِينَ. فَإِنْ قَدَرَ عَلَيْهِمْ؛ فَإِنَّهُ يَجِبُ أَنْ يُفَرِّقَ شَمْلَهُمْ وَتُحْسَمَ مَادَّةُ شَرِّهِمْ وَإِلْزَامُهُمْ شَرَائِعَ الْإِسْلَامِ وَقَتْلُ مَنْ أَصَرَّ عَلَى الرِّدَّةِ مِنْهُمْ. وَأَمَّا قَتْلُ مَنْ أَظْهَرَ الْإِسْلَامَ وَأَبْطَنَ كُفْرًا مِنْهُ وَهُوَ الْمُنَافِقُ الَّذِي تُسَمِّيهِ الْفُقَهَاءُ 
" الزِّنْدِيقُ "
: فَأَكْثَرُ الْفُقَهَاءِ عَلَى أَنَّهُ يُقْتَلُ وَإِنْ تَابَ كَمَا هُوَ مَذْهَبُ مَالِكٍ وَأَحْمَد فِي أَظْهَرْ الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ عَنْهُ وَأَحَدِ الْقَوْلَيْنِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ. وَمَنْ كَانَ دَاعِيًا مِنْهُمْ إلَى الضَّلَالِ لَا يَنْكَفُّ شَرُّهُ إلَّا بِقَتْلِهِ قُتِلَ أَيْضًا؛ وَإِنْ أَظْهَرَ التَّوْبَةَ وَإِنْ لَمْ يُحْكَمْ بِكُفْرِهِ كَأَئِمَّةِ الرَّفْضِ الَّذِينَ يُضِلُّونَ النَّاسَ كَمَا قَتَلَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ غَيْلَانَ الْقَدَرِيَّ وَالْجَعْدَ بْنَ دِرْهَمٍ وَأَمْثَالَهُمَا مِنْ الدُّعَاةِ. فَهَذَا الدَّجَّالُ يُقْتَلُ مُطْلَقًا. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and as Abū Bakr al-Siddīq—may Allah be pleased with him—fought the apostates. These people are to be fought so long as they resist submission. Their children are not to be taken captive, nor is their property that they have not used to support the fighting to be taken as spoils. As for the horses, weapons, and other things they have used to fight the Muslims, scholars disagree over whether these may be taken. It is reported that ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib’s army plundered what was in the Khawārij’s camp. If the ruler sees fit to authorize taking the property in their camp, that is permissible.

This applies so long as they resist submission. If the ruler gains control over them, he must disperse them, eliminate the source of their evil, compel them to observe the laws of Islam, and execute those among them who persist in apostasy.

As for executing someone among them who outwardly professes Islam but inwardly conceals unbelief—the hypocrite whom jurists call a “zindīq”—most jurists hold that he is to be executed even if he repents. This is the position of Mālik and of Ahmad according to the more established of the two reports from him, and one of the two positions within the schools of Abū Hanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī.

Anyone among them who calls others to misguidance and whose evil cannot be stopped except by executing him is also to be executed, even if he professes repentance and even if he has not been judged an unbeliever. This includes leaders of the Rāfida who lead people astray, just as the Muslims executed Ghaylān al-Qadarī, al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham, and others like them who propagated such teachings. Thus, this impostor is to be executed in any case. And Allah knows best.

 وَإِذَا دُعِيَ أَحَدُهُمْ إلَى الشَّرْعِ قَالَ:
 إنَّا الشَّرْعُ. إلَى غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ. فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ قِتَالُهُمْ وَالْحَالَةُ هَذِهِ؟ وَكَيْفَ الطَّرِيقُ إلَى دُخُولِهِمْ فِي الْإِسْلَامِ مَعَ مَا ذُكِرَ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
نَعَمْ، يَجُوزُ؛ بَلْ يَجِبُ بِإِجْمَاعِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ قِتَالُ هَؤُلَاءِ وَأَمْثَالِهِمْ مِنْ كُلِّ طَائِفَةٍ مُمْتَنِعَةٍ عَنْ شَرِيعَةٍ مِنْ شَرَائِعِ الْإِسْلَامِ الظَّاهِرَةِ
translated_text:
The shaykh was also asked:

There are people possessing armed strength who live in a certain territory but do not perform the prescribed prayers. They have no mosque, no call to prayer, and no call announcing its commencement. If any of them prays, he does so in a manner other than that prescribed. They do not pay zakat, despite their considerable wealth in livestock and crops. They fight among themselves, killing one another, plundering one another’s property, and killing children. They may show no restraint in shedding blood and seizing property, whether during Ramadan, the sacred months, or at any other time. When they take one another captive, they sell their captives to the Franks. They also openly sell their male and female slaves to the Franks, driving them along like livestock. They marry women during their waiting periods, deny women their inheritance, and do not submit to the Muslim ruler.

When one of them is summoned to abide by Islamic law, he says, “We ourselves are the law!” And they do other such things. Is it permissible to fight them under these circumstances? How can they be brought into Islam, given what has been mentioned?

He replied:

Yes, it is permissible. Indeed, by the consensus of the Muslims, it is obligatory to fight these people and others like them: any group that refuses to comply with any of the manifest ordinances of Islam

This accords with what Abū Bakr al-Siddīq and the other Companions—may Allah be pleased with them—said concerning those who withheld zakat, and with how ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib and the Prophet’s Companions fought the Khawārij, concerning whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“One of you would consider his prayer insignificant compared with theirs, his fasting compared with theirs, and his recitation compared with theirs. They recite the Quran, but it does not pass beyond their throats. They pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its quarry. Wherever you encounter them, kill them, for whoever kills them will have a reward with Allah on the Day of Resurrection.”

This is based on His words, Most High:

“Fight them until there is no more fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah.”

And His words, Most High:

“O you who believe, fear Allah and give up whatever remains of usury, if you are believers.”

“If you do not, then be warned of war from Allah and His Messenger.”

Usury was the last thing Allah and His Messenger prohibited; how much more, then, does this apply to things whose prohibition is graver!

Before fighting, they are to be called upon to commit themselves to the ordinances of Islam. If they do so, firm guarantees must be secured from them; their mere words are not enough. This is what Abū Bakr did with those whom he fought, after he had humbled them. He said:

“Choose: either a war that drives you from your homes or a peace that brings you humiliation.”

He also said:

“I am the successor of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

He replied:

“You must testify that our slain are in Paradise and yours are in the Fire. We shall take your mounts from you—meaning horses—and your weapons, until the successor of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the believers decide otherwise.”

This, then, is what must be done with such people when they profess obedience: someone is to be sent to teach them the ordinances of Islam, lead them in the prayers, and establish among them those Islamic ordinances that will benefit them. Alternatively, some of those who are obedient are to be enlisted in the Muslim army and incorporated into the Muslim community; or the weapons with which they fight are to be taken from them, and they are to be prohibited from riding horses; or they are to lay down their weapons until their conduct is set right; or those among them who refuse to commit themselves to the Sharia are to be killed. If they do not respond to Allah and His Messenger, they must be fought until they commit themselves to the manifest ordinances of Islam established by mass transmission. The scholars of the Muslims agree upon this. And Allah knows best.

Among them are also those in charge of lodges and hospices, who devote themselves exclusively to worship and receiving visitors: jurists, scholars, and other wayfarers. Others are the orphaned children of soldiers and others martyred in the path of Allah Most High, who have not left them enough to meet their needs. There are also those who request permission to bring uncultivated land into use and do so, or reclaim high-lying ahrās so that they may retain them after their reclamation. They have brought them into cultivation over many years, and their tenure has become established according to the prevailing customs in such matters.

Do these circumstances justify their receiving what they have been granted—what the Muslim kings and their deputies allocated to them in the public interest, and which has remained in their possession until now—or not? What is the ruling concerning someone who declares them ineligible despite their possessing these qualifications, and seeks favour with the sultan by striving to cut off their stipends, thereby causing the closure of the lodges and most of the lodges and hospices that benefit wayfarers and others devoted exclusively to worship, and in which the public observances of Islam are maintained? Is he thereby sinful and disobedient, or not?
